titre: Integrating Survival Modelling and Machine Learning to Unravel the Drivers of Geographic Disparities in COVID-19 Booster Vaccination Timing
resume: Background: Machine learning-based survival models provided modest predictive improvements over CoxPH in this study. However, combining RSF with SHAP offered complementary information about predictor contributions and their geographic distribution. These findings support using traditional survival analysis alongside explainable machine learning to examine sociodemographic and geographic disparities in booster vaccination timing. Methods: Individual-level vaccination records from Nueces County, Texas (n = 141,537) were linked to sociodemographic and geographic characteristics. A previously developed travel time discrepancy index was included alongside demographic variables, social vulnerability, and urban–rural residence. Kaplan–Meier analysis and Cox proportional hazards regression were used to examine booster vaccination timing. CoxPH, DeepSurv, DeepHit, and Random Survival Forests (RSF) were compared using the concordance index and Integrated Brier Score. SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) were applied to RSF to examine feature contributions and their geographic distribution. Results: RSF achieved the highest predictive performance (C-index = 0.610, IBS = 0.099), although its improvement over CoxPH was modest. Age, race, and travel time discrepancy were among the most influential factors in the RSF analysis. Higher travel time discrepancy was associated with delayed booster uptake. Mapping the SHAP values at census tract and block group levels showed differences in the contributions of selected predictors across Nueces County. Conclusions: Although RSF performed slightly better than CoxPH, the difference was relatively small. The SHAP analysis provided additional information about how individual predictors contributed to RSF predictions and how these contributions varied geographically. Together, the results show the value of examining booster vaccination timing using both traditional survival models and machine learning approaches.

titre: TrustID-WSN: code, processed data and results for lightweight identity-based signcryption with trust-aware, energy-efficient clustered routing in wireless sensor networks
resume: This record contains the complete code, processed data and result files that reproduce the experiments of the paper "TrustID-WSN: A Lightweight Pairing-Free Identity-Based Signcryption Scheme with Batch Verification and Trust-Aware Cluster-Head Selection for Secure Clustered Wireless Sensor Networks" (under preparation; journal and DOI to be added after acceptance). TrustID-WSN combines (i) a lightweight, pairing-free identity-based signcryption scheme with batch verification at cluster heads, (ii) a dual trust score built from a decision tree trained on WSN-DS (behaviour trust) and data-consistency residuals from real sensor traces (Intel Berkeley Lab, SensorScope), (iii) trust-aware, crypto-aware cluster-head selection and trust-aware multi-hop routing, and (iv) trust-triggered revocation and rekeying. The goal is resistance to impersonation, replay and man-in-the-middle attacks together with longer network lifetime, higher delivery ratio and higher energy-supply efficiency than LEACH, HEED and DEEC secured with ECDSA or pairing-based signatures. Contents: (1) Python preprocessing scripts for six public datasets (WSN-DS, Intel Berkeley Lab, SensorScope, ToN_IoT, Edge-IIoTset, CICIoT2023); (2) the trust-model training script and the trained decision trees; (3) a round-based WSN simulator with LEACH, HEED, DEEC, ECDSA, pairing-IBS and TrustID-WSN; (4) experiment runners (100- and 200-node networks, 0/10/20% insider attackers, 20 paired seeds, ablation and sensitivity studies); (5) ProVerif (Dolev-Yao) models and outputs; AVISPA models are included but were not executed; (6) all result CSV files, and the scripts and outputs for every figure and table of the paper; (7) a self-test (38 checks) and one-command run scripts. Everything runs on a laptop CPU in Python. Important notes: cryptographic energy costs are assumptions and are swept in a sensitivity study; the network is simulated; trust scores are sampled from the model evaluated on WSN-DS; insider data falsification is an assumed threat model; the processed datasets are derived from third-party datasets whose original licences and citations apply. See README.md for details, limitations and step-by-step instructions.
revue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

titre: Correction: Adhesive small bowel obstruction in a 3-year-old child with history of necrotizing enterocolitis: a case report
resume: Background and objectives: Adhesive small bowel obstruction (ASBO) is a serious complication following abdominal surgery in children, yet its presenting symptoms often mimic non-surgical conditions such as viral mesenteric adenitis and functional constipation. This diagnostic challenge is particularly acute in young children with a history of neonatal intestinal surgery who cannot reliably communicate their symptoms. This case report describes a former extreme preterm infant with surgical history of necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC) who presented with acute abdominal pain and was found to have complete mechanical small bowel obstruction due to postoperative adhesions. The objective is to highlight the diagnostic pitfalls in this population and to describe an unusual postoperative course complicated by three concurrent infections. Case presentation: A 3-year-7-month-old former preterm girl (23 weeks gestation) with a history of necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC) requiring jejunal resection and stoma closure presented with one day of colicky abdominal pain, vomiting, and constipation. Initial ultrasound showed reactive mesenteric lymph nodes and fecal loading, suggesting mesenteric adenitis and constipation. However, given her surgical history, she was admitted for observation. Abdominal x-ray revealed small bowel dilatation with air-fluid levels, and contrast-enhanced CT confirmed complete mechanical small bowel obstruction with pneumatosis intestinalis. She underwent emergent laparotomy, which revealed extensive adhesive bands causing obstruction without volvulus, and adhesiolysis was performed without complication. On postoperative day 17, she developed a one-day fever. Workup revealed three concurrent infections: ESBL-producing Escherichia coli urinary tract infection, adenovirus, and Entamoeba histolytica/dispar. She was treated with intravenous meropenem and metronidazole and recovered fully. Conclusion: Children with prior intestinal surgery can present with acute abdominal pain that mimics non-surgical conditions such as mesenteric adenitis and constipation while having a complete adhesive small bowel obstruction requiring emergent surgery. Normal or equivocal ultrasound findings do not exclude this diagnosis, and a low threshold for CT is essential. Postoperative fever in such patients warrants a broad infectious workup, as multiple concurrent pathogens may coexist.Adhesive small bowel obstruction (ASBO)is a common and potentially life-threatening complication following abdominal surgery in children (1). The formation of fibrous bands between loops of intestine, known as adhesions, occurs in virtually all patients after peritoneal injury, though only a subset develops clinically significant obstruction (2). Adhesions typically form within the first month after surgery as part of the normal peritoneal healing response, but their pathological progression into symptomatic obstruction can take months or even years to manifest, and obstruction can occur suddenly without prior warning symptoms (3). In the pediatric population, the incidence of adhesive obstruction following laparotomy ranges from 5% to 25%, with the highest risk observed in neonates who undergo intestinal surgery for conditions such as necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC), intestinal atresia, or gastroschisis (4,5).The diagnosis of Adhesive small bowel obstruction in young children presents unique challenges. Presenting symptoms, abdominal pain, vomiting, constipation, and abdominal distension, are non-specific and overlap substantially with far more common non-surgical conditions such as viral gastroenteritis, mesenteric adenitis, and functional constipation (2). Young children, particularly those of preschool age, cannot reliably articulate the quality, location, or severity of their pain, nor can they provide a detailed history of associated symptoms. This reliance on parental observation and physical examination alone introduces significant uncertainty into the diagnostic process (6). In a child with prior laparotomy, the consequences of missing an adhesive obstruction are severe, as delayed diagnosis can lead to bowel ischemia, perforation, peritonitis, sepsis, and death (7). This diagnostic dilemma is further complicated by the radiation exposure associated with computed tomography (CT) in young children and the difficulty of performing serial abdominal examinations in a distressed or uncooperative child (7,8).This case is noteworthy because it involves a child with a complex surgical history in whom the initial presentation mimicked non-surgical conditions, creating a diagnostic challenge with potentially serious consequences. Additionally, the postoperative course revealed an unusual combination of concurrent infections that are rarely described together in the literature. This report aims to describe the successful management of this complex case and to provide practical lessons for clinicians evaluating children with prior abdominal surgery who present with acute abdominal pain.A 3-year-7-month-old girl presented to the emergency department with a one-hour history of severe diffuse abdominal pain. According to her mother, the child had been constipated for the preceding two days but had eaten her breakfast normally and then began complaining of intense pain. The mother observed that the child attempted to have a bowel movement without success, and the pain worsened with straining. The child was noted to be curling her body in response to the pain, a posture consistent with significant intra-abdominal discomfort. There was no associated vomiting at the time of initial presentation, no fever, and no urinary symptoms. The initial emergency department examination revealed a well-appearing, alert child with stable vital signs, but there was notable abdominal guarding such that she cried when the abdomen was palpated. Based on these findings, the decision was made to transfer the patient via ambulance to another hospital for further evaluation.Upon arrival at the hospital later that same day, the history was further elaborated. The child had experienced central to epigastric colicky abdominal pain that was non-radiating and had been ongoing for approximately 24 h. One episode of vomiting had occurred. The mother reported that the child had not passed stool on the day of presentation and had decreased oral intake. There was a history of runny nose approximately one week prior to presentation, suggesting a possible preceding viral illness. Review of systems was otherwise negative for diarrhea and urinary frequency or dysuria. The patient's past medical history was remarkable for prematurity at 23 weeks gestation, with a birth weight of 435 grams, complicated by respiratory distress syndrome, persistent pulmonary hypertension, recurrent left pneumothorax, bronchopulmonary dysplasia, and patent ductus arteriosus that closed with paracetamol therapy. Most significantly, she developed NEC on day 52 of life requiring laparotomy with resection of 20 cm of jejunum and creation of a jejunostomy. By postoperative day 17, the stoma was successfully closed and she tolerated full oral feeding. Additional past medical history included anemia of prematurity which was resolved, borderline thyroid function tests that normalized, periventricular leukomalacia on neonatal brain ultrasound, mild speech delay, and no evidence of adrenal insufficiency. She had no hospitalizations since NICU discharge, and she was not on any regular medications at the time of presentation. Allergies included moderate reactions to beef and cow's milk, both manifesting as itching.Physical examination on admission to the hospital revealed an ill-appearing child in apparent pain with signs of mild dehydration. Vital signs were stable with heart rate, respiratory rate, blood pressure, and oxygen saturation within normal limits for age. Throat examination showed congestion. Chest auscultation revealed clear breath sounds bilaterally with no wheezes or crackles. Abdominal examination was notable for soft but tender abdomen, with tenderness localized to the central and lower abdomen. Importantly, there was no right iliac fossa tenderness, no guarding, no rebound tenderness, and bowel sounds were present. However, given the child's high-risk surgical history, the clinical team proceeded with admission for observation and serial abdominal examinations rather than discharge.The initial diagnostic workup included laboratory studies and abdominal ultrasound. Serum C-reactive protein was mildly elevated at 7 mg/L, a non-specific finding that could be consistent with either an inflammatory or infectious process.A complete blood count obtained on the day of admission showed a white blood cell count of 3.94 × 10 3 /μL, which is below the normal range of for age. The differential revealed 65.5% neutrophils, 28.2% lymphocytes (low), and 6.3% monocytes, with eosinophils and basophils at 0%. Hemoglobin was 13.2 g/dL (within normal range) and platelet count was 267 × 10 3 /μL (normal). Subsequent CRP monitoring showed a progressive rise to 42.2 mg/L, 126 mg/L, and 106 mg/L.Abdominal ultrasound performed on the day of admission was limited due to a gassy abdomen and fecal material, which are wellrecognized factors that reduce the diagnostic accuracy of ultrasound for bowel obstruction, but it revealed multiple hypoechoic periumbilical and right lower quadrant lymph nodes, the largest measuring 1.8 cm, which were interpreted as likely reactive. The appendix was not visualized. There was no free fluid or localized collection. The liver, gallbladder, pancreas, spleen, and kidneys were all unremarkable. The bladder was underfilled but appeared unremarkable. Based on these ultrasound findings combined with the history of constipation, the initial assessment was acute abdominal pain likely secondary to mesenteric adenitis and constipation with fecal loading. However, the clinical team explicitly noted that given the patient's past surgical history of NEC with bowel resection, it was necessary to exclude an evolving surgical abdomen or pancreatitis.The diagnostic turning point occurred when abdominal x-rays (supine and erect views) were obtained. The radiographs demonstrated few air-fluid levels in the mid abdomen and pelvis associated with small bowel dilatation measuring up to 3.5 cm in diameter. Additionally, a "peak sign" and abrupt obstruction of mid-abdomen small bowel loops were noted, findings highly suggestive of bowel obstruction, possibly due to volvulus. No pneumoperitoneum was observed. In response to these concerning findings, the surgical team was consulted, and a contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis with intravenous contrast was performed emergently. The CT scan confirmed mechanical complete small bowel obstruction. Small bowel loops were dilated to 3 cm in maximum diameter, and large bowel loops were dilated to 3.7 cm. More concerningly, the scan demonstrated wall edema of the rectum and sigmoid loops with air within the bowel wall, pneumatosis intestinalis, causing proximal dilatation of the large bowel. Rotating superior mesenteric vessels at the mid jejunal level and an adhesion band within jejunal loops with areas of narrowing were seen, suggestive of either volvulus or post-surgical adhesions. The impression was mechanical complete small bowel obstruction due to volvulus or adhesions, with pneumatosis intestinalis of the rectosigmoid colon. The surgical team was immediately notified.Following confirmation of complete small bowel obstruction, the patient was kept NPO (nil per os), intravenous fluids (D5% normal saline at 50 mL/hr) were continued, and she was prepared for emergency surgery. A chest x-ray obtained prior to surgery showed bilateral subtle granular opacities with rightsided predominance and mild pleural effusion, findings suggestive of an inflammatory or infectious process, though the patient was afebrile at that time. Intraoperative findings included extensive small bowel adhesions and multiple adhesive bands causing obstruction (Figure 1). The surgeon performed extensive small bowel adhesiolysis, excision of multiple bands, and an incidental appendectomy. The procedure was completed without complication and with minimal blood loss as documented by the operating surgeon. There was no volvulus identified intraoperatively; the obstruction was purely adhesive in nature. The patient tolerated the procedure well and was transferred to the surgical ward for postoperative care.On the first postoperative day, the patient was hemodynamically stable and appeared well, not in pain or distress. Her vital signs remained within acceptable parameters. The abdomen was soft but not fully examinable due to the fresh surgical site. She was maintained NPO with intravenous D5% normal saline and received regular paracetamol 170 mg intravenously every six hours as needed for pain control. The surgical team ordered monitoring of complete blood count and electrolytes, and they planned to follow the pediatric surgery plan closely.By postoperative day three, the patient showed significant clinical improvement. Abdominal distention had decreased, she had not vomited, she was ambulating, and she had been started on an oral soft diet. She was passing urine freely and regularly, and she had passed a moderate amount of more watery stool once during the night and once in the morning. She was receiving oral high-energy nutritional supplement, oral rehydration solution, intravenous fluids with potassium chloride, and oral macrogol for constipation prevention. The abdominal examination at this time showed a mobile abdomen with respiration, very mild distension, a clean dry and intact surgical wound, a soft abdomen, and audible bowel sounds on auscultation.The postoperative course was complicated by a one-day fever along with persistent abdominal distension that had been noted since the surgery. The viral respiratory panel returned positive for adenovirus. Urine culture grew extended-spectrum betalactamase (ESBL)-producing Escherichia coli, establishing the diagnosis of a urinary tract infection with a multidrug-resistant organism. Stool analysis revealed the presence of Entamoeba histolytica/dispar cysts and trophozoites, indicating possible intestinal amebiasis. The stool analysis also showed greenish, mucoid consistency with 7 pus cells and 2 + mucus. By the time these results were available, the patient's fever had resolved spontaneously. She had started oral intake without vomiting and had passed stool. Her vital signs were stable. The physical examination documented a soft abdomen with distention, normal bowel sounds, and no guarding.The treatment plan, as approved by the pediatric consultant, consisted of intravenous meropenem at 20 mg/kg/dose every 8 h (215 mg three times daily) for the ESBL E. coli urinary tract infection, combined with intravenous metronidazole for a total of 5 days to cover both anaerobic bacteria and the Entamoeba infection. The patient was encouraged to take oral intake gradually as tolerated. No specific antiviral therapy was administered for adenovirus. By the time of discharge, the patient had recovered fully, tolerating an oral diet, passing stool Frontiers in Surgery 04 frontiersin.org regularly, and afebrile off antibiotics. She was discharged home with outpatient follow-up arranged with both the surgery and pediatrics teams.This case describes a former preterm infant with surgical history of necrotizing enterocolitis who presented with acute abdominal pain mimicking mesenteric adenitis and constipation, but was found to have complete ASBO requiring adhesiolysis, complicated postoperatively by three concurrent infections. Each element of this case offers an educational value that aligns with and expands upon the existing evidence-based guidelines for ASBO management (8).A key learning point from this case concerns the diagnostic challenge of distinguishing ASBO from non-surgical causes of abdominal pain in children with a history of abdominal surgery. titre: THE MICROBIOTA–GUT–BRAIN AXIS IN STRESS AND ANXIETY: INTEGRATING NEURAL, ENDOCRINE, IMMUNE AND METABOLIC EVIDENCE
resume: Background: Stress and anxiety are complex neuropsychiatric conditions influenced by genetic, environmental, neuroendocrine, immune, and behavioural factors. Increasing evidence highlights the microbiota–gut–brain axis (MGBA) as an important bidirectional communication pathway linking the gastrointestinal tract and central nervous system through neural, endocrine, immune, metabolic, and barrier-mediated mechanisms. Objective: This review synthesizes recent evidence on the mechanisms connecting gut microbiota with psychological stress and anxiety, focusing on the hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal axis, vagal signalling, intestinal and blood–brain barriers, microbial metabolites, immune activation, neurotransmitter pathways, and dietary influences. Evidence for microbiota-targeted interventions, including probiotics, prebiotics, synbiotics, postbiotics, and dietary approaches, is also evaluated. Methods: A focused narrative review of recent literature indexed in PubMed and major biomedical databases was conducted, prioritizing studies published from 2021–2026, including systematic reviews, meta-analyses, randomized controlled trials, and mechanistic studies. Results: Evidence supports a bidirectional relationship between stress and gut microbial function. Stress can alter intestinal motility, permeability, immunity, and microbial ecology, while microbial metabolites and signalling pathways may influence neuroendocrine, immune, vagal, and brain-barrier functions. A 2023 meta-analysis of 29 randomized controlled trials involving 2,035 participants reported significant reductions in anxiety following probiotic and synbiotics interventions, although substantial heterogeneity was observed. Conclusion: The MGBA represents a promising interface between psychological stress and gastrointestinal physiology. However, clinical translation requires further mechanistic, longitudinal, and personalized research.
revue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

titre: Nutrition and Autism Spectrum Disorder: A Narrative Review of Dietary and Nutrient-Based Interventions in the Context of the Gut–Brain Axis
resume: Background/Objectives: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a neurodevelopmental disorder with a childhood onset. It manifests by delayed communication, stereotyping, and limited interests in activities. Genetic factors are known to be implicated in the ASD development. Nutrition-related features, including selective eating, nutrient insufficiency, and gut–brain axis (GBA) alterations, are increasingly studied as modifiable correlates. This narrative review summarizes previous studies on dietary deficiencies and/or nutrient-based interventions in ASD (gluten-free/casein-free and ketogenic diets, vitamins, minerals, omega-3 fatty acids, and antioxidants). Methods: The literature search was initiated on the 1 September 2025. A literature search was conducted across the Web of Science, PubMed, and Scopus. The search covered publication dates from 2000 to 2026. Our search utilized combined search terms such as “autism spectrum disorder,” “micronutrients,” “brain–gut-microbiota axis,” “ketogenic diet, KD”, “gluten-free/casein-free (GFCF)”, “vitamins”, and “antioxidants”. This narrative review reported previous research following the criteria of the Scale for the Assessment of Narrative Review Articles (SANRA). Records were screened by title and abstract, approximately 160 studies were included, and the findings were synthesized narratively. Results: The significance of nutrients as vitamins, minerals, GFCF diet, and KD is shown in ASD cases and trials. Conclusions: Nutritional assessment and correction of deficiencies are integral parts of care. However, the efficacy of dietary or supplement strategies for in alleviating ASD features has not been established, and the link between nutrition and ASD remains largely associative. Additional studies are needed to build up evidence on the correlation between nutrient deficiencies and ASD across a range of doses and populations. For enhancing our understanding of these nutrition interactions, upcoming investigations should focus on longitudinal studies performed in large scales.

titre: Correction: Santos et al. Beneficial Effects of Ginger Root Extract on Pain Behaviors, Inflammation, and Mitochondrial Function in the Colon and Different Brain Regions of Male and Female Neuropathic Rats: A Gut–Brain Axis Study. Nutrients 2024, 16, 3563
Microbiota intestinal em pacientes com transtorno do espectro autista: mecanismo e implicações clínicas
resume: Objective: To analyze the relationship between the gut microbiota and autism spectrum disorder (ASD), highlighting pathophysiological mechanisms and potential therapeutic approaches. Methodology: An integrative literature review was conducted, analyzing studies published over the past ten years in the PubMed, MEDLINE, and LILACS databases. The descriptors “gut microbiota,” “gut-brain axis,” and “ASD” were used, selecting articles that addressed pathophysiological mechanisms and therapeutic strategies related to the disorder. Results: Studies demonstrate that individuals with ASD frequently present intestinal dysbiosis, characterized by reduced microbial diversity and impaired intestinal barrier function, favoring systemic inflammatory processes. In addition, alterations in the gut microbiota may interfere with the regulation of neurotransmitters such as serotonin, dopamine, glutamate, and GABA, influencing behavior and cognition. Gastrointestinal symptoms, such as constipation and abdominal pain, have also been correlated with the severity of neurobehavioral manifestations. Therapeutic strategies, including probiotics, specific dietary interventions, and fecal microbiota transplantation, have shown promising results, although important methodological limitations remain. Conclusion: The gut microbiota exerts a significant influence on the pathophysiology of ASD through the gut-brain axis, contributing to inflammatory and neurochemical alterations associated with the disorder's symptoms. Despite advances in intestinal microbiota modulation strategies, further robust studies are needed to standardize therapeutic approaches and expand the prospects for individualized treatment for individuals with ASD.

titre: Lipopolysaccharide-binding protein is lower in sporadic Parkinson’s disease and inversely correlates with fecal biomarkers of intestinal inflammation and barrier permeability
resume: Parkinson’s disease (PD) is a highly heterogeneous disorder. In a subset of individuals, it may originate in the gut, spreading to the brain through the gut-brain axis. Intestinal endotoxin exposure, inflammation, and barrier dysfunction may contribute to its pathogenesis. We evaluated biomarkers of these processes in an exploratory pilot case-control study on 28 patients with sporadic PD and 28 unmatched controls. We assessed serum lipopolysaccharide (LPS) and LPS-binding protein (LBP) as markers of endotoxin exposure, serum and fecal calprotectin as markers of intestinal inflammation, and serum and fecal zonulin as markers of intestinal barrier permeability. Patients with PD had lower LBP and higher calprotectin and zonulin, with similar LPS levels, and LBP correlated directly with LPS and inversely with fecal calprotectin and zonulin. In the exploratory analyses, all biomarkers except LPS were associated with PD, the best model performance being achieved by combining serum LBP, fecal calprotectin, and fecal zonulin. To our knowledge, this is the first study to simultaneously evaluate all these widely available, relatively inexpensive biomarkers. Although limited by the cross-sectional unmatched design and small sample size, our findings add to the evidence of altered gut-related biomarkers in sporadic PD.

fiche.conclusion: Ces résultats soutiennent l'existence d'une altération des marqueurs intestinaux (perméabilité et inflammation) dans la maladie de Parkinson.

titre: Basti Therapy - A Comprehensive Review on its Principles, Therapeutic Mechanisms, and Clinical Applications
resume: Background: Basti therapy, a principal Panchakarma procedure in Ayurveda, is recognized as the most effective treatment modality for Vata dosha disorders. It is not merely an enema therapy but a systemic treatment influencing the entire physiology through the colon and gut-brain axis. Objective: This review aims to critically analyze classical concepts, pharmacological mechanisms, therapeutic indications, modern scientific interpretations, and clinical evidence supporting Basti therapy. Methods: Data were collected from classical Ayurvedic texts (Charaka Samhita, Sushruta Samhita, Ashtanga Hridaya), peer-reviewed journals, and recent clinical trials indexed in PubMed, Scopus, and AYUSH Research Portal. The collected data were synthesized under conceptual, pharmacological, and clinical headings. Results: Basti exhibits multidimensional actions — neuro-hormonal modulation, gut-microbiota regulation, detoxification, and rejuvenation. Clinically, it is effective in managing conditions such as arthritis, neurological disorders, constipation, infertility, and degenerative diseases. Modern studies reveal that Basti can modulate inflammatory mediators and gut-brain communication through mucosal absorption and neuroenteric reflexes. Conclusion: Basti therapy, when properly indicated and executed, acts beyond a local bowel cleansing procedure; it functions as a systemic therapy harmonizing Vata and restoring physiological homeostasis. Integration of Basti in modern practice holds promise for chronic, lifestyle, and neurological disorders.
revue: International Journal of Drug Delivery Technology

titre: Gut microbiota-derived 3HPPA rescues cognitive deficits in AD-like mouse models via ATP6V0C/USF1-mediated lysosomal regulation
resume: Context Alzheimer’s disease (AD), an intractable neurodegenerative pathology, represents a promising therapeutic contender in microbial metabolites such as 3-(3-hydroxyphenyl) propionic acid (3HPPA). Objective This investigation delineates the neuroprotective efficacy of 3HPPA in AD-like mouse models. Methods Glutamate-compromised HT22 neurons and LPS-activated BV2 microglia served as in vitro platforms to quantify cellular viability, reactive oxygen species (ROS) burden, and cytokine profiles. Concurrently, D-galactose/AlCl 3 or LPS-challenged murine models facilitated in vivo assessments of cognitive function, neuronal survival, superoxide dismutase (SOD) activity, p-tau hyperphosphorylation, and neuroinflammatory cascades. Integrating proteomics with 16S rRNA sequencing, we mapped molecular targets and microbiota dynamics, subsequently validating lysosomal competence and ubiquitination trajectories. Results 3HPPA enhanced HT22 viability, reduced ROS production, and suppressed IL-1β secretion in BV2 cells. It can cross the blood-brain barrier, improve cognitive function, mitigate neuronal loss, restore SOD activity, and decrease p-tau phosphorylation and microglial activation in AD-like mice. Mechanistically, 3HPPA may upregulate ATP6V0C by reducing its ubiquitination-dependent degradation, inhibit upstream stimulatory factor 1 (USF1) to preserve lysosomal integrity, and reshape gut microbiota by increasing Lactobacillus and decreasing pro-inflammatory genera. Conclusion 3HPPA exerts multi-target neuroprotection via the ATP6V0C/USF1-lysosomal axis, alleviates oxidative stress and neuroinflammation, and is associated with reshaped gut microbiota composition, providing novel evidence for its potential as a gut-brain axis-based therapeutic candidate for sporadic AD-like pathology.

fiche.conclusion: 3HPPA exerce une neuroprotection multi-cibles via l'axe ATP6V0C/USF1-lysosome et pourrait être un candidat thérapeutique basé sur l'axe intestin-cerveau pour la pathologie Alzheimer-like.

titre: The Role of Pelvic Floor Muscle Training in Preventing Pelvic Floor Dysfunction During and after Pregnancy: A Scoping Review
resume: Background: Pelvic Floor Dysfunction (PFD), including urinary incontinence, fecal incontinence, and pelvic organ prolapse, is common during pregnancy and after childbirth and often affects long-term health and quality of life. Pelvic Floor Muscle Training (PFMT) is widely recommended for prevention, but evidence on its effectiveness and implementation is mixed, particularly regarding long-term efficacy and adherence to home-based programs. Methods: This scoping review followed PRISMA-ScR and JBI guidelines. PubMed, Scopus, CINAHL, Cochrane Library, and Web of Science were searched for studies published from January 1999 to March 2024. Randomized controlled trials, quasi-experimental studies, and interventional programs evaluating PFMT during pregnancy and up to 12 months postpartum were eligible. Outcomes were urinary incontinence, fecal incontinence, pelvic organ prolapse, pelvic floor function, and quality of life. Results: Of 1,642 records, 15 studies met the inclusion criteria. Interventions lasted 8 weeks to 12 months and were supervised, home-based, or combined. Most studies showed that PFMT reduced postpartum urinary incontinence, improved pelvic floor strength, and enhanced quality of life. Additional benefits included better sexual function, fewer prolapse symptoms, and less pregnancy-related lumbopelvic pain. Supervised programs achieved higher adherence and better outcomes, although structured education and feedback also improved self-managed interventions. Conclusion: Long-term data, such as the six-year follow-up by Glazener et al, indicate that PFMT benefits may diminish without sustained adherence. PFMT is a safe, cost-effective, evidence-based approach to preventing PFD during and after pregnancy. Integrating PFMT into maternal care and strengthening adherence strategies are essential to maximize benefits and reduce the burden of pelvic floor disorders.

titre: Longitudinal changes in symptom clusters in ovarian cancer patients undergoing chemotherapy: a systematic review
resume: Ovarian cancer patients undergoing chemotherapy experience multiple co-occurring symptoms that change over time, but how these symptom clusters evolve across treatment phases remains unclear. This systematic review synthesizes longitudinal evidence on changes in symptom cluster composition in this population. We searched eight databases from inception to April 10, 2026, for longitudinal studies assessing symptom clusters at two or more time points in adults receiving chemotherapy for ovarian cancer. Two reviewers independently screened studies, extracted data, and assessed methodological quality using the NHLBI Quality Assessment Tool for Observational Cohort and Cross-Sectional Studies. Nine studies (1,139 patients) met inclusion criteria; methodological quality was good in four studies and moderate in five. One study identified a potential high-symptom subgroup, with 8%–25% of patients experiencing persistent burden across time points. Specifically, this study reported that 74.9% of patients remained in their assigned symptom class from pre-chemotherapy through cycle four. Symptom cluster composition shifted with treatment: psychological symptoms dominated early, while gastrointestinal and neurotoxic symptoms emerged later. Lower educational attainment, unemployment, anxiety, and depression were associated with persistent high symptom burden, which was consistently associated with poorer quality of life. Clinicians should assess symptoms before chemotherapy, prioritize psychological support early, and monitor gastrointestinal and neurotoxic symptoms as treatment progresses. Patients with anxiety, depression, or low education need closer monitoring. Future research should adopt person-centered approaches with adequate power and transparent reporting of participation rates and attrition. Systematic Review Registration https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/prospero/, identifier CRD420261281625.

titre: Structured Mixture Item Response Model (SMIRT) for structured DIF in HRQoL measurement
resume: Background Differential item functioning (DIF) is commonly observed in patient-reported outcome (PRO) measures across diverse populations. However, DIF analyses are mainly conducted in a post-hoc fashion and the most common practice is to revise or remove the item, without considering the systematic reason behind the DIF. This study investigated the possibility of using the structured mixture item response model to mitigate the issue by creating a composite scale applicable to heterogeneous groups. Methodology The structured mixture item response model was applied to address latent DIF, where a discontinuity parameter indicates the magnitude of the systematic difference in latent group responding. The analysis used PROMIS legacy anxiety and depression scale as illustrative examples (N = 740). In total, 27 items were classified into two groups: (a) 14 cognitive-affective items, reflecting affective, cognitive, and interpersonal appraisal symptoms; and (b) 13 somatic-physiological items, reflecting physiological, neurovegetative, behavioral, or bodily symptoms such as appetite changes, sleep disturbance, fatigue, gastrointestinal symptoms, muscle tension, and psychomotor slowing. Results The discontinuity parameter estimated for the anxiety subscale is 2.71 and 2.12 for the depression subscale, which is quite large. Given these estimates, a composite scale is created while taking the structured DIF into account for both scales. Moreover, the nature of the mixture model provides an estimate of patients’ latent group membership, and the validity of the estimate was investigated by comparing it with other background variables. Conclusions The results suggest that when latent DIF is caused by people’s varying sensitivities to different aspects of clinical diagnoses, SMIRT can be a solution because it offers (1) structural information that helps measurement developers create more appropriate scales for qualitatively different groups and (2) diagnostic information that shows patients’ sensitivity to different subdomains of symptoms, thereby supporting better intervention, particularly in mental health related disorders.

fiche.verdict: Le modèle SMIRT permet de distinguer la réponse aux symptômes cognitifs-affectifs vs somatiques dans les échelles d'anxiété et dépression.
fiche.population: 740 patients ayant complété les échelles PROMIS anxiété et dépression

titre: Perspective Chapter: Advanced Laparoscopic Management of Deep Endometriosis – Current Surgical Strategies and Outcomes
resume: Deep endometriosis represents one of the most challenging conditions in minimally invasive gynecologic surgery due to its complex anatomy, multisystem involvement, and significant impact on quality of life. This chapter will provide a comprehensive overview of the current principles and surgical management of deep endometriosis using advanced laparoscopic techniques. It will discuss preoperative evaluation, imaging-based surgical planning, patient selection, multidisciplinary collaboration, and standardized approaches to the excision of bowel, urinary tract, and pelvic sidewall disease. Particular emphasis will be placed on nerve-sparing techniques, surgical decision-making, complication prevention, and strategies to optimize functional, pain, and fertility outcomes. Current evidence regarding perioperative management, long-term results, recurrence, and quality-of-life measures will also be reviewed. By integrating contemporary evidence with practical surgical experience, this chapter aims to provide clinicians with an up-to-date reference for achieving safe, effective, and patient-centered laparoscopic management of deep endometriosis.

titre: Dietary Management of Hypothyroidism: A Review of Micronutrients, Dietary Patterns, Supplementation, and Levothyroxine Interactions
resume: Hypothyroidism is common and is usually caused by autoimmune thyroiditis in iodine-sufficient settings, whereas iodine deficiency remains an important cause globally. Nutrition is biologically relevant because iodine is a substrate for thyroid hormone synthesis. Selenium, iron, and zinc support enzymes involved in thyroid hormone production, conversion, and antioxidant defense. Dietary exposures can modify levothyroxine absorption. Biologic plausibility does not establish that supplements or restrictive diets prevent or reverse hypothyroidism. This review critically evaluates evidence on macronutrients, iodine, selenium, iron, zinc, vitamin D, vitamin B-12, dietary patterns, gluten-free and ketogenic diets, goitrogen-containing foods, and food-drug interactions. Recent systematic reviews suggest that selenium and vitamin D supplementation can lower thyroid antibody concentrations in some patients with Hashimoto thyroiditis, but effects on symptoms, progression, and levothyroxine requirements remain uncertain. Evidence for Mediterranean-style diets is promising but largely observational or based on small interventions. Routine gluten avoidance is not supported for patients without celiac disease, and ordinary consumption of cooked brassica vegetables or soy is unlikely to impair thyroid function when iodine intake is adequate. Clinical care should prioritize adequate, not excessive iodine intake, correction of documented nutrient deficiencies, cardiometabolic diet quality, and consistent separation of levothyroxine from interfering foods and supplements. Larger, longer randomized trials with patient-centered outcomes are needed.

titre: Osteopathy for neurological, gastro-intestinal, gynecological, neonatal and respiratory disorders: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
resume: Despite its increasing global popularity and the significant rise in scientific publications on osteopathy over the past decade, its effectiveness in treating neurological, gastrointestinal, gynecological, neonatal, and respiratory disorders (i.e., non-musculoskeletal disorders) remains unclear. Therefore, this study aimed to determine the effectiveness of osteopathy in managing non-musculoskeletal disorders. This review was conducted in accordance with the PRISMA guidelines. PubMed (Medline), Web of Science, Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, Embase, OSTMED.DR, Ostlib.de, and Osteopathic Research Web were searched from database inception to 19 March 2024. Two independent reviewers screened studies for randomized trials comparing osteopathy with inactive (e.g., sham) or active (e.g., physiotherapy) control in any non-musculoskeletal disorder. Two researchers independently extracted key information from eligible studies. Random-effects meta-analyses were performed to calculate pooled effect estimates at the end of the intervention and during follow-up. Two independent reviewers assessed the risk of bias using the Cochrane-Risk-of-Bias-Tool, and the certainty of the evidence was evaluated using the GRADE (Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development, and Evaluations) approach. One hundred forty-seven trials enrolling 8448 participants with various non-musculoskeletal disorders ranging from neurological and respiratory conditions to neonatal and gynecological issues were included in this review. Osteopathy, compared with inactive control, improved outcomes in tension-type headache at the end of intervention (intensity: standardized mean difference − 1.09, 95% CI [− 1.50, − 0.69], I 2 80%; frequency: − 1.44,[ − 2.10, − 0.78], I 2 90%; quality of life (QoL) 0.78,[0.41, 1.16], I 2 76%) and at short-term (intensity: − 1.07,[ − 1.84, − 0.30], I 2 89%; frequency − 1.30,[ − 2.25, -0.35], I 2 89%; QoL 1.23,[0.32, 2.14], I 2 :91%). Osteopathy may not improve outcomes in other non-musculoskeletal disorders including migraine (intensity − 1.60,[ − 3.26, 0.05], I 2 94%), infantile colic (crying − 1.14,[ − 3.84, 1.55], I 2 96%), pre-term infants (length of stay − 2.83,[ − 8.21, 2.54], I 2 69%), menopausal symptoms (− 1.38,[ − 4.65, 1.90], I 2 0%), pneumonia (length of stay − 1.04,[ − 3.85, 1.77], I 2 62%), but the evidence is very uncertain. For gastroesophageal reflux disease, menopause, and dysmenorrhea, the findings were inconsistent across outcomes and time points (e.g., dysmenorrhea pain intensity may improve [− 2.25, − 4.02 to − 0.48], but no effect was observed for pain duration or quality of life). Certainty of evidence was very low for all analyses, primarily due to imprecision, inconsistency, and poor methodological quality of studies. There is insufficient evidence to support the effectiveness of osteopathy for improving outcomes in neurological, gastrointestinal, gynecological, neonatal, and respiratory disorders, except for tension-type headaches. PROSPERO CRD42023397131

titre: The relationship between empathy and interoception: a systematic review
Assessing interoception in chronic pain: a systematic scoping review of instruments, construct coverage and psychometric evidence
resume: This registration records the a priori protocol for a scoping review entitled "Assessing interoception in chronic pain: a systematic scoping review of instruments, construct coverage and psychometric evidence". Interoception is indexed by a heterogeneous set of behavioural tasks (e.g., heartbeat counting and discrimination), physiological markers (e.g., heartbeat-evoked potentials), and self-report instruments (e.g., MAIA, Body Perception Questionnaire), which are frequently labelled with overlapping constructs such as accuracy, sensibility and awareness. In pain research these measures have been applied and interpreted inconsistently, which limits comparison across studies and obscures which facet of interoception is actually being assessed. Existing reviews of interoception and pain have largely been narrative or mechanism-focused; a systematic mapping of how interoception is operationalised and measured in relation to pain remains lacking. Using the Population-Concept-Context (PCC) framework, this review will map (1) the range and classification of interoception assessment methods used in pain-related research, (2) the constructs each method purports to measure and the reporting of its measurement properties, (3) the pain populations, experimental paradigms and pain outcomes with which these methods have been paired, and (4) conceptual and methodological gaps that constrain cross-study comparability. A secondary objective is to identify priorities for future methodological work. The review will be conducted in accordance with the JBI Manual for Evidence Synthesis (2024) for scoping reviews and reported against PRISMA-ScR (Tricco et al., 2018). Searches of major biomedical, psychological and multidisciplinary databases will be supplemented by grey literature and reference-list screening; title/abstract and full-text screening and a pilot-tested data-charting form will be used, followed by descriptive synthesis and an evidence-gap map. Consistent with JBI guidance, no formal critical appraisal of included sources and no meta-analysis are planned; conclusions will describe the breadth and gaps of the evidence rather than offer clinical or policy recommendations. Expected outputs are a structured taxonomy of interoception assessment methods, a charted dataset of included sources, a descriptive evidence map, a statement of research gaps, and a PRISMA-ScR-compliant manuscript for submission to a peer-reviewed journal. No directional effect estimates or confirmatory hypotheses are prespecified, as a scoping review maps evidence rather than tests hypotheses. This protocol is registered prospectively, before any database search or screening has commenced, to fix the eligibility criteria, search strategy and construct-classification rules in advance and to ensure that any subsequent deviations are documented and justified. The full protocol, search strings, screener instructions and charting codebook are attached to this registration.

titre: Translation and Validation of the Multidimensional Assessment of Interoceptive Awareness (Maia-2) in Urdu Among Patients with Polysubstance Use
resume: The study aimed to translate and validate the Multidimensional Assessment of Interoceptive Awareness (MAIA-2) in Urdu for patients with polysubstance use. The study was carried out in three phases. The first phase was the translation and tryout of the scale (N = 10), the second was the pilot study (N = 50) and the third was the main cross-sectional study (N = 300). Adult patients with polysubstance use (three or more substance classes) were taken from inpatient rehabilitation centres of Islamabad and Rawalpindi through convenience sampling. The scale was translated by forward translation, backward translation and expert review. The MAIA-2 has 37 items and eight subscales. Cronbach’s alpha, item-total correlation, confirmatory factor analysis and correlation analysis were used. The Urdu MAIA-2 showed good reliability in the pilot study (α = .82) and acceptable reliability in the main study (α = .77). The first factor model did not fit well. After the justifiable error terms were allowed to covary, the model fit improved (RMSEA = .07). The scale was negatively related to psychological distress (r = -.36), suicidal ideation (r = -.43), alexithymia (r = -.43) and emotion dysregulation (r = -.45), and positively related to perceived social support (r = .52). The Urdu MAIA-2 is a reliable and valid scale for measuring interoceptive awareness in patients with polysubstance use.

titre: Multimodal Assessment of Emotional Expression in Individuals with Depression and Emotional Alexithymia Through Embodied Performing Arts Intervention
resume: Alexithymic depression is marked by difficulties in identifying emotions, poor verbalization, and lack of nonverbal expression, while measurement of the latter with a scale has low utility for capturing the dynamics of intervention-related change. The effects of an eight-week performing arts program on behavior were analyzed by recording synchronously videoed facial expressions, speech, full-body poses, and heart rate variability in 60 adults assigned randomly to groups of intervention and controls. Visual, acoustic, postural, and physiological features extracted with MediaPipe, openSMILE, and RR-interval analysis were used for modeling with Elastic Net, XGBoost, and late multimodal fusion. Late fusion resulted in classification accuracy of 0.883, F1 of 0.879, and ROC-AUC of 0.918; regression models produced MAE of 2.12 (R2 of 0.62) for PHQ-9 and 3.47 (R2 of 0.58) for TAS-20. The intervention group exhibited gains of 0.63 in movement amplitude, 0.49 in postural openness, 0.46 in facial activity, 0.41 in F0 range, and 0.37 in RMSSD, which were superior to changes in the control group across all modalities. This combination of behavioral, vocal, and physiological changes suggests that performing arts could be evaluated not only by scales but also by objectively recorded indicators.

titre: A revised Polish version of the 20-item Toronto Alexithymia Scale (TAS-20-POL-R): Translation and validation
resume: The 20-item Toronto Alexithymia Scale (TAS-20) is the most widely used self-report measure for assessing alexithymia. Although there is a Polish version of the scale, close examination of its item content suggests that some items deviate from the original meaning of the English version and may affect the assessment of the construct in Polish-speaking populations. To address these issues, we developed a revised Polish translation (TAS-20-POL-R) and subsequently examined its psychometric properties in a sample of 591 Polish-speaking adults, who completed an online battery of self-report questionnaires, including the TAS-20-POL-R, a widely used measure of emotion regulation strategies (i.e., cognitive reappraisal and expressive suppression), a screening tool to assess anxiety and depression symptoms, and a measure of well-being. A series of confirmatory factor analyses supported the well-validated and replicable 3-factor model of the TAS-20. The internal consistency reliability of the TAS-20 total score was good. Higher scores on the TAS-20-POL-R were significantly associated with less adaptive emotion regulation patterns, higher levels of anxiety and depression symptoms, and poorer overall well-being. The externally-oriented thinking subscale demonstrated weaker psychometric performance (i.e., two items with low factor loadings and lower-than-acceptable reliability). Overall, the TAS-20-POL-R has adequate psychometric properties and shows a pattern of associations consistent with the alexithymia construct.

titre: Facilitating Movement through Design to Reduce Vulnerability in Chronic Conditions
resume: This chapter explores how design can facilitate movement as a means of reducing vulnerability in individuals living with chronic conditions. Drawing on design research, autoethnography, and interdisciplinary case studies, it argues that vulnerability is not eliminated through medical stabilization alone, but is actively negotiated through embodied experiences, learning, and agency. Across contexts including Type 1 diabetes, breast cancer, kidney disease, and gendered urban mobility, the chapter shows how movement supports interoception, self-efficacy, and autonomy—key mechanisms for living well with chronic illness. The projects presented illustrate how design interventions, ranging from visual narratives and participatory tools to garments, apps, and services, scaffold patients’ capacity to interpret bodily signals, manage uncertainty, and re-engage with movement on their own terms. Rather than prescribing behavior or optimizing performance, these “smart solutions” operate as relational and reflective scaffolds that make vulnerability negotiable and manageable. The chapter contributes a design-led perspective on movement as a site where care, learning, and bodily trust can be gradually rebuilt.

titre: Interaction of Mind and Body in Psychosexual Medicine
resume: Psychosexual medicine focuses on the complex and often unconscious interaction between mind and body as expressed through sexual symptoms. This chapter examines somatisation as a key psychological defence mechanism by which emotional conflicts are converted into physical symptoms that symbolise underlying distress. It highlights how difficulties in recognising and articulating emotions (alexithymia) predispose patients to experience and present psychological conflict somatically, leading them to seek medical explanations for psychosexual dysfunction. Through clinical examples, the chapter demonstrates how patients vary in their awareness of mind-body connections and underscores the importance of communicating at an appropriate emotional level to avoid defensiveness and foster insight. The role of the clinician is presented as one of observing symbolic bodily symptoms, containing emotional overwhelm and gradually introducing an understanding of unconscious processes. The chapter concludes that helping patients make less-conscious emotional experiences more conscious can reduce the need for physical symptom expression, thereby alleviating psychosexual difficulties and promoting a more integrated understanding of self.

titre: Parenting Styles, Attachment Relationship, and Self-Esteem in Adolescent Personality Development
resume: Individuals differ in their responses to relationship conflicts, intimacy, and self-evaluation. The factors underlying these differences warrant further investigation. Psychological research indicates that personality development is jointly influenced by parenting styles, attachment relationships, and self-esteem. However, current studies mostly separately explore individual factors and lack a systematic integration of the influence paths of the three. This paper adopts the literature review method to systematically explore the research on the relationship between parenting styles, attachment relationships, and self-esteem and personality development from three levels: parenting styles, attachment relationships, and self-esteem. The study found that authoritative parenting is associated with better social adaptation and healthy personality, while neglectful parenting is associated with the worst adaptation results, and authoritarian psychological control is linked to covert narcissism and alexithymia; insecure attachment is positively correlated with impaired personality functions, with emotional dysregulation serving as a mediating factor, and attachment anxiety is also related to emotional manipulation behaviors in intimate relationships through dark personality traits; self-esteem has a bidirectional association with each dimension of the Big Five personality traits and plays a mediating role in the influence of personality traits on creativity as well as depression. The research shows that parenting styles, attachment relationships, and self-esteem jointly influence personality development through different paths. Future research can further integrate these three factors and explore protective factors and intervention paths.
revue: Lecture Notes in Education Psychology and Public Media

titre: Monitoring depth of anesthesia in the operating room and sedation in intensive care: a SIAARTI Consensus Statement
resume: The brain is the primary target organ of hypnotic and analgesic drugs administered during general anesthesia and sedation; yet cerebral function remains less systematically monitored than other systems. Processed electroencephalography (pEEG) allows for individualized titration of sedatives and analgesics, identifies inadequate hypnosis and sedation, and improves recognition of electroencephalographic (EEG) patterns associated with adverse outcomes (e.g., burst suppression/suppression). The Italian Society of Anesthesia, Analgesia, Resuscitation and Intensive Care (SIAARTI) developed a consensus statement to provide pragmatic guidance on the clinical use of EEG monitoring during general anesthesia and sedation in the intensive care units (ICUs) and perioperative settings. This consensus statement was developed in accordance with the methodology of the Italian National Health Institute for the preparation of consensus-based documents. A structured literature search was conducted. A multidisciplinary panel with expertise in the topic identified key clinical items through a modified Delphi process. Consensus was predefined as ≥ 75% agreement within the same Likert-scale range. Statements and rationales were drafted, subjected to blinded voting and external peer review before final approval. Six items were considered. Statements address: (1) pEEG technology; (2) pEEG in adult anesthesia; (3) pEEG in pediatric anesthesia; (4) pEEG in adult and pediatric intensive care; (5) artifact recognition; (6) neurological and hemodynamic outcomes. The panel supported pEEG monitoring to reduce intraoperative awareness, burst suppression, and hemodynamic instability, and emphasized interpretation of numerical indices, EEG raw traces, and derived parameters (e.g., density spectral array, spectral edge frequency, burst suppression, electromyography, artifact detection, quality signal, asymmetry). This consensus statement provides updated, pragmatic guidance on pEEG monitoring during general anaesthesia and sedation. Implementation should consider clinical settings, patients’ characteristics, dosing risks, and training in the interpretation of raw EEG and derived parameters.
revue: Journal of Anesthesia Analgesia and Critical Care

titre: Communication in psychotherapy for depression: a systematic review of conversation analysis studies
resume: The interaction between therapists and clients is fundamental to determining the effectiveness of treatment and has clinical significance in psychotherapy for depression. Conversation analysis (CA) has emerged as a vital methodology for understanding therapeutic interactions in psychotherapy. Nevertheless, the existing body of CA research on the therapist-client interaction in the context of depression remains fragmented and lacks systematic synthesis. Thus, we conducted the first systematic literature review of CA research on psychotherapy for depression. By searching nine databases, we identified 18 empirical studies published in English to date. We adopted thematic analysis to discuss and categorize these 18 studies into five themes: emotion talk, management of participation, psychotherapeutic changes in the interaction, dynamic relationship in psychotherapy, and introduction of CA to psychotherapy research. This study introduced the unique contribution of CA to psychotherapy research for depression and provided the latest advancements in CA studies in this context. It further offered valuable insights into the psychotherapeutic treatment of depression and future research directions in psychotherapy.

titre: Acceptability and feasibility of a universal online preventive intervention for depression and anxiety among university students: protocol of a pilot randomized controlled trial
resume: The mental health of university students is a global concern, with high rates of depression, anxiety, and stress significantly impacting their well-being and academic performance. Several studies reveal high prevalence rates, highlighting the need for effective prevention strategies. Evidence shows that digital interventions incorporating mindfulness, emotional regulation, and cognitive-behavioral techniques can reduce symptoms of mental illness. However, such programs are scarce in Latin America. This study proposes developing and evaluating "CUIDATE," a brief online universal preventive intervention targeting depression and anxiety among university students, focusing on acceptability, feasibility, and potential improvements in mental health and quality of life. This is a pilot randomized controlled trial, parallel-group type, where students using CUIDATE, a 6-session online self-guided universal preventive intervention, are compared to students doing regular academic work. 50 students in a private university in Santiago, Chile, are expected to be recruited and randomized with 1:1 allocation. Assessments of acceptability and feasibility during the whole project will be collected at the end of the intervention. Measurements of depression and anxiety symptoms, quality of life, and several mindfulness, emotional regulation, and cognitive-behavioral skills will be conducted among students of both groups at baseline, post-intervention and 12-week follow-up. This pilot Randomized Controlled Trial aims to evaluate the acceptability and feasibility of "CUIDATE," a self-guided online intervention promoting cognitive-behavioral therapy skills, emotion regulation, and a healthy lifestyle to prevent depression and anxiety. Unlike existing programs, often limited to developed countries, CUIDATE is designed for accessibility and cost-effectiveness, using the widely adopted Canvas platform to engage university students. While challenges like recruitment and task adherence are anticipated, proactive measures, including student leaders’ network support, will mitigate these risks. The study's findings will produce relevant information about these novel designs and may help guide future studies, such as a randomized controlled trial on a large scale. Clinical Trials NCT06419868, May 14. 2024 [ https://www.clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06419868 ].

titre: Peer-led intervention for individuals with major depression: post-intervention and implementation outcomes from the SUPEERMood randomized controlled trial
resume: Depressive disorders represent a major global public health challenge, affecting an estimated 280–300 million people worldwide and constituting a leading cause of disability. Major depressive disorder (MDD) is associated with substantial clinical, social, and economic burden. Consequently, clinical guidelines emphasize the need for adjuvant, recovery-oriented interventions that promote self-management, lifestyle changes, and symptoms reduction, including peer support. However, high-quality evidence for structured peer-led interventions in MDD remains limited. To evaluate post-intervention and implementation outcomes of a structured peer-led intervention on depressive symptoms in individuals with MDD compared with a cognitive-behavioural therapy (CBT)-based mHealth application. SUPEERMood was a two-arm, parallel randomized controlled trial conducted in three primary care Mental Health Units (MHUs) in Mallorca, Spain. Adults (≥18 years) with MDD were randomized to a peer-led intervention weekly sessions over 6 weeks or to a CBT-based mHealth application used for the same duration. Outcomes were assessed at baseline and post-intervention (6 weeks). The primary outcome was depressive symptoms measured by the Beck Depression Inventory-II (BDI-II). Secondary outcomes included quality of life, medication attitudes, lifestyle behaviours, and alcohol consumption. Implementation outcomes included adoption, reach, adherence, fidelity, and maintenance. Eighty-one participants were randomized (intervention n = 41; control n = 40). After adjusting for baseline BDI-II scores, a significant between-group difference was observed at post-intervention (6-week follow-up), with participants in the intervention group showing greater reductions in depressive symptoms than the control group (Adjusted Mean Difference [AMD] = −5.82, 95% CI −8.72, −2.93; F(1,71) = 16.06, p < 0.001; partial η 2 = 0.185). Improvements in quality of life were also observed (AMD = −0.352, 95% CI −0.646, −0.059; p = 0.019; partial η 2 = 0.074). Adherence was higher in the peer-led intervention (65.8% completed the programme) than in the mHealth group (54% reported at least moderate use). Overall, 66.6% of invited primary care MHUs adopted the intervention, fidelity was high with one minor adaptation, and maintenance was supported by their continuation beyond the trial. The peer-led intervention significantly reduced depressive symptoms immediately post-intervention and demonstrated feasibility and promising implementation outcomes in primary care mental health units. These findings suggest that peer support may represent an effective, recovery-oriented adjuvant approach for MDD, warranting further evaluation in larger and more diverse populations. NCT06398561. Date of registration: 05/01/2024.

titre: Evaluating the effectiveness of a digital therapy intervention (iCARE) to treat symptoms of postpartum depression: study protocol for a two—armed randomized controlled trial
resume: Postpartum depression (PPD) is a common condition that can negatively affect maternal well-being and child development. Cognitive behavioral therapy an effective psychological treatment, but access is limited in many settings. Internet-based cognitive behavioral therapy offers a scalable alternative that can be delivered flexibly at home. This trial aims to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of a self-guided internet-based intervention, iCARE, compared to treatment as usual for mothers with symptoms of PPD. This is a two-arm, parallel-group, randomized controlled superiority trial. Mothers within 6 months postpartum with an Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale score of 7–30 will be recruited through health nurses in 21 Danish municipalities and nationwide via self-recruitment through a project website. After baseline assessment, participants will be randomized 1:1 to iCARE plus usual care or usual care alone, stratified by symptom severity and recruitment pathway. The primary outcome is change in depressive symptoms from baseline to two months, with a secondary endpoint at 6 months. Key secondary outcomes include anxiety, functioning, automatic negative thoughts, and parental stress. Analyses will follow the intention-to-treat principle. Missing data will be handled with multiple imputation. Safety procedures include monitoring of symptom scores and predefined referral pathways for participants reporting self-harm thoughts or deterioration of depressive symptoms. This trial will provide evidence on the effectiveness and safety of a self-guided digital intervention for PPD in a real-world setting. If effective, iCARE could improve access to psychological support and reduce treatment gaps for mothers experiencing symptoms of PPD and potentially be implemented in a stepped care approach. Findings will inform future implementation strategies in public health systems. ClinicalTrials.gov ID: NCT07384273

titre: Resilience, Insight, Self-Compassion, and Empowerment (RISE): a prospective study of a psychoeducational retreat program for physicians experiencing burnout
resume: Background Physician burnout is a critical public health crisis affecting approximately 50% of physicians. The RISE (Resilience, Insight, Self-Compassion, and Empowerment) program is a psychoeducational intervention previously found effective for nurses and nurse leaders. This study examined the impact of a 2.5-day retreat-style adaptation of this program on burnout and well-being outcomes among physicians. Methods A prospective single-group pretest-posttest study was conducted with physicians experiencing predominantly moderate-to-high burnout symptoms. Participants completed validated assessments measuring burnout, professional quality of life, resilience, insight, self-compassion, self-efficacy, perceived stress, work-life balance, moral injury, anxiety, and depression at baseline, 1-month, and 3-month follow-up. Repeated-measures ANOVA was used to evaluate changes across timepoints, with 95% confidence intervals. Pairwise comparisons among the three timepoints were adjusted using the Bonferroni method within each outcome. Effect sizes for the overall time effect were reported using eta squared (ηp²). Results 39 participants attended the intervention. Analyses of the primary outcome of burnout included 34 participants. Scores changed significantly over time across all three Maslach Burnout Inventory domains. Emotional Exhaustion decreased from baseline to 1- and 3-month follow-up (35.53 vs. 27.76 vs. 27.18; F[2,66] = 15.454; p <.001; ηp²=0.319), as did Depersonalization (12.18 vs. 9.32 vs. 8.88; F[1.503,49.605] = 6.365; p =.007; ηp²=0.162). Personal Accomplishment increased from baseline (31.26 vs. 39.44 vs. 38.91; F[2,66] = 42.641; p <.001; ηp²=0.564). Significant changes over the three timepoints were also observed in exploratory secondary outcomes including professional quality of life, insight, self-compassion, self-efficacy, perceived stress, work-life balance, moral injury, anxiety, and depression. Conclusions The study results demonstrated improvements in participant scores across multiple dimensions of physician well-being. This retreat-style psychoeducational intervention shows promise as an approach to help reduce physician burnout and promote healthier alignment between work and home life. This study can inform a future randomized controlled trial to establish intervention effectiveness. Trial registration number (TRN) NCT06462443, Date registered 6/17/2024.

titre: Cost-Effectiveness of Digital Mental Health Interventions in Community-Based Care: Systematic Review
resume: Background Mental health conditions are a leading cause of disability and economic burden worldwide. Digital mental health interventions (DMHIs) may widen access, but economic evidence from community mental health settings, including low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), has not been synthesized by perspective, time horizon, and comparator type. Objective This study aimed to assess the cost-effectiveness of DMHIs delivered in community mental health settings. Methods This systematic review followed the PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses) 2020 guidelines and was registered with the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO CRD420251141326). PubMed, Scopus, the Directory of Open Access Journals, and the Cochrane Library were searched for economic evaluations published from January 2010 to June 2025 involving adolescents (aged 10 years and older) through older adults with mental disorders. Two reviewers independently screened studies, and the quality was appraised using the Consensus on Health Economic Criteria (CHEC) list. Costs were standardized to 2025 US $, and findings were synthesized narratively. Results Of 2478 records identified, 20 economic evaluations were included: 16 randomized controlled trials, 3 decision-analytic models, and 1 uncontrolled single-arm study, conducted in high-income countries and LMICs (Kenya, Lebanon, China, and Southeast Europe). Depression (n=11, 55%) and anxiety (n=7, 35%) were the most frequent targets. Of 20 studies, 10 (50%) used a health care payer perspective only, 1 (5%) study used a societal perspective only, and 9 (45%) used both perspectives; time horizons ranged from 2 weeks to 10 years. Thirteen (65%) studies were cost-effective at the willingness-to-pay thresholds applied, and 4 (20%) were not; 3 (15%) did not state a threshold. Among the 16 studies reporting quality-adjusted life years, 4 (25%) were dominant (less costly and more effective), 11 (69%) were more costly and more effective, and 1 (6%) was less costly and less effective. The BlueIce smartphone app for self-harm and the NIDUS-Family (New Interventions for Independence in Dementia Studies) dementia intervention were dominant, whereas a societal perspective made some interventions cost-saving, such as Step-by-Step in Lebanon. Interventions that were not cost-effective included those evaluated in Germany, the United States, and Southeast Europe, and 1 psychosis trial with a high incremental cost-effectiveness ratio. Methodological quality was high in 15 (75%) studies, moderate in 4 (20%), and low in 1 (5%). Conclusions DMHIs in community settings can offer good value for money, particularly guided internet-based cognitive behavioral therapy for depression and anxiety, and may be cost-saving from a societal perspective. The evidence is limited by short time horizons (often 12 months or less), waitlist and usual care comparators, and heterogeneous outcome measures. Future evaluations should use longer follow-ups, active comparators, and a common utility measure, ideally the EQ-5D questionnaire.

titre: Feasibility study of an online mindfulness group intervention for people with aphasia
resume: Background People with aphasia (PWA) can struggle with mental health symptoms and loneliness, as post-stroke communication challenges can lead to stressful changes and losses across multiple facets of their lives. Unfortunately, little research has implemented interventions to address these issues, in part because PWA are often excluded from clinical research studies due to their language deficits. This study begins to address this gap by assessing the feasibility of an online mindfulness-based group intervention tailored specifically for PWA.Methods We designed an 8-week, online, group intervention for PWA focused on teaching three key practices adapted from Kabat-Zinn’s Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction protocol: sensory awareness, breath awareness, and nervous system regulation. The intervention was further adapted for PWA by having 90-minute, once-weekly sessions to reduce fatigue and by using aphasia-friendly communication strategies.Results Seven participants completed the intervention and the pre- and post-intervention measures assessing feasibility, satisfaction, mental health, and loneliness outcomes. We also elicited feedback from participants post-intervention. Findings revealed good feasibility and satisfaction, as participants had > 80% attendance, retention, and class/instructor satisfaction scores. Participants also reported reduced stress and improved scores of depression, anxiety, and loneliness. During our feedback interviews, some participants expressed challenges related to technology and home practice. These issues and potential solutions are discussed.Conclusions The online group mindfulness intervention demonstrated good feasibility (i.e. recruitment, retention) and participant satisfaction. These findings provide support for further study of online interventions such as mindfulness for PWA using randomized controlled trials.
