titre: Robustness Analysis of XDJZ (Lam & Chung, 2019)
resume: Paper, analyst, and focal result Analyst Ruben Lopez-Nicolas Paper ID XDJZ Date 2 November 2026 The focal result: The effect of IPSRT on overall functioning (occupational, social, and impaired functioning) was significant (g = -0.344, 95% CI: -0.546 to -0.141; p = 0.001).... p.160, ‘Results’, ‘Treatment Effect of IPSRT on Patients with Bipolar Disorders’. Figure 2b, overall functioning, bottom pooled row: Hedges’ g = -0.344, SE = 0.103, 95% CI [-0.546, -0.141], p = .001; three independent trials. The figure labels negative effects as favoring IPSRT (Lam & Chung, 2021). The analysis that produces it: The unit of analysis is one independent trial-level functioning contrast. The synthesis concerns the three trials included in Figure 2b: Frank (2008), Inder (2015) and Miklowitz (2007). Their outcomes are occupational functioning on the UCLA Social Attainment Scale, social adjustment on the SAS, and impaired functioning on the LIFE-RIFT, respectively. Primary reports determine the analysis populations; the trials do not all estimate an identical endpoint contrast. Frank compares acute IPSRT with intensive clinical management through a treatment-by-time mixed-model interaction across baseline, end of acute treatment and two maintenance follow-ups. Inder compares IPSRT with specialist supportive care using baseline-adjusted ANCOVA of the weeks 26–78 SAS composite. Miklowitz compares intensive psychotherapy (IPSRT, CBT and family-focused therapy combined) with collaborative care over months 3, 6 and 9, adjusting for baseline functioning, concurrent depression, site, bipolar subtype and pharmacotherapy-study assignment. The meta-analysis uses random-effects inverse-variance pooling in Comprehensive Meta-Analysis 2.0. The unspecified between-study variance estimator is provisionally assumed to be DerSimonian–Laird (DL), and the reported confidence intervals are assumed to be based on normal/Wald inference. There are no study-level covariates in the pooled model. The focal estimate: The focal estimate is the pooled mean standardized functioning effect, Hedges’s g, estimated by the intercept in an intercept-only random-effects meta-analysis. Record g, SE, the two-sided test, p-value and 95% CI. 2. Data Data source: The source data are the primary reports’ F tests, counts, functioning means, SDs and plotted endpoints: Frank et al. (2008), pp. 1560–1561 and Figure 1; Inder et al. (2015), pp. 130–134 and Tables 1–2; Miklowitz et al. (2007), pp. 1341–1344. These reports were available to the meta-analysts. Risk-of-bias labels for d01 are extracted from the meta-analysis’s Table 3. Author materials. Did you consult any author materials, whether replication code, data documentation, appendices, supplements, or other relevant materials? ☐ Yes ☒ No Prior work with this paper or these data. Aggregate summaries do not permit alternative clinical cutpoints or responder classifications for the same outcome. d06 Covariate set No alternative available: No defensible meta-regression with only 2–3 trials. Original primary-model adjustments are inherited in the original-effect branch; raw-change alternatives in d03 also alter adjustment and timing, which are disclosed rather than treated as isolated covariate choices. d07 Estimator and functional form: Varied d08 Clustering, nesting, and standard errors: Varied d09 Sampling weights and complex design: Not applicable No survey weight, strata or PSU variables are supplied. Usual meta-analytic inverse-variance weighting is retained; with no reasonable alternative weighting scheme. 4. The five you are varying d01 — Analytic sample construction Option Original? What it does Why it is a reasonable choice for this question orig_all: Yes Include all three functioning trials in Figure 2b. — alt_RoB: No Exclude any trial rated high risk in at least one domain of the meta-analysis’s Table 3. This excludes Frank (high risk for random sequence generation) and retains Inder and Miklowitz. Unclear risk alone does not trigger exclusion. Tests whether restricting the synthesis to trials without an explicitly high-risk rating changes the focal result, using a rule fixed before pooled analysis. d03 — Outcome operationalization Option Original? What it does Why it is a reasonable choice for this question orig_F: Yes Reconstruct the apparent original conversions from the primary F tests and nominal arm counts. Effect-size signs will follow the directions indicated in the primary study reports, correcting an apparent coding error in the original meta-analysis (see Section 7). — alt_recon: No Reconstruct all three trials using ANCOVA- and gain-score-based estimates of Hedges’s g: Inder ANCOVA, Miklowitz nine-month gains, and Frank baseline-standardized controlled change. Assesses the sensitivity of the results to alternative methods for estimating treatment effects. d04 — Focal predictor operationalization Option Original? The article specifies random effects but not the tau-squared estimator; DL is the provisional reading of the original analysis. — alt_REML: No Use restricted maximum likelihood to estimate tau-squared, keeping the same study inputs and intercept-only mean model. REML offers a standard alternative estimate of between-study variance within the same random-effects model. d08 — Clustering, nesting, and standard errors Option Original? What it does Why it is a reasonable choice for this question orig_Wald: Yes Use standard Wald-type 95% CI and two-sided significance test, based on the normal distribution. — alt_mKH: No Use the modified Knapp-Hartung adjustment for 95% CI and two-sided significance test, based on the t-distribution. titre: Obsessive-compulsive disorder with impossible content: a case report of an adolescent boy’s fear of becoming pregnant
resume: Background Sexual obsessions are common in young people with obsessive-compulsive disorder, yet they remain poorly documented. When their content is biologically impossible, they are easily taken for an emerging psychosis. Case presentation A 14-year-old boy with no psychiatric history was referred after about eight months of worsening anxiety, avoidance and repetitive washing, which had begun after his first masturbatory experience. He feared that his own semen would spread through the house, carried by his mother and everyday objects, and find its way back into his body to make him pregnant. Each of his rituals blocked one step of this imagined route. A second theme concerned whether a pleasurable sensation proved he had a particular sexual orientation. At baseline, his Children’s Yale-Brown Obsessive Compulsive Scale (CY-BOCS) score was 40/40 and his Clinical Global Impression-Severity (CGI-S) score 7. The content and the severity raised the question of psychosis at first contact, but the symptom was obsessional in form from the start. He doubted rather than believed, saw his thoughts as unreasonable, neutralized them with matching rituals, and showed no psychotic feature. He received sertraline 200 mg/day, olanzapine 5 mg/day as augmentation after a partial response, and about twenty sessions of cognitive-behavioral therapy with exposure and response prevention. His CY-BOCS score was 10 at the end of the program and 12 one year after all treatment had stopped. No psychotic feature appeared over three years of follow-up. Conclusions Biologically impossible content alone does not make an obsession psychotic. What separates an obsession from a delusion is the form and function of the symptom, not its content.

titre: Can an app change obsessive beliefs in adolescents? The GGOC-AD trial
resume: Adolescence is a period of vulnerability to obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD). Maladaptive beliefs about intrusive thoughts are one of several factors thought to contribute to OCD. A new randomised controlled trial suggests that two weeks of app-based cognitive training (GGOC-AD) was associated with lower OCD-related beliefs and symptoms in community adolescents. It appears to be a preliminary yet promising tool for addressing and modifying an important cognitive risk factor for OCD, though more testing is necessary.

titre: Dietary Supplements, Gut Microbiota and ADHD
resume: Dietary supplement, gut microbiota and ADHD (short title: Gut microbiota and ADHD) Background and hypothesis ADHD is the most prevalent neurodevelopmental disorder in child psychiatry (about 7.2% of the world population); its aetiology is multifactorial and still poorly understood. The gut microbiota (GM) modulates the gut-brain axis; the 7 available studies report differences in bacterial composition in ADHD, without consensus. Pycnogenol, a polyphenol-rich French maritime pine bark extract, is a dietary supplement (no marketing authorisation, no therapeutic claim) whose biotransformation depends on colonic microbial enzymes. Previous trials show a reduction of ADHD symptoms after 4 to 10 weeks and a very low rate of adverse effects (about 1.8%, minor). Hypothesis: Pycnogenol modulates the GM and regulates the gut-brain axis, improving the clinical symptoms of ADHD and the associated cognitive functions. Objectives (1) To identify a possible bacterial signature (dysbiosis) linked to ADHD symptoms and/or associated cognitive functions, by comparing the GM of children with ADHD with that of typically developing children; (2) to explore whether the presumed efficacy of Pycnogenol on clinical symptoms and cognitive functions is associated with a rebalancing of the GM. Population 100 French-speaking children aged 6 to 12 years inclusive, girls and boys: 50 with ADHD, combined presentation (child psychiatry outpatient clinic, Erasme Medical Center) and 50 typically developing (advertisements, investigators' acquaintances). Consent of the child and of the legal representatives. Exclusion: psychiatric comorbidity, significant eating disorders, lactose intolerance or cow's milk protein allergy, gluten intolerance, prematurity, IQ \ 50 kg). Provided free of charge. The control group receives no Pycnogenol. Visits: T0 inclusion; T1 week 1; T2 week 5; T3 week 10. Assessments Clinical: DSM-5 criteria and child psychiatric examination (T0, T2, T3); clinician-rated ADHD-RS IV (T0, T2, T3 in ADHD; T1 in controls); Physical Complaints Questionnaire for side effects (T2, T3, ADHD); Food Frequency Questionnaire and Bristol stool scale (T1, T2, T3 ADHD; T1 controls). Neuropsychological: WISC-V (estimated IQ), TAP battery (visual and auditory selective attention, divided attention, vigilance, flexibility, Go/NoGo inhibition, working memory) and MIDA (delay aversion), at T1 and T3 in ADHD, T1 in controls; Go/NoGo and vigilance also at T2 (ADHD). Microbiota: stool collected at home (OMNIgene-GUT kit, stable 60 days), stored at -80 °C; DNA extraction (QIAamp DNA Stool Mini Kit), 16S rRNA V1-V3 amplification, Illumina MiSeq sequencing, QIIME2 pipeline. Laboratory and biostatistical analyses: Prof. A. Everard (UCLouvain/LDRI). Biobank: UCLouvain Biothèque (Prof. E. Marbaix); samples destroyed after analysis. Expected results Replication of a distinct GM composition in ADHD; confirmation of a beneficial effect of Pycnogenol; identification of the cognitive indices most sensitive to it; demonstration of GM modulation correlated with clinical and cognitive improvement. Data, ethics, risks REDCap eCRF, pseudonymisation by code; the key file is held by the PI only and destroyed after publication. Conducted according to GCP and the Declaration of Helsinki, submitted to the Ethics Committee. Risks: possible mild gastrointestinal complaints or allergy; no incidental findings expected (group-level analyses). No cost to participants; cognitive test results returned to families. Funding: Fund Claude \& Marie-Hélène Lelièvre-Meurée.

titre: Synergistic Nutrition and Early Rehabilitation for Guided Recovery in Critically Ill Patients: The SYNERGY Multicenter Randomized Controlled Trial
resume: Critically ill patients lose muscle mass rapidly during their intensive care unit (ICU) stay, which contributes to prolonged mechanical ventilation, longer hospital stays and lasting functional limitations. Nutrition therapy and early mobilization each help, but they have mostly been tested separately and only during the ICU stay. The SYNERGY trial tests whether combining personalized nutrition, guided by indirect calorimetry, with early mobilization improves quality of life 6 months later in adults who need mechanical ventilation. The combined program continues after ICU discharge, up to day 28 or hospital discharge. A total of 224 adults in four Swiss ICUs will be randomly assigned (1:1) to the combined program or to standard nutrition and physiotherapy care. The main outcome is quality of life measured with the EQ-5D-5L questionnaire at 6 months. Other outcomes include muscle mass and function, physical recovery, inflammation, gut microbiota, survival, length of stay, infections, and functional, mental and cognitive health at 6 months.

titre: The Samal-FLARE Technique for Parastomal Hernia: A Prospective Study of a Four-Layer Laparoscopic Repair
resume: Parastomal hernia is a common complication in patients with a permanent abdominal stoma. It can cause discomfort, difficulty in stoma care, and impaired quality of life. Surgical repair remains challenging because of the risk of recurrence, even after mesh reinforcement. Various laparoscopic techniques, including keyhole, Sugarbaker, and sandwich mesh repairs, have been described, but no single technique has consistently eliminated the risk of recurrence. The Sasmal-FLARE (Four-Layer Anti-Recurrence Repair) technique is a novel laparoscopic surgical approach designed to address multiple anatomical factors contributing to parastomal hernia recurrence. It combines four sequential steps: (1) obliteration of the parastomal hernia cavity using transfascial sutures; (2) reinforcement of the widened hernia neck by polypropylene suture darning; (3) placement of a composite intraperitoneal mesh in a keyhole configuration around the stomal bowel; and (4) placement of a second intact composite mesh using the Sugarbaker technique, with lateralization of the bowel and adequate mesh overlap. This multilayered approach is intended to reinforce the hernia defect and potentially reduce recurrence. This prospective, single-centre, interventional pilot study will be conducted in the Department of General Surgery, All India Institute of Medical Sciences (AIIMS), Bhubaneswar, India. A minimum of 10 consecutive adult patients (aged 18 years or above) with uncomplicated parastomal hernia associated with a permanent stoma, who are suitable for elective laparoscopic repair, will be enrolled after obtaining written informed consent. The primary objective is to determine the recurrence rate of parastomal hernia following the Sasmal-FLARE repair during a follow-up period of 24 months. Secondary objectives include assessing the technical feasibility and safety of the procedure, operative and postoperative complications, postoperative pain, duration of hospital stay, return to routine activities, stoma function, and patient satisfaction. Patients will undergo standard preoperative assessment followed by laparoscopic repair using the four-layer technique. Clinical follow-up will be performed at approximately 1, 3, 6, 12, 18, and 24 months after surgery. Hernia recurrence will be assessed clinically, with ultrasonography or computed tomography performed when clinically indicated or when recurrence is uncertain. Postoperative complications, including surgical site infection, seroma, bowel obstruction, mesh-related complications, stoma-related problems, readmission, and reoperation, will be recorded. As an initial pilot study, the findings will be analysed primarily using descriptive statistics. The study aims to generate preliminary evidence regarding the feasibility, safety, and short- to intermediate-term outcomes of the Sasmal-FLARE technique and provide a basis for future larger clinical studies. The study has received approval from the Institutional Ethics Committee, AIIMS Bhubaneswar, effective October 27, 2026.
auteurs: All India Institute of Medical Sciences, Bhubaneswar

titre: A Parallel Study of Hypnotherapy and Dialectical Behavior Therapy for Emotional Wellbeing Among University Students With Migraine
resume: This study evaluated the effectiveness of hypnotherapy and Dialectical Behavior Therapy (DBT) in managing migraine symptoms and improving psychological wellbeing among university students diagnosed with migraine without aura. Migraine can interfere with academic activities, emotional functioning, stress management, and quality of life. A randomized, three-group, parallel-assignment study was conducted with 60 university students. Participants were assigned to hypnotherapy, DBT, or psychoeducation, with 20 participants in each group. Each group received six intervention sessions. Hypnotherapy focused on relaxation, guided imagery, pain management, and cognitive reframing. DBT focused on mindfulness, distress tolerance, emotion regulation, and interpersonal effectiveness. Psychoeducation provided information about migraine, stress, lifestyle modification, and coping strategies. Migraine frequency, migraine severity, migraine-related disability, perceived stress, emotional distress, and migraine-specific quality of life were assessed before and after the interventions. The study aimed to compare changes across the three groups and examine the potential usefulness of these psychological approaches for university students experiencing migraine.

titre: Mobile-based Preventive Digital Mental Health Intervention for Depression and Anxiety in Malaysian Adolescents and Young Adults
resume: Early symptoms of depression and anxiety often emerge during adolescence and young adulthood, yet stigma, limited access to services, and reluctance to seek professional help frequently delay support. This study evaluates DAYA, a self-guided, Malay-language digital intervention grounded in Cognitive Behavioural Therapy (CBT), designed to reduce depressive and anxiety symptoms and to improve functioning and psychological well-being among Malaysian adolescents and young adults aged 13 to 24 years. The intervention is delivered through a web-based platform accessible on any internet-enabled device and is completed independently, without direct professional involvement. The study is a randomised controlled trial conducted in two stages. A pilot trial first assesses the feasibility, usability, and acceptability of the intervention and study procedures. A main trial with new participants then compares DAYA with a waitlist control that receives standard health information. The primary outcomes are depressive and anxiety symptoms, and the secondary outcomes are functional impairment and psychological well-being.

titre: "Toujours Dimanche": A Nature-Based Mindfulness and Self-Compassion Meditation Program Delivered Through Immersive Virtual Reality During Hemodialysis. A Pilot Randomized Controlled Feasibility Trial
resume: The goal of this pilot clinical trial is to learn whether a virtual reality mindfulness and self-compassion program can be used during hemodialysis, whether patients find it acceptable, and whether it is safe. The study will include 26 adults who have received in-center hemodialysis for at least 3 months at Hôpital du Haut-Richelieu in Quebec, Canada. The program, called "Toujours Dimanche," combines guided meditation with videos and sounds of nature. Participants wear a virtual reality headset that makes them feel surrounded by natural landscapes. Mindfulness means paying attention to the present moment without judgment. Self-compassion means treating yourself with kindness during difficult experiences. The main questions are: Can researchers recruit patients, and can patients complete the planned virtual reality sessions? How do patients feel about the program, and how well does it fit into their dialysis treatments? Does the program cause unwanted effects, such as nausea, dizziness, or discomfort? Researchers will also collect information about anxiety, depression, stress, emotional well-being, physical symptoms, quality of life, and physical activity. This small pilot study is not designed to determine whether the program improves these outcomes. Its findings will help researchers plan a larger trial. Participants will be assigned by chance to one of two groups, with an equal chance of joining either group: Virtual reality group: Participants will use the headset during their regular hemodialysis treatments for 20 minutes, twice a week, for 16 weeks. Each session includes 10 minutes of guided meditation followed by 10 minutes of freely exploring the virtual nature setting. A research team member will help participants use the equipment and will be available during sessions. Comparison group: Participants will receive an educational brochure about caring for their mental health during hemodialysis. They will be offered free access to the virtual reality program after the study. Participants in both groups will: * Complete questionnaires before the program, around its midpoint, at its end, and about 10 weeks after it ends. * Wear a wrist-worn activity tracker to record their steps, including for 2 weeks before the program begins. After the final data collection, a sample of patients and nurses will take part in interviews to share their experiences with the program and suggest improvements before a larger study. The research team will ask participants in the virtual reality group about their comfort and emotional well-being before and after each session. The team will also monitor blood pressure and other unwanted effects during dialysis. Study participation will last about 28 to 34 weeks, including initial assessments, the 16-week program, and follow-up. Virtual reality sessions will take place during regular dialysis treatments and will not require extra trips. Researchers will compare the two groups to explore changes in the outcomes measured and assess how practical the study procedures are. They will also interview dialysis staff to understand how the program could fit into routine care.

resume: ARFID (Avoidant Restrictive Food Intake Disorder) is when a person eats only a small amount of food, or only a few types of food. titre: Pathophysiology of slow-transit constipation: from cellular mechanisms to personalized therapy
resume: Slow-transit constipation (STC) represents a severe and often refractory subtype of chronic constipation, defined by markedly prolonged colonic transit and a poor response to standard therapies. It is estimated to affect ∼15%-30% of patients with chronic constipation. Despite extensive investigation, its underlying pathogenesis has yet to be fully elucidated. In this review, we synthesized recent advances in the multidimensional pathophysiology of STC, encompassing dysfunction of the enteric and autonomic nervous systems, injury to interstitial cells of Cajal and smooth muscle, imbalances in neurotransmitter and hormonal signaling, gut microbiota dysbiosis, and low-grade inflammation, with an emphasis on how these factors interact to generate substantial inter-patient heterogeneity. Given the limited and often variable efficacy of existing treatments, there is an urgent need for mechanism-based, precision-targeted therapies. Emerging approaches, including neuromodulation, regenerative cell-based therapies, and microbiome modulation, have shown encouraging signals, although their efficacy and safety require confirmation in larger, well-designed clinical trials. Future research should integrate molecular omics with clinical phenotyping to stratify patients with STC and identify robust biomarkers, thereby guiding personalized interventions. Continued translational efforts are expected to bridge molecular insights with clinical practice, laying the groundwork for precise and durable therapies that ultimately improve outcomes and quality of life for individuals with STC.

titre: Cardiac PIEZO 1 Channels Modulate Anxiety
resume: BACKGROUND: Conscious cardiac interoception explains the ability of some individuals to "feel" their heartbeat without taking their pulse. Subconscious cardiac interoception detects heart signals from baroreceptors without subjective awareness. METHODS: We used photoplethysmography to determine if contrasting sensitivity of PIEZO 1 (human mechanosensitive stretch channels) mediates each form of cardiac interoception and feelings of anxiety. RESULTS: In healthy volunteers, conscious cardiac interoception was increased with lower heart rates and greater stroke volumes but not associated with anxiety. Disruption of Piezo 1 (rodent mechanosensitive stretch channel) in cardiac sensory neurons enhanced anxiety in rodents. PIEZO 1 sensitivity correlated inversely with state anxiety scores in men and women (r=-0.6495, P=0.0004, n=25). Cold pressor test-induced changes in cardiac work were greater in subjects with lower PIEZO 1 sensitivity when compared with subjects with higher PIEZO 1 sensitivity (values expressed as median percentage increase in rate pressure product, 27.6 [interquartile range, 19.2-35.8] versus 8.4 [interquartile range 0.38-19.13], P=0.0093). Those with lower anxiety also had enhanced coefficients of variation in their instantaneous baroreceptor gain at rest (values expressed as medians, 1.417 [interquartile range 0.8482-1.585] versus 0.7518 interquartile range [0.5947-0.8226], P=0.0082). CONCLUSIONS: We propose that a reduction in PIEZO 1 sensitivity causes errors in subconscious interoception and leads to anxiety and increased cardiac workloads. We also report testosterone, which is anxiolytic, enhanced, whereas the stress hormone corticosterone, decreased Piezo 1 gene transcription. Selectively enhancing subconscious interoception by increasing PIEZO 1 sensitivity may reduce anxiety and improve cardiovascular health outcomes.
revue: Journal of the American Heart Association

titre: ABORDAGEM LOW FODMAP NO MANEJO DA SÍNDROME DO INTESTINO IRRITÁVEL: UMA REVISÃO DA LITERATURA SOBRE EFEITOS, LIMITAÇÕES E INDIVIDUALIZAÇÃO NUTRICIONAL
resume: The irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) is a chronic gastrointestinal disorder associated with abdominal pain, bloating, and changes in bowel habits. This study aimed to analyze, through a literature review, the effectiveness and limitations of the low-FODMAP diet in managing IBS symptoms, considering dietary individualization. The studies analyzed indicate that the diet may help reduce symptoms in some individuals; however, responses vary, and prolonged restriction may reduce nutrient intake and affect components of the gut microbiota. It is concluded that the diet may be a useful strategy when implemented in stages, with food reintroduction and professional guidance, avoiding unnecessary restrictions.

titre: Dietary and Lifestyle Factors Associated with Irritable Bowel Syndrome among Egyptian Medical Students Using Rome IV Criteria: A Multicenter Cross-Sectional Study
resume: Background: Irritable Bowel Syndrome (IBS) is a multifactorial gastrointestinal disorder that has been associated with various dietary and lifestyle factors. Several studies have investigated IBS among medical students, including studies conducted in Egypt. The present study aimed to estimate the prevalence of IBS and examine its dietary and lifestyle correlates in a large multicenter sample of Egyptian medical students recruited from 28 universities across different regions of the country using the Rome IV criteria and a standardized dietary assessment tool. Methods: This study was a multi-center cross-sectional study involving 5883 Egyptian medical students and interns who completed a validated self-administered questionnaire assessing socio-demographic data, dietary habits, sleep patterns, and the Rome IV criteria for IBS. The study used a binary logistic regression model to examine factors independently associated with IBS, estimated as odds ratios (ORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Results: Among 5,883 medical students and interns, the prevalence of IBS was 39.9%. In the adjusted logistic regression model, increasing age was associated with higher odds of IBS . Higher fast-food consumption was also associated with increased odds of IBS: 1–3 times per week (adjusted OR = 1.238, 95% CI: 1.090–1.406) and ≥4 times per week (adjusted OR = 1.485, 95% CI: 1.243–1.774), compared with less than once per week. Food intolerance (adjusted OR = 2.953, 95% CI: 2.505–3.481) and medication use (adjusted OR = 1.815, 95% CI: 1.586–2.077) were also associated with higher odds of IBS. Conversely, male sex and regular sleep were associated with lower odds of IBS.
revue: Journal of High Institute of Public Health

Molecular Convergence of Periodontitis and Stroke: Shared Signaling Nodes Along the Oral–Gut–Brain Axis and Their Modulation by Probiotics and Antioxidants
resume: Periodontitis and stroke are prevalent chronic diseases managed by separate clinical disciplines, yet both involve microbial, inflammatory, and oxidative mechanisms. This structured narrative review, self-appraised with the Scale for the Assessment of Narrative Review Articles, examines whether periodontitis contributes to stroke and whether probiotics and antioxidants could interrupt it. A 2025 meta-analysis of 22 observational studies associated periodontitis with incident stroke (cohort relative risk 1.49), most clearly for ischemic stroke and in cohorts followed beyond ten years. Mendelian randomization did not support a causal effect on overall ischemic stroke. Because null genetic estimates cannot identify a mediating pathway, action through modifiable intermediate states, notably hypertension, is treated here as a hypothesis requiring direct testing. Six molecular nodes recur in periodontal and cerebrovascular systems: Toll-like receptor signaling, gingipain proteolysis of endothelial junctions, redox control of nitric oxide, nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2 (Nrf2) signaling, inflammasome-dependent interleukin-1β maturation, and ferroptosis. Documented in parallel experimental systems rather than in the same tissue, their convergence is a potential mechanism rather than an established one. In randomized trials, intensive periodontal therapy improved endothelial function and lowered blood pressure. A phase II trial after stroke or transient ischemic attack found no superiority of intensive over standard periodontal treatment for a composite of recurrent ischemic stroke, myocardial infarction, and cardiovascular death. Adjunctive probiotics and polyphenols produced only small periodontal gains. Because several polyphenols interact with the antithrombotic drugs that stroke survivors receive, we propose a tiered, risk-stratified framework. The evidence generates testable hypotheses but does not yet support routine clinical use.

titre: Fructooligosaccharides Beyond Conventional Prebiotic Effects: Immune and Gut–Brain Mechanisms, Bioprocessing, and Advanced Delivery Systems
resume: Fructooligosaccharides (FOS) are among the most extensively studied prebiotics, traditionally associated with bifidogenic effects and modulation of the intestinal microbiota. Emerging evidence suggests that their biological activities extend beyond conventional microbiota-centred explanations and involve interconnected immune, neuroactive, and metabolic pathways. This review critically examines recent advances in the biological mechanisms, bioprocessing, and translational applications of FOS. Particular attention is given to evidence linking FOS-mediated microbial changes with type 2 conventional dendritic cell responses, the aryl hydrocarbon receptor–interleukin-22 axis, and microbiota–gut–brain communication, including the production of neuroactive metabolites such as gamma-aminobutyric acid. The strength and limitations of the evidence are evaluated across in vitro, animal, and human studies, with emphasis on distinguishing direct FOS effects from findings obtained with related fermentable carbohydrates. Advances in FOS production and in situ recovery, together with their incorporation into hydrogels and nanoscale delivery systems for intestinal and colonic applications, are also assessed. By connecting molecular mechanisms with bioprocess design and delivery technologies, this review identifies evidence gaps and priorities for developing tailored FOS preparations for precision nutrition and intestinally targeted biomedical applications.

titre: Synbiotic Formulations with Lactic Acid Bacteria to Modulate GLP-1/PYY Pathways in Obesity
resume: Obesity is an escalating global public-health challenge, closely linked to gut-microbiota dysbiosis and disruption of the gut–brain axis. Intestinal L cells secrete the incretins GLP-1 and PYY, which suppress appetite, slow gastric emptying, and improve glucose–insulin balance. Their activity is strongly modulated by short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs-acetate, propionate, butyrate) generated by fiber fermentation. Via FFAR2/FFAR3 receptors, SCFAs increase GLP-1/PYY secretion, strengthen the intestinal barrier, and dampen low-grade inflammation, enhancing insulin sensitivity and weight control. Growing evidence shows that SCFA-producing probiotics (e.g., Bifidobacterium animalis, Clostridium butyricum, Butyricimonas virosa), fermentable prebiotics (inulin/FOS), and polyphenols can synergistically potentiate this pathway. Polyphenols act through two routes: direct activation of L cells (taste/GPCR signaling) and indirect promotion of SCFA production by reshaping the microbiota. This review examines the potential for developing a functional symbiotic, combining SCFAs producing strains with an appropriate prebiotic and bioactive polyphenols as a natural strategy to enhance appetite regulation, glycemic control, and energy homeostasis through modulation of the GLP-1/PYY pathway. Keywords: GLP-1, short-chain fatty acids, obesity, probiotics, satiety hormone regulation

titre: Malabsorption Syndrome and Xerostomia: Nutritional Deficiencies, Salivary Gland Dysfunction, Neuroimmune Mechanisms, and the Gut–Salivary Axis
resume: BACKGROUND Malabsorption syndrome encompasses a heterogeneous group of gastrointestinal disorders characterized by impaired digestion or intestinal absorption of nutrients, potentially resulting in systemic nutritional deficiencies, metabolic disturbances, and extraintestinal manifestations. Xerostomia, defined as the subjective sensation of oral dryness, may occur with or without objectively reduced salivary flow (hyposalivation) and can substantially affect oral comfort, swallowing, speech, taste perception, and quality of life. Although malabsorption syndrome and xerostomia have not been established as directly causally related conditions, several potentially relevant biological pathways may connect intestinal dysfunction with oral and salivary abnormalities. Deficiencies of vitamins, minerals, and proteins may compromise oral epithelial integrity, tissue maintenance, and immune function, while systemic inflammation and autoimmune mechanisms may contribute to salivary gland dysfunction. In addition, alterations in intestinal microbiota, epithelial barrier function, and neuroautonomic regulation may influence systemic immune and physiological processes involved in salivary secretion. The proposed gut–salivary axis offers an emerging conceptual framework for investigating these interactions. Understanding these potential relationships may improve the recognition of oral manifestations in patients with gastrointestinal disorders and support further research into the mechanisms linking intestinal malabsorption and xerostomia.
revue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

titre: Early Adaptive Withdrawal: Reframing 18-Month Autistic Regression and Adult Somatic Transitions as Lifespan Resource Optimization
resume: This conceptual paper proposes that 18-month autistic regression ("First Regression") represents an early adaptive resource-optimization capacity triggered by somatic, interoceptive, and environmental overload, predicting favorable long-term developmental trajectories once bodily regulation is achieved. Drawing on multi-generational autistic observation across both sexes, it extends this same adaptive energy-conservation mechanism to somatic suffering and transitions across the lifespan—including acute illness in childhood or adolescence, painful postoperative states (situational mutism/shutdown), motherhood, menopause, and aging—while upholding strict third-party privacy.
revue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

titre: DCBRA: Divinely Created Biological Regulatory Architecture — A Proposed Event-Level Functional Coding and Evidence-Tracing Framework for Biological Regulation (Version 2.1)
resume: Background: Biological regulation involves interacting molecular, cellular, tissue, organ and organism-level processes. Homeostasis, allostasis, interoception, systems biology and biological control theory already describe important aspects of sensing, signaling, integration, response and feedback. Objective: To present the Divinely Created Biological Regulatory Architecture (DCBRA) as a proposed event-level functional coding and evidence-tracing framework for organizing selected biological regulatory events across domains. Framework: DCBRA uses five functional categories: Recognition (REC), Signal Transmission (SIG), Integration (INT), Activation (ACT), and Regulation and Feedback (REG). They are analytical categories, not a mandatory linear sequence. Methods: This manuscript provides a conceptual comparison with established frameworks, illustrative mappings for glucose-stimulated insulin secretion and acute wound repair, an evidence-status system (D, I, H, NE, NA, A0), a preliminary literature mapping structure, and a protocol for independent coding and reliability assessment. Results: No new experimental results are reported. The five functions overlap with established biological concepts. The proposed methodological contribution is the combination of event-level functional coding, separate evidence and mapping statuses, source traceability, contextual biological-scale annotation, and structured disagreement analysis. Conclusion: DCBRA is a proposed analytical framework, not an established biological law or newly demonstrated mechanism. Its value must be assessed through independent reproducibility, comparative performance and evidence of incremental research utility.
revue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

titre: What We Know About Psychotherapies
resume: What We Know About Psychotherapies is a plain-language booklet with evidence summaries for mental health professionals, patients, and policymakers. How well does therapy work, and for whom? What makes therapies work, and what makes a good therapist? In short essays, Pim Cuijpers answers questions that patients and clinicians often ask, based on what meta-analytic research tells us about psychological treatments. The knowledge draws mainly on the collective work of the Metapsy collaboration over at least 15 years. The texts were first published as evidence summaries on the Metapsy patient portal and are collected here as a printable first edition (2026). What’s inside Fundamentals — Does psychotherapy work? Placebo effects, alliance, digital tools, AI, and whether benefits are exaggerated What to expect — Negative effects, when evidence-based care still fails, and broader life outcomes Choosing a treatment — Medication vs psychotherapy, CBT, brief vs long-term care, finding a good therapist, severe depression, and more Special populations — Older adults, adolescents, and partners who do not want treatment Next steps — When therapy does not seem to work, and “treatment-resistant” depression In total, the booklet brings together 32 evidence summaries. titre: Beyond body image: Environmental factors in feeding and eating disorders, with a focus on ARFID, and an LLM-assisted protocol for early recognition and referral
resume: AbstractPublic debate on young people, social media and eating is framed almost entirely around body image. Avoidant/restrictive food intake disorder (ARFID), added to the diagnostic manuals in 2013, falls outside that frame by definition: restriction is driven by sensory sensitivity, fear of aversive consequences such as choking or vomiting, or low interest in food, not by concern about weight or shape. This open, evidence-graded book examines the environmental conditions in which feeding and eating disorders arise in adolescence, with a focus on ARFID. It combines an academic essay, a practical guide for health and education professionals and an interactive toolkit. Part I reviews prevalence and how it is measured, the family of related disorders and the groups at elevated risk, and the interplay between genetic liability and environments. Part II turns to digital environments. A dated bibliometric check finds only 14 PubMed records combining ARFID with social-media terms, and seven candidate digital pathways are graded in an evidence-gap map. The book then sets out a protocol in which a large language model acts as a scribe rather than a judge: fixed rules decide urgency, observations are organised by dimension without scores, a second model audits each draft, and an evaluation with synthetic vignettes and pre-registered criteria is specified before any claim of effectiveness. The toolkit implements a base-rate (positive predictive value) simulator and a referral-note prompt composer in English and Spanish, and a bilingual page offers guidance to anyone who is worried. The book does not provide diagnosis. Version 0.9 is a pre-review edition: it has not yet been peer reviewed, and the toolkit has not yet been evaluated. Online edition: https://arfid26.vercel.app/ (canonical), with mirrors on GitHub Pages, Netlify and Cloudflare. This archive contains the rendered edition and the Quarto and R source files.
revue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

titre: HBRAN Stage 20: the five disorders of thinking as lesions of a trained pipeline, measured with the MTSR metrics
resume: Summary: Registered test of the five metrics of "Measuring Temporal Self-Reference" (TMI peak, recurrence density, half-life, effective dimensionality, SNR; EEG test registered as OSF 10.17605/OSF.IO/C5GJF) in a system whose self-referential loop is known: the eight registered pipelines of HBRAN configuration K (Stage 15) are run over their texts intact and under five lesions of the recurrent state built from the paper's characterisations (noise in blocks = delirium; half the workspace silenced = dementia; leak = ADHD; inertia = OCD; random self-model feedback = schizophrenia), all at strength 0.5. Predictions L1-L5: each lesion's observed signature matches its predicted signature (cosine above a sign-flip null), is closest to its own among the five, and moves its defining metric in the predicted direction in at least 7 of 8 pipelines; L6: at least 4 of 5 recovered. A test of the instrument and the pattern logic, not of the disorders. A pilot measured only task cost (stated in the PDF); no metric was computed on a lesioned trained pipeline before registration. Attached: registration PDF and manifest with SHA-256 hashes. Foreknowledge: Data does not yet exist (no lesioned trained pipeline has been measured with these metrics). titre: Ground-truth benchmarking of signed, directed lagged connectivity: TemporalSignedMBB from a simulated gut-br​ain model to neural data
resume: Methods inferring signed, directed, window-specific connectivity are rarely tested against a known answer. We benchmarked TemporalSignedMBB, which combines Gaussian conditional transfer entropy, tracking of edge-sign transitions, persistent homology and a Laplacian perturbation score, against planted ground truth: independent replications of a gut-brain model of depression, an inferential null, seven misspecified generators, heterogeneous subject-specific couplings and a Wilson-Cowan neural-mass model. Under correct latent specification, transfer entropy recovered planted directed couplings with precision 0.91 and recall 0.67 to 0.91; detected edges had correct signs in over 99.9% of cases. A cluster-robust edge test was calibrated under the null, but the realized false discovery rate was 0.09 at nominal 0.05, owing to subject-demeaning bias in short panels. Sign tracking detected 76% of true reversals with 5 false reversals in 180 network comparisons. Lag mismatch, saturating or abundance-scale coupling and latent drivers lowered recall to 0.46 or raised false discoveries to 0.19. Persistent homology missed planted directed loops that a directed cycle count detected, and the perturbation score did not predict perturbation responses. Individual networks recovered subject-specific couplings poorly, and with matched learners, network features gave case-control AUROCs of 0.56 to 0.59, against 0.97 to 0.98 for abundance features exploiting planted mean shifts, and 0.56 to 0.58 when groups differed only in coupling. In the neural-mass model, excitatory and inhibitory signs were recovered with an adequate lag order but not under volume conduction or hemodynamic observation. The results support group-level transfer entropy and sign tracking under favorable conditions, not the complete framework.

titre: IBS BAG
resume: The IBS BAG includes teams from IBS (Grenoble) and external groups from CEA-Cadarache (St Paul lez Durance), CEA-Grenoble, CERMAV (Grenoble) et IRBA (Brétigny-sur-Orge). We study the structure-function relationships of proteins and biological macromolecular complexes with a focus on human health, biotechnology and methodology. Most of the projects are a continuation of the MX-2686 proposal and can be grouped under the following themes: host-pathogen interaction, new therapeutic targets, fundamental cellular mechanisms, membrane proteins, biotechnological applications and methodology. Some of these projects use integrative approaches (X-ray crystallography, cryo-EM, SAXS and NMR) together with other biophysical and biochemical studies and, more recently, the use of AI (e.g. AlphaFold, Chai-1) to fully understand the complexity of the biological systems under study.

titre: Weitai’an Alleviates Functional Dyspepsia-like Phenotypes in Mice: An Exploratory Multi-Omics Analysis of the Microbiota–Metabolite–Gene Network
resume: Background/Objectives: Weitai’an (WTA), a modified Sijunzi Decoction-based formulation, is clinically used for functional dyspepsia (FD) with liver depression and spleen deficiency, but its mechanisms remain unclear. This study aimed to evaluate the efficacy of WTA in an FD-like mouse model and to explore its potential mechanisms using multi-omics approaches. Methods: Five groups of C57BL/6J mice (control, model, WTA-L (3.198 g/kg), WTA-H (6.396 g/kg), domperidone) were studied. Therapeutic effects were assessed by gastric residual rate, intestinal propulsion rate, behavioral tests, histopathology, serum gastrin levels, and gastric IL-1β mRNA expression. Multi-omics analyses, including 16S rRNA sequencing, serum metabolomics, and gastric transcriptomics, were employed to identify key pathways and potential associations. Results: WTA significantly improved gastrointestinal motility, reduced mucosal inflammation, ameliorated mucosal damage, and alleviated depressive-like behaviors. Exploratory multi-omics analysis indicated that WTA treatment was associated with multi-level alterations. Specifically, it was associated with changes in gut microbiota, including the enrichment of Lachnospiraceae and Faecalibaculum. It also correlated with shifts in serum metabolic profiles, particularly the enrichment of amino acid and energy metabolism pathways such as glutamate metabolism and the TCA cycle. Furthermore, WTA treatment was associated with the modulation of gastric transcriptional disturbances related to circadian rhythm, oxidative phosphorylation, and inflammation. Integrated analysis further suggested potential associations between specific gut genera and glutamate metabolism. In vitro experiments showed that WTA-containing serum and several specific absorbed compounds exerted selective inhibitory effects on LPS-induced cytokine expression in GES-1 cells. Conclusions: This study provides preliminary evidence that WTA alleviated FD-like phenotypes in mice, which was associated with the modulation of the microbiota–metabolite–gene network. These findings offer exploratory insights into the multi-target therapeutic actions of WTA in FD-like phenotypes and provide a scientific basis for its further clinical investigation.

titre: Estudio Comparado de Regímenes Fiscales Favorables al Sector de las Micro, Pequeñas y Medianas Empresas en Latinoamérica
resume: Este trabajo compara los regímenes fiscales simplificados dirigidos a las micro, pequeñas y medianas empresas (MIPYMES) en seis países latinoamericanos México, Colombia, Argentina, Brasil, Chile y, como referencias complementarias, Ecuador y Perú con énfasis en el Régimen Simplificado de Confianza (RESICO) mexicano. Mediante un enfoque documental-comparado se analizan variables macroeconómicas (informalidad laboral, presión fiscal, apertura comercial), el diseño normativo de cada régimen y un caso hipotético de una microempresa ("Cafetería Ruta 90") replicado bajo las reglas de cada país. Los resultados muestran que la carga fiscal efectiva de una microempresa comparable oscila entre 1.1% (Monotributo argentino) y 6.0% (Simples Nacional brasileño) de las ventas anuales, y que la simplicidad normativa por sí sola no garantiza permanencia en la formalidad si no se acompaña de seguridad social, progresividad gradual y acompañamiento digital. Se incorpora evidencia hasta septiembre de 2026, incluida la propuesta de reforma a RESICO contenida en el Paquete Económico 2026-2027 y la transición de Brasil hacia el IVA dual (IBS/CBS). El estudio concluye con recomendaciones de política fiscal para México y señala líneas de investigación futura.

fiche.intervention: Comparaison des régimes fiscaux simplifiés (RESICO, Monotributo, etc.)

fiche.conclusion: La simplicité fiscale seule ne garantit pas la formalisation sans sécurité sociale et accompagnement digital.

titre: Cefazolin Versus Alternative Antimicrobial Prophylaxis for Upper Gastrointestinal and Hepatobiliary Surgery: A Multicenter Retrospective Cohort Study Spanning the Cefazolin Shortage
resume: Background/Objectives: Cefazolin is recommended as the standard surgical antimicrobial prophylaxis for several upper gastrointestinal and hepatobiliary procedures. However, the 2019 nationwide cefazolin shortage in Japan created an externally driven shift from cefazolin to alternative agents, thereby providing an opportunity to examine the clinical consequences of such substitution in routine practice. Herein, we evaluated whether antibiotic substitution was associated with surgical site infection (SSI) incidence compared with cefazolin. Methods: This multicenter retrospective cohort study included adults who underwent cholecystectomy, gastrectomy, esophagectomy, or hepatectomy between February 2018 and June 2020. The primary outcome was SSI within 30 days postoperatively. The association between prophylactic antibiotic regimen and SSI was assessed using multivariable logistic regression, adjusting for patient-, procedure-, calendar period-, and institution-related factors. Results: Among 3259 patients, 2218 and 1041 received cefazolin and alternative antibiotics, with SSIs occurring in 127 (5.7%) and 61 (5.9%) patients, respectively. Among the 3210 patients in the primary multivariable analysis, alternative prophylaxis showed no significant associations with SSI compared with cefazolin (adjusted OR, 1.06; 95% CI, 0.74–1.52; p = 0.735). Further, there was no statistically significant evidence of effect modification by calendar period (p for interaction = 0.165). Clostridioides difficile infection and antibiotic-related allergic events were uncommon in both groups. Conclusions: Alternative prophylactic antibiotics were not significantly associated with SSI incidence compared with cefazolin in the upper gastrointestinal and hepatobiliary procedures for which cefazolin is the standard prophylaxis. These findings may inform procedure-specific contingency planning during future antimicrobial supply disruptions while supporting avoidance of unnecessary broadening of prophylaxis under usual supply conditions.

titre: Novel light shed on the cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic syndrome
resume: For the podcast associated with this article, please visit https://academic.oup.com/eurheartj/pages/Podcasts. This Focus Issue on Diabetes and metabolic disorders starts with a Special Article entitled ‘Novel cardiovascular metabolic risk factor mechanisms and therapeutic opportunities: a scientific statement of the ESC Council on Basic Cardiovascular Science, the ESC Working Group on Atherosclerosis and Vascular Biology, the ESC Working Group on Cellular Biology of the Heart, the ESC Working Group on Myocardial Function, and the ESC Working Group on Cardiac Cellular Electrophysiology’, by Paul Evans from Queen Mary University of London, UK, and colleagues. The authors aim to categorize and delineate the mechanisms that link metabolic disorders with cardiovascular (CV) risk.1 Metabolic disorders such as obesity, type 2 diabetes, and dyslipidaemia are major drivers of CV risk and have reached epidemic levels in Western populations.2–9 Recent advances in clinical research have uncovered unexpected and often beneficial effects of pharmacological classes of metabolic drugs on CV outcomes, revealing complex interactions between metabolism and cardiac pathology. Despite their clinical efficacy, the molecular and cellular mechanisms through which many of these agents act remain only partially understood. This gap in knowledge underscores the urgent need for fundamental research that not only dissects the biology of metabolic disorders and CV disease (CVD) but also reveals the mechanistic basis of existing and emerging therapies, thereby enabling rational therapeutic development. This scientific statement, developed by researchers from the European Society of Cardiology (ESC) Council on Basic Cardiovascular Science and several ESC Working Groups, provides a state-of-the-art overview of the emerging molecular and cellular pathways linking metabolic abnormalities with vascular and cardiac disease. By illuminating these critical connections and unresolved questions, this article aims to catalyse innovation in the prevention and management of CVD in the context of metabolic dysfunction and to suggest new directions for future research. Diabetes and heart failure (HF) are closely intertwined, with diabetes increasing the risk for all forms of HF, i.e. HF with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF), as well as HF with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF), and vice versa. Approximately one-third of patients with diabetes suffer from HF, and a similar number of HF patients are affected by diabetes or at least by dysglycaemia. In a Great Debate article entitled ‘Great debate: diabetic cardiomyopathy is a distinct disease’ Petar Seferovic from University Belgrade, Serbia, and colleagues aim to evaluate whether diabetic cardiomyopathy (DCM) is a distinct disease entity, separate from other causes of myocardial dysfunction, through a Pro–Con debate examining the available scientific evidence.10 The European Society of Cardiology (ESC) Guidelines for the management of CVD in patients with diabetes as well as the ESC Guidelines for the management of HF recommend a proactive search for HF in patients with diabetes and vice versa. The term ‘diabetic cardiomyopathy’ still receives a lot of attention, despite the lack of a clear definition and uncertainty about whether such an entity exists. In the ESC Guidelines for the management of cardiomyopathies, a cardiomyopathy is defined as ‘a myocardial disorder in which the heart muscle is structurally and functionally abnormal, in the absence of coronary artery disease, hypertension, valvular disease, and congenital heart disease sufficient to cause the observed myocardial abnormality’. Diabetic cardiomyopathy is not mentioned as an entity there. The consensus statement of the Heart Failure Association of the ESC and the ESC Working Group on Myocardial and Pericardial Diseases proposed a definition, whereby ‘diabetic myocardial disorder’ is defined as systolic and/or diastolic myocardial dysfunction in the presence of diabetes. Thus, the current Great Debate ‘Diabetic cardiomyopathy is a distinct disease’ with the Pro and Contra written by top experts in the field is timely and important to all physicians involved in the treatment of patients with diabetes. A review of recent literature reveals considerable variability in the terminology used to describe the adipose tissue (AT) depots. Terms such as intrathoracic, paracardial, pericardial, mediastinal, epicardial, and cardiac AT have been applied inconsistently and are often used interchangeably, despite not always referring to the same AT depot. In a Viewpoint article entitled ‘Epicardial and pericardial adipose tissue: a plea for standardized definitions and assessment’ Michelle Lobeek, Jeroen van Vugt, and Thomas Gorter from the University of Groningen, The Netherlands, propose the use of the terms epicardial and pericardial adipose tissue (AT) when referring to AT depots in proximity to the heart.11 In recent years, increasing attention has been given to the specific fat depots surrounding the heart, which are suggested to exert direct effects on cardiac structure and function. However, a lack of consistency in the terminology used to describe these depots hinders the clarity and comparability of research in this field. In this viewpoint, the authors argue for the consistent use of the terms epicardial adipose tissue (EAT) and pericardial adipose tissue (PAT), and offer the rationale for this terminology. They believe that standardised terminology will facilitate clearer communication and enhance comparability across studies. This perspective is particularly timely given the expanding body of literature on EAT and PAT and the growing interest in its clinical relevance. The epidemiological and pathophysiological links between obesity, type 2 diabetes, CVD, and chronic kidney disease (CKD) have been recognized for decades.8,12–16 However, the emergence of therapies that simultaneously target multiple aspects of these interconnected conditions has catalyzed a shift in clinical thinking. In a Viewpoint article entitled ‘Randomized trials in cardiovascular, kidney, and metabolic diseases: rethinking late-phase drug development’ Brendon Neuen, Hiddo Heerspink, and Muthiah Vaduganathan from the University of New South Wales in Sydney, Australia, University Medical Center Groningen, The Netherlands, and Harvard Medical School, Boston, MA (USA), propose innovative late-phase clinical trial designs.17 By leveraging novel trial designs that enrol overlapping patient populations, they propose a more integrated approach to clinical research that better reflects real-world disease overlap and opportunities to address systemic drivers of cardiometabolic disease. As the prevalence of multimorbidity rises, traditional trial paradigms—where investigational therapies are tested in distinct, single-disease populations—may be limiting the full realization of therapeutic potential. They argue that novel trial designs, including basket trials that enrol overlapping patient populations, could optimize the efficiency and rigor of evidence generation. By rethinking trial methodology to better reflect real-world disease overlap, the authors propose a framework that aligns with the broader goals of integrating trials into clinical practice. No tools are available for identifying patients with CKD and type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) at high risk of hyperkalaemia. Using the FIDELITY pooled patient data set, a risk model for incident hyperkalaemia was developed and validated. In a Clinical Research article entitled ‘Incident hyperkalaemia risk model in chronic kidney disease and diabetes: the FIDELITY programme’ João Pedro Ferreira from Porto University, Portugal, and colleagues aim to develop an easy-to-implement risk model for incident hyperkalaemia in patients with CKD and T2DM and analyse the efficacy and safety of finerenone across patients with varying levels of hyperkalaemia risk.18 The primary outcome was new-onset hyperkalaemia (serum potassium >5.5 mmol/L). Data from the placebo arm were used for derivation and from the finerenone arm for validation. An integer risk score was built and divided into low-, intermediate-, and high-risk hyperkalaemia categories. Assessed efficacy outcomes included CV and kidney composites. Seven baseline covariates (serum potassium >4.5 mmol/L, prior history of hyperkalaemia, no sodium–glucose co-transporter-2 inhibitor use, urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio >1000 mg/g, haemoglobin 2 million adults with T2DM who underwent health examinations between 2015 and 2016, sourced from the Korean National Health Insurance Service database. Participants were classified by body mass index into underweight, normal weight, overweight, and obesity, with underweight further stratified into mild, moderate, and severe. Primary outcomes were CVDs, including myocardial infarction and ischaemic stroke, assessed using Cox proportional hazards models adjusted for demographic, clinical, and lifestyle factors. During a mean follow-up of 5.7 years, 111 522 CVD events, were documented. Compared with the normal weight group, all underweight groups showed significantly higher CVD risks (adjusted hazard ratio 1.49, 1.47, and 1.19 for severe, moderate, and mild underweight, respectively). These risks exceeded those for body mass index ≥35 kg/m2 (1.14), showing a reverse J-shaped association. Stratified analyses indicated stronger associations in younger individuals and non-smokers (Figure 2). Association between body mass index and cardiovascular risk in patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus from a nationwide cohort study focusing on underweight status. BMI, body mass index; CVD, cardiovascular disease; MI, myocardial infarction; CI, confidence interval; aHR, adjusted hazard ratio.4 The authors conclude that underweight status in T2DM patients is significantly associated with increased risk of CVDs, particularly in those severely underweight, exceeding the risks observed with obesity. These findings emphasize the need for dedicated guidelines for managing underweight T2DM patients in order to mitigate CV risks. The manuscript is accompanied by an Editorial by Joshua Barzilay from Kaiser Permanente of Georgia, Atlanta, GA (USA).22 The author notes that underweight in individuals with diabetes is an amalgamation of many types of disorders and pathological processes that can interact with the CV system. Some of these mechanisms may be related to metabolic derangements in the muscle and adipose tissue. Other factors not directly related to diabetes, muscle, and adipose tissue, such as poverty, smoking, eating disorders (e.g. anorexia nervosa), depression, dementia, cancer, liver and gastrointestinal diseases, chronic infections, and an overactive thyroid, can also be present to initiate and propagate weight loss. Regardless of the mechanism(s), the reader should be aware that low body weight carries an elevated risk of CVD. In the SELECT trial, subcutaneous semaglutide (target dose 2.4 mg) weekly in adults with pre-existing CVD and body mass index ≥27 kg/m2 without diabetes significantly reduced major adverse CV events (MACE) by 20% vs placebo. This analysis explored potential mediators of this CV benefit. titre: Premetric Affective Modulation Beyond Emotion: Constitutive Modulation and the Failure of Affect-Emotion Identity
resume: This paper reconstructs a basal affective architecture at a level prior to scalar valence, semantic labeling, conscious feeling, and one universal biological mechanism. PremetricConstitutiveValuation is defined as non-metric classification of typed relational contexts by their consequences for a declared constitutive continuation burden. The object is relational and claim-indexed: the scientific content lies in how a context bears on continuation rather than in a numerical value assumed to belong intrinsically to the state. PremetricAffectiveModulation is the stronger active architecture. It requires a typed relational context to change continuation-relevant transition admissibility, selection, stabilization, degradation, or failure direction at the declared system and grain. Classification, readout, prediction, or correlation without transition change remains outside the modulation object, while transition change unrelated to the declared continuation burden remains generic dynamics rather than PremetricAffectiveModulation. The paper establishes PremetricAffectiveModulationEmotionNonIdentityTheorem through a claim-relative separating construction. PremetricAffectiveModulation can close under its own continuation and transition burden while HostRelativeEmotionQualification has not closed for the same claim. At that scientific claim state EmotionArchitectureFamily membership is unassigned, so PremetricAffectiveModulation closure is insufficient for assignment of Emotion membership. This result does not convert unclosed qualification into ontic absence of Emotion from the host. A second boundary concerns universal parentage. The host-relative Emotion family permits host-native mechanism and differential plurality and does not entail one universal PremetricAffectiveModulation mechanism as a necessary parent of every independently qualified member. This is a non-entailment result rather than an empirical assertion that a particular qualified Emotion case has been demonstrated with PAM absent. Local overlap, causal participation, and recurrent biological mechanisms remain fully admissible. The phrase “Beyond Emotion” therefore denotes extension beyond the surface of already closed Emotion qualification rather than universal set containment. PremetricAffectiveModulation may coincide with HostNativeAffectiveBasis in particular claims, but no such coincidence creates universal identity between the two offices. The architecture preserves host-specific mechanism research while keeping scientific status, realization, and parentage separately typed. Interoception, core affect, homeostatic regulation, survival circuitry, component-process organization, response-system coherence, and dynamic biological patterning remain external scientific neighbors. They can realize, constrain, measure, or elaborate the architecture in particular hosts. Contemporary interoception and dynamic-emotion research strengthens the importance of context-sensitive bodily and neural modulation while leaving the generic constitutive identity of PremetricAffectiveModulation independently defined. Consciousness, Feeling, semantic appraisal, and explicit labels are not generic prerequisites. PremetricAffectiveModulation can be evaluated in hosts or grains where conscious access is absent or unresolved, while emotional Feeling can be studied downstream under its own transduction burden. Metric, semantic, phenomenological, or biological enrichment is therefore compatible with the premetric architecture when it is added as a host-specific specialization rather than retroactively imposed as the generic definition. The public Emotion-series parents are Non-Derivability of a Universal Emotion Criterion from the Current Affective Discriminant Grammar: Necessity, Sufficiency, and Host-Diversity Countermodels and Host-Relative Emotion Qualification: Host-Native Differentials, Same-Host Contrast, Alternative Explanations, and Non-Transfer. They supply the bounded negative criterion result and the positive host-relative Emotion comparator respectively. Lawhood Before Laws: Invariance, Admissibility, and Regime Transformation is consumed conditionally for declared-domain and status discipline. The maximum public result is a machine-reconstructible distinction among premetric relational valuation, active continuation-relevant modulation, and host-relative Emotion membership. The paper closes generic non-identity without universal parentage while making no stronger claim about one universal biological affect mechanism, scalar valence, interoception, homeostasis, survival circuitry, Consciousness, Feeling, cross-host realization. The separation remains compatible with later host-specific mechanistic enrichment.
revue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

fiche.verdict: Article théorique conceptualisant la modulation affective prémétrique et séparant formellement l'architecture affective de base de la qualification d'émotion.
resultats_cles: Définition de la valence prémétrique constitutive comme classification non métrique de contextes relationnels.
Démonstration théorique d'une non-identité entre modulation affective prémétrique et émotion.
Compatibilité de l'architecture avec l'intéroception et l'affect fondamental sans réduire l'émotion à un mécanisme universel unique.

titre: Emotion as a Host-Relative Architecture Family: Generic Non-Derivability, Qualification, and Relations to Affect, Consciousness, and Feeling
resume: This paper establishes the public synthesis architecture for Emotion at the current generic scope. It begins with a target-blind question: whether a host-general necessary-and-sufficient criterion can be derived across declared host diversity without treating human taxonomy, report, feeling, physiology, or a host-specific Emotion label as constitutive evidence. EmotionDiscriminantGrammar supplies the bounded candidate surface; no tested route yields the required generic criterion. The negative result is explicitly grammar-bounded. It does not establish metaphysical impossibility of a future invariant and preserves a prospective reopen condition for a genuinely new discriminant whose constitutive content lies outside the current grammar. The paper therefore distinguishes failure of the present universal-criterion route from failure of Emotion science itself and uses the negative result to motivate a positive host-relative qualification architecture. EmotionArchitectureFamily is presented as the family architecture whose candidate members enter only through independently closed HostRelativeEmotionQualification at declared host, grain, domain, candidate, contrast, differential, and evaluation coordinates. Qualification requires a predeclared host-native differential and a destructive same-host alternative-explanation audit. EmotionQualificationNonTransferRule prevents an established qualification from migrating automatically across hosts, bearers, grains, scales, species, collectives, substrates, or realization maps. The synthesis separates Emotion from neighboring offices that frequently co-occur in biological and human cases. PremetricAffectiveModulation is a distinct relation-conditioned constitutive-modulation office that can close in claims for which HostRelativeEmotionQualification has not closed, while qualified Emotion is not universally reducible to one PremetricAffectiveModulation mechanism. The relation is therefore one of generic non-identity without universal parentage rather than universal containment. A conscious relation-dependent self-state change forms a conditional specialization rather than the generic definition of Emotion. DomainRelativeConsciousSelfStateDelta requires the conscious relational branch and same-bearer discipline; stronger DomainRelativeEmotionDelta status additionally requires HostRelativeEmotionQualification. Consciousness therefore remains branch-local: it can be essential to a declared conscious self-state Emotion claim without becoming a prerequisite of every member of EmotionArchitectureFamily. Emotional Feeling is placed downstream of an already qualified Emotion delta. ConditionedEmotionalFeelingTransduction relates a qualified DomainRelativeEmotionDelta, under a declared FeelingTransductionCondition, to EmotionalFeelingResponse while preserving host- and condition-specific variation. ExactFeelingTransductionFunction remains OPEN / SYSTEM-SPECIFIC. Feeling report, peripheral physiology, interoception, representation, readout, and semantic label may support attribution or mechanism studies but cannot retroactively create upstream Emotion qualification. The architecture is compatible with mechanism plurality and with several contemporary research neighborhoods. Constructionist, basic and evolutionary, dimensional, component-process, interoceptive, comparative, semantic-space, and dynamic biological approaches are treated as scientific comparators, mechanisms, evidence classes, or host-specific hypotheses rather than as authorities that define the generic target by affiliation. The paper therefore supports comparative integration while preserving office separation and host-relative burden. Public parentage is bounded. The Consciousness papers Bearer-Relative Presence and the Minimal Constitutive Relation of Consciousness: Necessity, Sufficiency, and Irreducibility, Conscious Content and Conscious Occurrence: Content Optionality and Relational Specialization, and Bearer-Specific Consciousness: Reinstantiation, Non-Transfer, Grain, Composition, and Continuity supply only the already closed results needed by the branch-local conscious specialization. The maximum public result is a machine-reconstructible host-relative Emotion architecture with bounded generic non-derivability, explicit member-level qualification, non-transfer, non-identity boundaries for affective modulation, branch-local Consciousness, conditioned downstream emotional Feeling, and an open exact Feeling-transduction function. The paper introduces no new theorem authority beyond the specialized series controls and makes no stronger claim about one universal mechanism, substrate, taxonomy, phenomenology, biological realization, cross-host transfer.
revue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

fiche.verdict: Modèle théorique formalisant l'émotion comme une famille d'architectures relative à l'hôte, indépendante d'un critère universel unique.
resultats_cles: Impossibilité de dériver un critère d'émotion universel et unique valable pour tous les hôtes.

titre: Conditioned Emotional Feeling as Downstream Realization: Transduction from Qualified Emotion Deltas and System-Specific Feeling Functions
resume: This paper defines a generic scientific architecture for emotional Feeling only after upstream Emotion status has independently closed. DomainRelativeEmotionDelta is the qualified input. FeelingTransductionCondition declares the host-, system-, state-, contextual-, environmental-, recent-history-, support-, and other claim-relevant variables under which downstream realization is evaluated. ConditionedEmotionalFeelingTransduction then relates that qualified input, under the declared condition, to EmotionalFeelingResponse without specifying one universal exact mechanism. EmotionalFeelingResponse is a provenance-indexed downstream response-class primitive. Its emotional status derives from conditioned downstream realization of a qualified DomainRelativeEmotionDelta, not from an ordinary-language Feeling label. Positive attribution requires a host-specific response criterion. The paper does not derive a universal constitutive definition of Feeling and does not assign ConsciousOccurrence, ConsciousContentRelation, ConsciousRelationalRealization, or conscious access merely because a response is described as felt. Three comparative transduction classes make condition dependence testable. EmotionalFeelingTransmissionAttenuation records a reduced or weak response for an equivalent or matched upstream Emotion delta under one declared condition relative to another. EmotionalFeelingTransmissionAmplification records the corresponding enhanced response. EmotionalFeelingTransmissionFailure records a non-null qualified Emotion delta that yields no discriminable EmotionalFeelingResponse under the active criterion and condition. Condition sensitivity is distinguished from mapping non-injectivity. When a matched DomainRelativeEmotionDelta yields different responses under different FeelingTransductionCondition values, the full exact-function input has changed. The result therefore demonstrates condition sensitivity rather than a one-to-many mapping of one fixed full input. Any exact inverse inference must specify the condition and the host-, system-, and state-specific coordinates consumed by the active mapping. A separate same-condition convergence countermodel establishes the inverse-uniqueness boundary. Within one host/system validity domain, under one fixed FeelingTransductionCondition and one stable EmotionalFeelingResponse criterion, two distinct qualified DomainRelativeEmotionDelta inputs with non-equivalent upstream differentials or domain-relative contents may yield the same discriminable EmotionalFeelingResponse. The generic architecture therefore does not guarantee injectivity or a unique inverse from Feeling to upstream Emotion. The convergence result does not impose non-injectivity on every host-specific ExactFeelingTransductionFunction. ExactFeelingTransductionFunction remains OPEN / SYSTEM-SPECIFIC, and a restricted function may be injective or support a validated inverse within an independently demonstrated validity domain. The generic result localizes mechanistic openness rather than prohibiting precise host-specific reconstruction. EmotionalPeripheralPhysiologicalRealization remains an optional downstream realization class encompassing autonomic, endocrine, vascular, cardiac, respiratory, sudomotor, motor, or expressive involvement. Peripheral physiology, interoception, representation, readout, semantic label, and report can support evidence or mechanism studies while remaining distinct from EmotionalFeelingResponse and from upstream Emotion identity. Transmission failure likewise does not retroactively negate the already qualified Emotion delta. The direct public Emotion-series parents are Host-Relative Emotion Qualification: Host-Native Differentials, Same-Host Contrast, Alternative Explanations, and Non-Transfer and Conscious Self-State Change as an Insufficient Criterion for Emotion: Domain-Relative Deltas, Host-Relative Qualification, and the Consciousness Boundary. They supply HostRelativeEmotionQualification and DomainRelativeEmotionDelta respectively. The paper Premetric Affective Modulation Beyond Emotion: Constitutive Modulation and the Failure of Affect-Emotion Identity is not consumed by this argument and therefore is not activated as a public parent. The maximum public result is a machine-reconstructible conditioned emotional-Feeling architecture with protected upstream qualification, claim-local condition dependence, provenance-indexed downstream response, comparative attenuation/amplification/failure, optional peripheral realization, no generic guarantee of injectivity or unique inverse, and an exact transduction function left open for host-specific science. Downstream Feeling evidence therefore cannot manufacture the upstream Emotion status on which the transduction model depends.
revue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
