Une revue IRMf (11 études) montre des modifications fonctionnelles dans 8 régions cérébrales
Quatre articles non-acupuncture dont un essai randomisé sur la thérapie cognitive basée sur la pleine conscience
fiche.conclusion: L'acupuncture et les approches complémentaires montrent des résultats prometteurs dans l'insomnie, mais des essais supplémentaires sont nécessaires.
limites: Hétérogénéité très élevée (I² jusqu'à 91 %) dans les analyses citées
fiche.pertinence_raison: Centré sur l'insomnie et l'acupuncture, éloigné de la psychogastroentérologie.
fiche.titre_court: Insomnie chronique : éditorial sur les traitements
fiche.conclusion_simple: Cet éditorial rapporte des effets positifs mais très hétérogènes de l'acupuncture dans l'insomnie, et mentionne la pleine conscience.

titre: Functional outcomes after transperineal anterior levatorplasty for symptomatic rectocele with perineal descent: a retrospective study
resume: Transperineal repair is a surgical option for symptomatic rectocele refractory to conservative therapy. In patients with perineal descent (PD), the impact of transperineal anterior levatoroplasty (TPAL) on recurrence and functional outcomes is uncertain. This study evaluated 12-month patient-reported functional outcomes and clinical symptom relapse after TPAL in patients with symptomatic rectocele and PD following failed conservative treatment. This single-center retrospective cohort study included women undergoing TPAL for symptomatic rectocele with PD after failed conservative management (2014–2024). Outcomes were assessed preoperatively and at 3 and 12 months using the Altomare Obstructed Defecation Score (ODs), Cleveland Clinic Fecal Incontinence Score (CCFIS), Patient Assessment of Constipation-Quality of Life (PAC-QoL), Pelvic Floor Distress Inventory-20 (PFDI-20), and Pelvic Organ Prolapse/Urinary Incontinence Sexual Questionnaire (PISQ-12). Clinical symptom relapse was defined as worsening ODs (increase or return to within 10% of baseline). Postoperative magnetic resonance (MR) defecography was obtained selectively. Of 63 women undergoing TPAL, 50 had complete 12-month data. Baseline MR defecography showed moderate rectocele (2–4 cm) in 84% and large (> 4 cm) in 16%; PD was grade 1 in 88% and grade 2 in 12%. Mean ODs improved from 15.8 ± 1.4 preoperatively to 6.6 ± 1.3 at 3 months and 5.9 ± 1.5 at 12 months ( p < 0.001). PFDI-20 and PAC-QoL improved (both p < 0.001). CCFIS was unchanged ( p = 0.943). Thirty-day morbidity was limited to Clavien–Dindo grade I events (24%). No clinical symptom relapse was observed through 12 months; asymptomatic anatomic recurrence and objective anatomic durability could not be systematically assessed. TPAL was associated with favorable 12-month changes in obstructed defecation symptoms and quality of life, with low short-term morbidity. Because routine postoperative imaging was not performed, asymptomatic anatomic recurrence and objective anatomic durability could not be assessed. This study provides 12-month patient-reported outcomes following transperineal anterior levatoroplasty in women with symptomatic rectocele and perineal descent. It demonstrates sustained improvement in obstructed defecation symptoms and quality of life with low short-term morbidity, while highlighting the need for further evaluation of long-term anatomical durability

titre: Effects of lidocaine combined with dexmedetomidine or remimazolam on early quality of recovery in older adult patients undergoing lumbar spine surgery: a six-arm randomized controlled trial
resume: Optimization of postoperative recovery in older adult patients is a clinical priority. This study investigated the effects of intraoperative lidocaine combined with dexmedetomidine or remimazolam on postoperative rehabilitation in elderly patients undergoing lumbar spine surgery. In this randomized controlled trial, 270 older adult patients were randomly assigned to six groups based on the intraoperative intravenous anesthetic used: lidocaine (Group L), dexmedetomidine (Group D), remimazolam (Group R), lidocaine plus dexmedetomidine (Group LD), lidocaine plus remimazolam (LR), and and normal saline (Group C). The primary outcome was the global quality of recovery-40 (QoR-40) score at postoperative day 1 (POD 1). Secondary outcomes included gastrointestinal recovery, inflammatory cytokine levels (IL-6, TNF-α), and long-term quality of life (SF-12) at POD 180. The modified intention-to-treat population included 265 patients. Group LD achieved significantly higher global QoR-40 scores than Group C at both POD 1 and POD 3 (all P 0.05). The combination of lidocaine and dexmedetomidine significantly improves early recovery in elderly patients through an additive interaction. This combination outperforms lidocaine and remimazolam, which exhibited sub-additive effects. Although no long-term benefits were observed, the lidocaine-dexmedetomidine regimen is a safe, mechanism-based approach for optimizing early functional restoration after major spine surgery. Trial registration number: ChiCTR2200062226, 30/07/2022. Title: “Effects of lidocaine in combination with dexmedetomidine or remimazolam on postoperative recovery and pulmonary function in elderly patients undergoing posterior lumbar spine surgery. Available online: https://www.chictr.org.cn .

titre: Extending Healthspan Through Lifestyle: Nutrition, Physical Activity, Sleep, and Other Modifiable Behaviors—A Narrative Review
resume: Population aging has increased interest in extending healthspan, defined here as the period of life characterized by preserved physical and cognitive function, independence, and well-being. This narrative review examines major modifiable determinants of healthspan and critically evaluates how established lifestyle strategies compare with newer approaches promoted within the longevity field. A structured, topic-driven search of PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, and Web of Science focused primarily on publications from January 2015 to August 2026, with earlier studies included when relevant. To provide a mechanistic and translational frame, the major interventions were mapped to the hallmarks of aging and stratified by level of evidence, distinguishing human clinical outcome data from biomarker, mechanistic, and animal findings. The most consistent human evidence supports high-quality dietary patterns, regular physical activity, and healthy sleep as central components of healthy aging. Stress management, social connection, avoidance of harmful exposures, and the physical and socioeconomic environment are also relevant to healthy aging and influence the context in which these behaviors occur. Observations from long-lived real-world populations, such as the blue zones, are consistent with this evidence. The gut microbiome represents an important interface between lifestyle and host physiology, although changes in microbial composition should not be assumed to translate into improved healthspan. Evidence for dietary supplements is strongest when use addresses deficiency, inadequate intake, or a defined clinical indication. Intermittent fasting and time-restricted eating can improve selected weight and cardiometabolic outcomes, but evidence that they extend healthspan remains limited. Similar uncertainty applies to several emerging longevity practices, where biomarker changes or short-term physiological responses often precede evidence of meaningful clinical benefit. Greater personalization may refine lifestyle and nutritional interventions, but its added value over well-designed standard care requires further study. Healthy aging is therefore best supported by sustained, evidence-based lifestyle behaviors, while newer strategies should be judged by their ability to improve long-term function, disease burden, and independence rather than by biological plausibility alone.

titre: *Bone Marrow Transplantation as a Curative Intervention for Hematological Malignancies and Disorders: Clinical Protocols, HLA Matching, and Post-Transplant Care Protocols (A Clinical Review Based on Expert Insights)**
resume: ### Alternative Titles 1. **Rebooting the Blood System: A Comprehensive Analysis of Autologous and Allogeneic Bone Marrow Transplants in Modern Hematology**2. **Beyond Chemotherapy: The Role of Bone Marrow Transplantation in Curing Blood Cancers and Severe Anemias**3. **The Lifesaving Science of Stem Cell Transplants: Navigating HLA Compatibility, Recovery Challenges, and Long-Term Patient Care**4. **Clinical Perspectives on Bone Marrow Transplantation: Indications, Procedural Risks, and Essential Post-Operative Lifestyle Modifications** --- ### Sub-titles (Section Structure) 1. **Introduction: The Burden of Blood Cancers and the Promise of BMT**2. **Understanding Bone Marrow and Hematological Disorders** * 2.1 The Function of Bone Marrow * 2.2 Indications for Transplantation (Leukemia, Thalassemia, Aplastic Anemia)3. **Types of Bone Marrow Transplants** * 3.1 Autologous Transplantation (Self-Donor) * 3.2 Allogeneic Transplantation (Donor-Dependent)4. **The Critical Role of HLA Matching**5. **The Transplant Procedure: A Step-by-Step Clinical Pathway** * 5.1 Pre-Transplant Conditioning * 5.2 Stem Cell Infusion * 5.3 Engraftment and Hospitalization6. **Risks, Complications, and Graft-versus-Host Disease (GVHD)**7. **Post-Transplant Care: Lifestyle, Diet, and Hygiene** * 7.1 Dietary Restrictions and Food Safety * 7.2 Vaccination Schedules and Infection Control8. **Conclusion: Expanding Access and Improving Outcomes** --- ### Detailed Description #### AbstractBone Marrow Transplantation (BMT) has emerged as a revolutionary medical procedure offering a potential cure for patients suffering from blood cancers—such as leukemia and lymphoma—as well as severe, non-malignant blood disorders like thalassemia and aplastic anemia. By replacing diseased or damaged bone marrow with healthy stem cells, the procedure effectively "reboots" the body's blood production system. This paper synthesizes clinical insights, procedural steps, risk factors, and post-transplant care guidelines provided by Dr. K. Kiran Kumar, Hematologist and Bone Marrow Transplant Specialist at Yashoda Hospital, Secunderabad. The report details the critical role of Human Leukocyte Antigen (HLA) matching, the distinction between autologous and allogeneic transplants, the arduous recovery process, and the imperative of long-term lifestyle modifications to ensure graft survival and patient health. **Keywords:** Bone Marrow Transplant (BMT), Blood Cancer, Stem Cells, HLA Matching, Autologous, Allogeneic, Graft-versus-Host Disease, Hematology. #### 1. Introduction: The Burden of Blood Cancers and the Promise of BMTBlood cancers and severe hematological disorders have historically been among the most challenging conditions to treat. Traditional approaches like chemotherapy and radiation, while effective in controlling the disease, often fail to provide a permanent cure and cause significant collateral damage to the body's hematopoietic system. Bone Marrow Transplantation (BMT) represents a paradigm shift in this field. As highlighted in recent medical literature, BMT provides a definitive cure for conditions where the bone marrow—the spongy tissue inside bones responsible for producing blood cells—is damaged, diseased, or malfunctioning. This paper outlines the fundamental mechanics, indications, and clinical realities of BMT, drawing on expert medical insights regarding the procedure's life-saving potential. #### 2. Understanding Bone Marrow and Hematological Disorders**2.1 The Function of Bone Marrow:** Bone marrow is a vital organ responsible for the production of red blood cells (which carry oxygen), white blood cells (which fight infection), and platelets (which help in blood clotting). **2.2 Indications for Transplantation:** When this production system is compromised by diseases such as blood cancer (leukemia, lymphoma), genetic disorders (thalassemia, sickle cell anemia), or autoimmune conditions (aplastic anemia), the body loses its ability to fight infections and transport oxygen effectively. Bone marrow transplantation is the process of infusing healthy blood-forming stem cells into the body to replace the damaged or diseased marrow. #### 3. Types of Bone Marrow TransplantsThe procedure is broadly categorized into two primary types, depending on the source of the stem cells:**3.1 Autologous Transplantation (Self-Donor):** In this method, the patient's own healthy stem cells are harvested before undergoing high-dose chemotherapy or radiation. After the treatment eliminates the diseased cells, the harvested stem cells are reintroduced into the patient's body. This approach is generally preferred for certain types of lymphomas and multiple myeloma.**3.2 Allogeneic Transplantation (Donor-Dependent):** This involves harvesting stem cells from a genetically matched donor (usually a sibling or an unrelated volunteer from a donor registry). This is the standard treatment for diseases like leukemia and aplastic anemia. The donor's immune cells can also help attack any remaining cancer cells in the patient's body, a phenomenon known as the "graft-versus-tumor" effect. #### 4. The Critical Role of HLA MatchingThe success of an allogeneic transplant hinges on Human Leukocyte Antigen (HLA) matching. HLA markers are proteins found on the surface of cells that help the immune system distinguish between "self" and "non-self." A high degree of compatibility (ideally a 10/10 match) between the donor and recipient is essential to minimize the risk of the recipient's body rejecting the donor cells or the donor's immune cells attacking the recipient's body. #### 5. The Transplant Procedure: A Step-by-Step Clinical PathwayThe BMT process is a multi-stage, rigorous medical intervention:**5.1 Pre-Transplant Conditioning:** Before the infusion, the patient undergoes "conditioning"—intensive chemotherapy or radiation therapy designed to destroy diseased marrow cells and suppress the immune system to prevent graft rejection.**5.2 Stem Cell Infusion:** The harvested stem cells are infused into the patient's bloodstream via a central venous catheter. The cells naturally migrate to the bone marrow cavities where they begin to grow and produce new blood cells.**5.3 Engraftment and Hospitalization:** The period following infusion is critical. The patient remains under strict isolation to protect against infection, as their immune system is virtually non-existent. Engraftment—the point at which the new stem cells begin producing healthy blood cells—typically takes two to four weeks. #### 6. Risks, Complications, and Graft-versus-Host Disease (GVHD)BMT is a high-risk procedure associated with several potential complications:* **Infection:** Due to the complete suppression of the immune system during conditioning.* **Graft-versus-Host Disease (GVHD):** A common complication in allogeneic transplants where the donor's immune cells attack the recipient's organs (skin, liver, gastrointestinal tract).* **Graft Failure:** The risk that the new stem cells fail to engraft or produce healthy cells.* **Organ Toxicity:** Damage to the liver, kidneys, or lungs caused by the intense conditioning regimen. #### 7. Post-Transplant Care: Lifestyle, Diet, and HygieneAccording to Dr. K. Kiran Kumar, maintaining strict post-transplant protocols is vital for long-term survival. Key recommendations include:**7.1 Dietary Restrictions and Food Safety:** Patients must consume thoroughly cooked, pasteurized food. Raw or undercooked items (meat, eggs, seafood), unwashed fruits, and raw salads should be strictly avoided to prevent foodborne infections.**7.2 Vaccination Schedules and Infection Control:** Because the immune system is essentially "reset," patients must follow a specialized vaccination schedule post-transplant. Regular handwashing and maintaining a clean environment are paramount. Patients are advised to avoid crowded places and sick individuals for the first few months. Regular follow-ups with the transplant team are mandatory to detect any signs of relapse or GVHD early. #### 8. Conclusion: Expanding Access and Improving OutcomesBone Marrow Transplantation represents a beacon of hope for patients facing terminal blood disorders and cancers. While the journey is physically demanding, requiring extensive pre-conditioning, high-risk surgery, and a prolonged recovery phase, the potential for a complete cure is significant. Public awareness regarding stem cell donation and the importance of donor registries is crucial to expanding access to this life-saving procedure. With advancements in medical technology and post-transplant care, the survival rates and quality of life for BMT recipients continue to improve steadily. ---**References*** *Based on the article "Bone Marrow Transplant tho Blood Cancer ki Check" (Namaste Telangana E-Paper, Hyderabad Main, Page 11, Dated 17/11/2026).** Insights provided by Dr. K. Kiran Kumar, Hematologist and Bone Marrow Transplant Specialist, Yashoda Hospital, Secunderabad.

titre: Learning and feedback processing: Contextual influences and clinical implications for obsessive-compulsive disorder
resume: Motivational biases describe a tendency in learning and decision-making to perform an action to obtain a reward and to withhold an action to avoid punishment. These biases have been linked to striatal mechanisms and are generally considered robust across task contexts, although alterations have been reported in several mental disorders. Although generally thought to reflect anticipatory Pavlovian response biasing of action selection, recent accounts suggest that they also involve biased instrumental learning of responseoutcome associations. This raises the possibility that motivational biases may already emerge during feedback evaluation and processing, possibly reflected in the feedback related negativity/reward positivity (FRN/RewP) of the eventrelated potential. Across four consecutive studies, this dissertation investigated motivational biases across different learning contexts and the role of feedback processing in these biases, while also exploring their clinical relevance in obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), alongside broader alterations in instrumental learning and feedback processing. Despite previous evidence highlighting their robustness, Study I demonstrated that motivational biases were attenuated when learning from emotional compared to neutral facial cues. Study II found that motivational biases emerged independently of feedback timing, despite learning from delayed feedback being associated with reduced striatal engagement. It also provided only limited support for a substantial role of biased instrumental learning to motivational biases while motivational biases were not reflected in altered feedback processing. Study III explored instrumental learning and feedback processing in OCD, showing impaired learning, across active and observational task contexts, increased indecisiveness and altered reward processing in the FRN/RewP. Finally, Study IV investigated motivational biases in OCD but found no evidence for alterations in OCD, although they were generally attenuated for observational compared to active learning. Consistent with Study II, motivational biases were not reflected in altered feedback processing. Interestingly, however, OCD patients showed altered self-other distinction in the FRN/RewP for self- versus other-related outcomes. Taken together, while partially sensitive to the learning context, motivational biases persisted across contexts, highlighting them as a particularly robust hallmark of learning and decision-making, that may most substantially reflect a Pavlovian response bias on action selection. Findings from OCD patients suggest that, although associated with alterations in learning and decisionmaking, these alterations are not general but rather context-dependent, converging with the notion of cognitive inflexibility in OCD.

titre: Anterior cingulate gyrus surgery for intractable pain-related suffering in pediatrics: clinical and ethical justifiability
resume: The anterior cingulate gyrus (ACG) is a forebrain structure located in the mesial frontal lobe comprised of anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) and the associated portion of the cingulum comprising similar cytoarchitectural tissue defined as Brodmann's Areas 24, 32, and 35. 1,2 Functional MRI (fMRI) studies exploring neuroanatomical correlates of pain show Blood Oxygen Level-Dependent (BOLD) elevations in the ACC in response to painful stimuli and decreased BOLD activity with nonpainful stimuli. 3,4 Animal models demonstrate that excitation of the ACC increases aversive behavior in response to painful stimuli. [5][6][7][8] Adult patients with obsessive compulsive disorder (OCD), 9,10 major depressive disorder (MDD), 11 and chronic pain disorders such as back pain, migraine, and craniomandibular disorders 12 consistently reveal abnormal resting-state activity in the ACC. Recently, ACG surgery has been attempted to address intractable pain-related suffering in adults, via either laser interstitial thermal therapy (LITT) and neuromodulation via deep brain stimulation (DBS). The neurosurgical evidence suggests that ablative or neuromodulatory ACG surgery can significantly improve pain and quality of life in adult patients 13 with chronic and refractory neuropathic pain, 14,15 cancer-related pain, 16 non-cancer pain, 17 or severe depression. 15,18 As a whole, the current neuroscientific literature suggests the ACC plays a central role in the negative, affective component of pain, and that surgical targeting of the ACG can significantly reduce pain-related suffering.While data primarily supports ACG surgery in adults, children with cerebral palsy (CP), 19-21 chronic regional pain syndrome (CRPS), 22 advanced cancer, 23,24 and treatment-resistant major depressive disorder 25 also experience chronic, medically intractable pain. Additionally, ethnographic research shows that in pediatric critical care contexts, "suffering" --which is notoriously difficult to define or quantify 26 -is invoked three times more often to justify withdrawal of care than to sustain a child's life. 27 This research suggests intractable pediatric pain and suffering are principal factors in determining survival outcomes for critically ill children and remain inadequately addressed, underscoring an urgent duty to improve the treatment of intractable pain and suffering in pediatrics. This literature raises the following question: can we -and should we -perform ACG surgery to target and treat refractory pain or pain-related suffering in children?Various frameworks help determine the clinical and ethical justifiability of pediatric ACG (Table 1). Davidson et al. have proposed that the ethical justifiability of any innovative form of pediatric DBS surgery requires five specific expectations be met: (1) the protection of the child's best interest, (2) consideration of developmental context, (3) mitigation of "relative" known and unknown risks, (4) avoidance of overreliance on the adult literature, and (5) communication of trial results and collaboration with other practitioners. 28 Similarly, Lipsman et al. proposed the ethical permissibility of any form of pediatric psychosurgery requires meeting seven criteria: (a) proper discussion of patient selection, (b) evidence-based rationale surpassing a consensus-driven threshold for surgical intervention, (c) demonstration of the disease burden, (d) transparent informed consent, (e) multidisciplinary review of individual cases, (f) proper oversight of all aspects of the research, and (g) routine scheduled evaluations focused ensuring ethical trial design. In tandem, these frameworks suggest pediatric ACG surgery is ethically justifiable if it, firstly, serves the best interest of the child (1). Given ACG surgery's elevated degree of invasiveness and experimental nature, neurosurgically addressing pain-related suffering would only serve the pediatric patient's best interest in the following clinical scenarios: if medical analgesic therapy is ineffective or insufficient, compromises the child's conscious state via oversedation, or produces intolerable side effects significantly impairing quality of life such as respiratory depression, hyperalgesia, urinary retention, nausea, vomiting, pruritis, or withdrawal; or if other interventional/surgical pain interventions have also failed or are unsuitable. These scenarios may arise in the setting of intractable chronic pain syndromes such as CRPS, end-stage sickle cell disease, or peripheral nerve injury, refractory psychiatric disease such as OCD, or terminal cancer. Though instances of massive analgesic therapy for these diseases are rare, they do occur and are ethically controversial given the nonzero probability of oversedation or precipitate pharmacological dependence. As has been proposed regarding cordotomies in adults with terminal cancer, 30 neurosurgery for medically intractable pain is clinically and ethically justifiable as it addresses the patient's primary concern of pain, often greater than the fear of death, 31 and minimizes use of opioid therapy. While children may not fear pain as much as adults, minimizing pain-related suffering when safe and possible is morally uncontroversial. Regarding patient selection (a), only pediatric patients with convincing signs of pain-related suffering, whose medical or procedural pain regimen is either ineffective, undesirably sedating, or significantly impairing, should be considered, given the highly experimental and invasive nature of the procedure. Finally, whether the patient is chronically versus terminally ill may be of ethical import. The severity of the patient's pain burden carries great weight in light of the "rule of rescue" described in the bioethical literature, 32 and patients with non-cancer pain may by definition suffer for longer. For that very reason, however, the current lack of procedure-specific efficacy and side-effect data calls for a tiered roll-out of this experimental surgery, described below.Developmentally (2), research demonstrates the sulcal structure of the ACG is relatively stable from early infancy into adulthood, suggesting robust neuroanatomic and functional development before birth or shortly thereafter. 33 However, sulcal stability alone does not ensure anatomical landmarks are similar in pediatric patients compared to adults. We propose that the ACG target be defined on a case-by-case basis using patient-specific, intraoperative MRI as opposed to relying on adult anatomical landmarks.Similarly, given the experimental nature of this surgery, we propose that initial candidacy be limited to adolescent patients with mature, MRI-confirmable cingulate anatomy.Post-operative cognitive functioning also warrants particular caution. Though ablating or modulating the ACG may lead to a reduced ability to distinguish favorable versus unfavorable experiences after surgery, protecting this function may pale in comparison to the immediate imperative to address the child's intractable suffering, especially at the end of life. Though adult studies have not shown significant cognitive post-operative deficits, such lack of positive results may reflect developed learned decisionmaking skills; as such, children may be at greater risk. On the other hand, children are more neuroplastic than adult counterparts, supporting surgical intervention in hopes of neuroplastic compensation. To this caution, we propose a "smallest effective lesion" goal and explicit disclosure of this possibility during the informed consent process.Clinically, the evidence (b) for pediatric ACG surgery currently rests on three pediatric cingulotomy case reports [34][35][36] and the favorable safety outcomes of a long history of DBS surgery on pediatric patients. 37,38 The literature also contains Level III efficacy and safety outcomes for pediatric stereotactic ablation via laser interstitial thermal therapy (LITT) or radiofrequency ablation (RF) of various neuroanatomical targets, 15,[39][40][41][42][43] supporting the clinical feasibility of pediatric ACG surgery. On the other hand, in adults, the efficacy of ACG surgery is also limited to case report data, [13][14][15][16][17][18] reducing the likelihood of overreliance on adult literature (4) but reinforcing the surgery's experimental nature. Infection, blood loss, adverse neurological side effects, and caregiver conflict in surgical decision-making are all risks requiring effective mitigation strategies (3). Infection can be mitigated by carefully selecting intervention type per patient needs. DBS leads to hardware-dependent infection (approximately 5%), a risk that is higher than with LITT or RF, 44 though LITT or RF may produce higher rates of infection than high intensity focused ultrasound (HIFU), another non-invasive, stereotactic procedural modality. Long-term adult data on anterior cingulate DBS also show that the risk of seizure induction is not null (approximately 8-18%), 14 and incident seizures may be irreversible.As such, we propose ablative cingulotomy (via LITT, RF, or HIFU, depending on the clinical and demographic picture) as the primary candidate procedure, and DBS only as a theoretical alternative. While neurological side effects of ablation are not perfectly predictable given ACG surgery's innovative nature, they may be mitigated by ensuring optimal stereotactic precision, utilizing intraoperative neuromonitoring, and avoiding other neuroanatomical structures during surgery. Blood loss can also be mitigated by setting surgical time-goals and optimizing pre-operative hemoglobin levels.Of all recommended justifiability criteria, demonstration of disease burden (c) is perhaps the hardest to meet in this patient population, as pain and suffering are notoriously difficult to quantify in any patient population. Pain is best measured in children via age and developmentally appropriate self-reported scales, such as the Visual Analog Scale (VAS) for verbal children, and observational scales for pre-or non-verbal patients such as the Faces, Legs, Activity, Cry, Consolability (FLACC) scale, but is still significantly challenging. Suffering is even harder to measure, as it is operationally challenging, requires subjective self-reporting, and is influenced by cultural values. 45 Shared decision-making with parents, along with child assent, may thus play a larger role in the justifiability of this procedure, as it may serve as both consent and third-party confirmation of sufficient disease burden. In this manner, while pain and suffering may be difficult to quantitatively measure in non-verbal and verbal pediatric patients, their empirical elusiveness does not negate neither their existence nor the duty to treat them, especially given their centrality in determining survival outcomes at the end of life and their effect on the well-being of both patient and family.Given the notable lack of procedure-specific efficacy data, we propose a tiered roll-out of this investigational surgery. Since the risk of operating on patients with longer expected survival is ethically suspect in an invasive, experimental surgery of this kind, patients with limited life-expectancy indications should be considered first. After robust pilot outcomes data is established and favorable, patients with intractable non-terminal pain ought to be considered Finally, the communication of trial results (5), transparent informed consent (d), multidisciplinary review (e), proper oversight (f), and routine scheduled evaluation of ethical design (g) are all reasonably achievable and expected by following the clinical guidelines for any surgical trial set by the Idea, Development, Exploration, Assessment, and Long-term Follow-up (IDEAL) Framework and Recommendations. 46 We also propose three other safeguards: (a) detailed pre-and post-operative neuropsychological assessment where appropriate; (b) restriction of these procedures to academic centers operating under strict governance frameworks; and (c) methodical registry of all cases to generate evidence on the efficacy and side effects of this treatment. IRBs or other institutional regulatory bodies may serve as final arbiters of the justifiability of each surgical case per the aforementioned criteria, especially during the surgery's investigational stage.As such, we propose that pediatric ACG surgery is clinically and ethically justifiable if the outlined criteria are met (Table 2). Anterior cingulate surgery produces favorable outcomes in adults; children also suffer from intractable pain-related suffering. Pediatric ACG surgery is clinically and ethically justifiable in the medically appropriate circumstances. Ablative ACG surgery should be considered, within a tiered roll-out beginning with palliative indications, for carefully selected patients to treat pain-related suffering, with the goal of improving quality of life and preventing premature withdrawal of care.

titre: Goat milk fat globule membrane attenuates D-galactose-induced cognitive decline in mice in association with gut microbiota remodeling, increased fecal SCFAs, and GPR41/43-related signaling
resume: The global rise in aging-related cognitive decline necessitates effective preventive strategies. The gut microbiota modulates brain function via the microbiota-gut-brain axis, yet the role of goat milk fat globule membrane (GMFGM) in this crosstalk remains to be fully elucidated. This study investigated neuroprotective effects of GMFGM in a D-galactose-induced aging mouse model and examined changes in gut microbiota composition, fecal short-chain fatty acid (SCFA) concentrations, and G protein-coupled receptor 41/43 (GPR41/43) expression. GMFGM supplementation alleviated D-gal-induced cognitive deficits, as evidenced by improved behavioral performance, accompanied by ameliorated hippocampal histopathological damage and restored synaptic protein expression including synaptophysin and postsynaptic density protein 95. GMFGM reshaped gut microbiota and increased fecal SCFA concentrations. These changes coincided with increased colonic levels of tight junction proteins including zonula occludens-1, Occludin, and Claudin-1, and elevated GPR41/43 expression in the colon and hippocampus. GMFGM also increased serum superoxide dismutase and glutathione peroxidase activities, but reduced malondialdehyde. In the hippocampus, GMFGM decreased 8-hydroxy-2'-deoxyguanosine levels, restored brain-derived neurotrophic factor/tropomyosin receptor kinase B/cAMP response element-binding protein-related signaling, and suppressed neuroinflammation by reducing ionized calcium-binding adaptor molecule 1 expression and toll-like receptor 4/nuclear factor kappa-B signaling. Notably, GMFGM at 200 mg/kg·BW produced greater improvements than goat buttermilk at the same dose in several outcomes. Collectively, these findings suggest the potential involvement of SCFA-GPR41/43 signaling in the neuroprotective effects observed following GMFGM supplementation and highlight GMFGM's potential as a functional ingredient for neuroprotection.

titre: Japanese encephalitis virus infection reshapes the gut microbiome and induces colonic inflammation in neonatal mice
resume: Japanese encephalitis virus (JEV), a neurotropic flavivirus, predominantly causes severe infection in children, leading to neuropsychiatric complications. Given that the juvenile period is a transitional window for the gut microbiota to develop into a stable community profile, any alterations to the microbiota during infections can result in chronic inflammation. Therefore, we investigated changes in the gut microbiota of neonatal mice during the early and late stages of JEV infection. Postnatal day 10, BALB/c mice challenged with JEV succumbed to acute infection at 6 to 7 days post-infection. This severity was marked by a surge in systemic pro-inflammatory cytokines (TNF-α, IFN-γ, IL-6, and MCP-1) and reduced food intake. Fecal 16S rRNA V3-V4 sequencing revealed distinct β-diversity between mock and JEV-infected groups, with the dominant phyla being Firmicutes, Bacteroidota, and Proteobacteria. The relative abundance of these phyla shifted, with Firmicutes decreasing from ~63.7% (control) to ~39% (JEV), whereas Proteobacteria remained unchanged in JEV. The Firmicutes/Bacteroidota ratio decreased in JEV, along with a reduction in Lactobacillus. Simultaneously, altered mucosal secretion, reduced tight-junction protein ZO-1, increased pNF-κB, and cleaved caspase-3 together indicated colonic inflammation. Prediction of microbial pathways using PICRUSt2 suggested a reduction in specific pathways associated with beneficial secondary metabolites and short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) in JEV. Intragastric administration of the SCFA cocktail prolonged survival and delayed the onset of clinical signs and the inflammatory response. Our findings suggest that systemic inflammation and reduced feeding during an acute infection could result in colonic dysbiosis, reduced beneficial bacteria, and trigger inflammation. SCFAs displayed a transient therapeutic effect in JEV infection, highlighting the potential of gut microbiota modulation to manage acute viral infection.IMPORTANCEJapanese encephalitis remains a leading cause of viral encephalitis in children across the Asia-Pacific region, with new outbreaks driven by evolving demographic factors. The need for targeted therapies beyond existing supportive care underscores the need for new host-directed interventions. Our findings suggest that gut-brain axis interactions may play a role in acute viral infections, potentially amplifying disease severity through infection-driven reduction in feeding, increased cytokine production, and shifts in the gut microbiome. We propose that SCFA supplementation can serve as a microbiota-modulating strategy that offers a safe, translatable approach to managing inflammation and JEV outcomes in pediatric viral encephalitis. This could be utilized as a supplement along with supportive care in other flavivirus infections.

titre: [First intestinal autotransplantation in the Netherlands]
resume: Benign mesenteric lesions may still become life-threatening when they cause chronic bleeding, transfusion dependency, malnutrition or impending intestinal failure. We describe a patient with an extensive benign veno-lymphatic lesion in the mesenteric root who was referred for intestinal transplantation. Conventional in-situ resection was considered unsafe because of the risk of major bowel loss. Allogeneic intestinal transplantation was deemed disproportionate for a benign indication. After multidisciplinary, multicentre evaluation, bowel autotransplantation was performed. The postoperative course was favorable: the patient returned to full enteral nutrition, no longer required blood transfusions, and regained quality of life. This case illustrates that early interhospital consultation and multidisciplinary decision-making can reveal treatment options beyond standard pathways when conventional approaches are insufficient. Bij complexe mesenteriale aandoeningen moeten de gevolgen van conventionele resectie, parenterale voeding en allogene transplantatie expliciet tegen elkaar worden afgewogen. Bij patiënten met een mesenteriale afwijking die met conventionele methoden niet te reseceren is kan ex-situresectie en darmautotransplantatie een methode zijn om de afwijking te verwijderen en functionele darm te behouden. Door explantatie en koude preservatie kan de darm buiten het lichaam van alle kanten worden benaderd, waardoor complexe tumorresecties, dissectie van vaten en vaatreconstructies mogelijk worden. Darmautotransplantatie vereist zorgvuldige patiëntselectie en gespecialiseerde transplantatie- en microchirurgische expertise.

titre: Schaftoside, a functional flavonoid from fenugreek (Trigonella foenum-graecum L.), alleviates depression and cognitive deficits via the microbiome-gut-brain axis in stressed mice
resume: Depression involves dysregulation of central and peripheral networks, with gut microbiota alterations increasingly implicated in pathogenesis. Trigonella foenum-graecum L. (fenugreek), a functional food and medicinal herb, has been used traditionally for neurological disorders, yet its specific neuroprotective constituents remain poorly characterized. This study evaluated the antidepressant potential of schaftoside, the predominant flavonoid of fenugreek seed flavonoids, and explored its mechanisms involving the microbiome-gut-brain axis in a chronic restraint stress (CRS) mouse model. Male Kunming mice were subjected to CRS and orally administered schaftoside (20, 50, and 125 mg kg -1 ) or fluoxetine (10 mg kg -1 ) for 28 days. Behavioral assessments (tail suspension, forced swim, novel object recognition, and Y-maze) demonstrated that schaftoside dose-dependently ameliorated depressive-like behaviors and cognitive impairments. It attenuated hippocampal neuronal damage and neuroinflammation, restoring hippocampal 5-HT, NE, and ACh levels. Intestinal barrier integrity was improved, evidenced by enhanced tight junction proteins (ZO-1, occludin) and mucin (MUC2) expression, alongside reduced colonic pro-inflammatory cytokines and elevated IL-10. 16S rRNA profiling revealed that schaftoside reshaped gut microbiota composition, notably suppressing stress-enriched Bacteroides and promoting butyrate-producing Butyricicoccus . Untargeted metabolomics identified restoration of tryptophan and α-linolenic acid metabolism pathways. Spearman correlation analysis revealed significant associations between specific gut genera, fecal metabolites, and host inflammatory/neurochemical markers. Hippocampal transcriptomics indicated enrichment of cAMP signaling, dopaminergic, and serotonergic synapse pathways. Fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) from schaftoside-treated donors partially recapitulated the behavioral, anti-inflammatory, and intestinal barrier-protective effects in antibiotic-pretreated recipient mice, accompanied by restoration of the gut microbiota and metabolite profiles. These findings demonstrate that schaftoside, the major flavonoid of fenugreek seeds, exhibits promising antidepressant-like potential through modulation of the microbiome-gut-brain axis, supporting the functional food application of fenugreek-derived flavonoids for stress-related mood disorders.

titre: ФУНКЦІОНАЛЬНА ДИСПЕПСІЯ: ЕТІОЛОГІЧНІ, ПАТОГЕНЕТИЧНІ, КЛАСИФІКАЦІЙНІ ТА КЛІНІЧНІ МОМЕНТИ РОЗУМІННЯ І ЗДОБУТКИ НА СУЧАСНОМУ ЕТАПІ (коментар до статті професора В. П. Образцова (1915 р.))
resume: This paper presents a comparative analysis of the concept of functional dyspepsia at the beginning of the 20th century versus its current state, based on an article by Professor V. P. Obraztsov published in 1915. The authors accessed the original content through its republication in the journal «Bulletin of the Pancreatologists’ Club» (2025, No. 4). A key finding of this study is that the fundamental approach to perceiving this condition has remained largely unchanged for over a century. Functional dyspepsia continues to be characterized by independent gastric clinical manifestations in the absence of morphological changes in the gastric mucosa or other diagnosable diseases that could mimic its symptoms. The authors emphasize that contemporary advancements in gastroenterology — particularly instrumental diagnostic methods — have expanded knowledge regarding the risk factors, etiology, pathogenesis, clinical presentation, and therapy of the disease. A parallel is drawn between "neurasthenic" and "hysterical" dyspepsia (as categorized by Prof. Obraztsov) and modern functional dyspepsia. The authors suggest that neurasthenic dyspepsia can be interpreted as functional dyspepsia accompanied by anxiety or depressive syndromes. Regarding hysterical dyspepsia, its interpretation remains dualistic: in therapeutic practice, it is viewed as functional, whereas from a psychiatric perspective, it may be considered a consequence of an underlying disorder (secondary), which complicates its classification. Notably, the presence of constipation in functional dyspepsia was already recognized in the early 20th century. Today, functional dyspepsia and functional chronic constipation are increasingly categorized as manifestations of functional gastrointestinal disorders (FGIDs). The authors identify the development of a simplified clinical classification and the identification of "alarm symptoms" as significant modern achievements essential for medical strategy and tactics. However, the study notes that despite modern progress, the importance of objective examination methods in the diagnostic process has diminished, which is viewed as a limitation. The authors propose reviving these methods in clinical practice, particularly at the primary care level. Significant contemporary achievements include instrumental diagnostics and pharmacological advances that enable effective, evidence-based recommendations for treating subtypes of functional dyspepsia. Furthermore, dietary and rehabilitative guidelines have been developed to prevent the onset and progression of the disease. Finally, the paper addresses unresolved issues, including post-infectious functional dyspepsia and the ongoing debate regarding the concept of Helicobacter pylori-associated functional dyspepsia.

titre: Римські критерії V: оновлені погляди на порушення сфінктера Одді
resume: In May 2026, the Rome Foundation published the Rome V Criteria, which substantially revised the current understanding of sphincter of Oddi disorders (SOD). This review analyzes the evolution of concepts regarding SOD, from the Milwaukee classification and the Rome II–IV criteria to the current Rome V recommendations. Particular attention is given to the updated pathophysiological concepts based on disorders of gut–brain interaction, which have led to the replacement of the terms functional and sphincter of Oddi dysfunction with the broader concept of sphincter of Oddi disorders. The review discusses the contemporary principles of positive diagnosis, the updated definition of typical biliary pain, the revised diagnostic criteria for biliary and pancreatic SOD, and the changing role of invasive diagnostic procedures. The rationale for abandoning the routine use of sphincter of Oddi manometry and hepatobiliary scintigraphy is analyzed, as is the current role of endoscopic ultrasound and magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography in the modern diagnostic algorithm. Special emphasis is placed on the major revisions concerning pancreatic SOD. According to the Rome V Criteria, this diagnosis should be considered exclusively in patients with documented recurrent acute pancreatitis after thorough exclusion of all other potential etiologies. Current therapeutic strategies, the substantially narrowed indications for endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography and sphincterotomy, and the practical implications of these changes for clinical practice are also discussed. The implementation of the Rome V recommendations supports a transition toward a more evidence-based, safer, and personalized approach to the management of patients with SOD.

titre: Perinatal Mental Health in Emergencies: An EvidenceCalibrated Biosocial Framework
resume: Public health emergencies expose pregnant and postpartum women to disrupted maternity care, food insecurity, violence, displacement, bereavement, social isolation, infection, and loss of income. Mental health and psychosocial support remains essential, but the same exposures also disturb sleep and affect stress, immune, and metabolic pathways, with possible effects on the microbiota-gut-brain axis. Biological plausibility does not make a biomarker clinically useful. This Perspective sets out an evidence-calibrated biosocial framework that separates services that should be delivered now, routinely available information that should alter care, and technologies that remain investigational. It also defines a minimum workflow for disrupted systems and treats digital tools as ways to extend care rather than prerequisites for it. Biomarkers, microbiome profiling, multi-omics, and targeted biological interventions should remain research tools until they show incremental clinical value, feasibility, safety, reproducibility, affordability, and equity across settings.

titre: Bromelain-digested casein peptide pool (BDCPP) as a natural neuroprotective compound: an in silico study to explain its mechanism of action
resume: Bromelain-digested casein peptide pool (BDCPP) has been shown to alleviate chronic stress-induced behavioral and neurobiological alterations in rats; however, the molecular basis of these effects remains unclear. In the present study, an integrated in silico approach was used to investigate the possible neuroprotective mechanisms of BDCPP. Peptides generated following simulated bromelain digestion of casein were screened for safety, gastrointestinal stability, physicochemical properties, and predicted neuroprotective activities. We identified 11 peptides with favorable characteristics and selected two representative peptides (β-casein-P2 and κ-casein-P19 ) for molecular docking and molecular dynamics analyses. Both peptides showed strong and stable interactions with dipeptidyl peptidase-4 (DPP4) and glutamate carboxypeptidase II (GCPII), proteins involved in gut–brain axis communication, neuroinflammation, and glutamatergic signaling. Molecular dynamics simulations suggested the stability of the selected peptide–receptor complexes throughout the simulation period. Importantly, several peptides within the BDCPP pool displayed similar predicted biological activities, suggesting that the observed effects of BDCPP are likely mediated by the collective action of multiple bioactive peptides rather than a single dominant component. The identified interactions with DPP4 and GCPII may provide a potential molecular basis for the previously reported behavioral, cognitive, and neurobiological benefits of BDCPP and support its potential as a food-derived neuroprotective ingredient. However, these computational predictions should be considered as a hypothesis-generating framework and require further experimental validation.

titre: Induction of multilevel multi-organ eutrophic synergies: an organ-network hypothesis for simultaneous preventive and therapeutic physiological optimization
resume: Organ-specialized medicine has achieved remarkable diagnostic and therapeutic precision, yet it rarely considers the functional state of interconnected organs in the absence of overt disease. We hypothesize that simultaneous, low-intensity and directionally coherent stimulation of the major organs and systems induces eutrophic states, that is, states of optimal functional efficiency, whose network effects exceed the sum of the effects obtained by stimulating each organ in isolation. The Inducer of Multilevel Multi-organ Eutrophic Synergies (ISEMM) framework models the organism as a network of interdependent organ-nodes in which the autonomic nervous system, and the vagus nerve in particular, acts as the primary hierarchical node. A corollary is that inter-organ functional incoherence, the loss of coupling among physiological systems, is an autonomous and measurable pathological state distinct from individual organ dysfunction. The hypothesis is supported by documented neural, endocrine, immune-inflammatory and metabolic crosstalk (cardiorenal, gut-liver and microbiota-gut-brain axes), by the cholinergic anti-inflammatory reflex, by network physiology showing that health corresponds to specific patterns of inter-system coupling, and by data on organ functional reserve. Six falsifiable predictions are derived, including superiority of simultaneous over sequential stimulation at equal cumulative dose, a network-dose effect, transitive effects on unstimulated organs, an inverse relation between baseline performance and response, and slower washout than supra-threshold interventions. If confirmed, the hypothesis would support a complementary category of sub-threshold multi-target interventions, termed network normo-physiotherapy, for prevention and as an adjunct to organ-specific therapy, monitored through a proposed Systemic Eutrophy Index.Preprint, not peer reviewed. titre: Lack of healthy gut microbiota species in autism: A large cohort study
resume: Abstract Background Autism Spectrum Disorder is a neurological disorder that affects social interaction, behavior, and sensory processing. In recent years, the gut brain axis has come into focus because of its direct associations with neural mechanisms. Gut microbiome dysregulation, including depletion of beneficial probiotics, may contribute to gastrointestinal disturbances, altered metabolite production, immune dysregulation, and behavioral symptoms. It is important to see whether the gut probiotic changes in ASD reflect any pattern of deficiency across individuals or are associated with clinical symptoms and severity. Methods We performed a cross-sectional analysis of gut probiotic profiles in 1,072 individuals with ASD using a panel of 36 clinically reported probiotic species. Overall probiotic absence patterns were characterized across the cohort and compared according to demographics, dietary factors, and clinical symptoms. Organism-level associations were evaluated using contingency table analyses. Cumulative probiotic absence was quantified using an Absence Burden Score, its associations with clinical symptoms and severity were examined using logistic and multiple linear regression analyses. Results A conserved pattern of probiotic absence was observed across the cohort, predominantly involving lactic acid-producing bacteria, spore-forming Bacillus species, beneficial yeasts, and Bifidobacterium species. Similar overall patterns were observed across demographic and symptom-defined subgroups. Both organism-level analyses and the Absence Burden Score demonstrated significant associations with picky eating behavior. Picky eating behavior also increased with ASD severity, and individuals with severe ASD demonstrated significantly greater variability in the Absence Burden Score. However, absence burden score did not show consistent positive association with overall autism severity. In multivariable analyses, Absence burden score showed a small inverse association with CARS score, while no significant association was observed with GARS scores. Conclusions Children with ASD demonstrated variation within cohort in probiotic absence profile, with picky eating showing robust clinical association with absence burden score. These findings should be interpreted as pattern variation within ASD cohort observed in retrospective observational study. Further prospective controlled studies are needed to determine the clinical and biological significance of these findings.

titre: Editorial: Traditional medicine inspired drug development against central nervous system (CNS) disorders
resume: neurotransmitter regulation. Importantly for CNS drug development, ATL-III has demonstrated bloodbrain barrier penetration, although the authors identify pharmacological and toxicological characterisation, bioavailability, brain retention, and clinical evaluation as necessary next steps. Zhang et al. (2026) similarly examine Astragaloside IV as a potential neuroprotective agent for stroke, highlighting anti-inflammatory, antioxidative, and other pharmacological effectsdrawing on in vitro and in vivo studies to highlight anti-inflammatory, antioxidative, and other pharmacological effects and its potential role as an adjunctive therapy.The multi-target nature of natural products and botanical medicines is particularly evident in the contributions concerning Alzheimer's disease (AD). Wang et al. (2026) systematically analyse 28 preclinical studies of Kai-xin-san, reporting improvements in behavioural measures and changes involving Aβ and tau pathology, inflammation, oxidative stress and cholinergic function. The authors nevertheless caution that high risk of bias may result in overestimation of these effects and call for higher-quality preclinical evidence before clinical efficacy is considered. Li et al. (2026) examine botanical metabolites targeting programmed cell death pathways including apoptosis, ferroptosis, autophagy and pyroptosis, while also identifying important limitations including pan-assay interference compounds, inadequate representation of sporadic AD in existing models, bioavailability and brain targeting. Ntsapi et al. (2026) focus specifically on the potential relationship between cannabinoids, autophagy and neuronal survival, proposing multi-cannabinoid approaches as an area requiring further experimental investigation. Xu et al. (2025) provide an important reminder that therapeutic activity cannot be separated from safety. Using metabolomic, histological, and molecular approaches, the authors report that Huang-Lian-Jie-Du Decoction reduced Aβ deposition, inflammation, and neuronal damage and preserved bloodbrain barrier integrity in an AD rat model. However, administration to normal rats was associated with inflammation, impaired neuronal function, compromised blood-brain barrier integrity, and organ damage. These differential effects demonstrate why biological context and toxicity assessment must form part of the development pathway rather than being considered only after efficacy has been established. Experimental models provide another critical bridge between candidate identification and translation. Shao et al. (2026) highlight zebrafish as a platform for investigating neuroprotective traditional medicines, particularly for high-throughput screening, real-time imaging, and rapid safety assessment. At the same time, they identify limitations in neuroanatomy, drug metabolism, and the predominance of acute disease models, supporting the need for model standardisation and cross-species validation. Ranjbari et al. (2026), using a rat model, report anxiolytic-and antidepressant-like effects of astaxanthin associated with GABAergic, cholinergic and opioid pathways as well as antioxidant and anti-inflammatory mechanisms. Wang et al. (2026) similarly synthesise preclinical evidence for Sinisan in depression models, reporting changes in behavioural outcomes, monoamine neurotransmitters, hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis hormones and inflammatory markers, while cautioning that heterogeneity, risk of bias and inadequate phytochemical characterisation limit interpretation.Stroke-related contributions illustrate particularly well how evidence can progress from mechanistic investigation towards clinical evaluation. Lee et al. (2026) report that Chunghyul-dan reduced infarct volume and provided multi-level neurovascular protection in experimental ischemia, includingin preclinical models of ischemia, including effects on collateral perfusion, vascular adaptation, neuroinflammation and endothelial barrier integrity. Huang et al. (2025) integrate clinical and preclinical evidence concerning traditional Chinese medicine interventions for post-stroke cerebral edema, identifying potential effects involving ion homeostasis, aquaporins, neuroinflammation, oxidative stress, apoptosis and blood-brain barrier protection. Ren et al. (2025) extend this to comparative clinical evidence through a network meta-analysis of 70 randomised controlled trials involving 6,227 patients with acute ischemic stroke. Although several Fuzheng traditional Chinese medicine injections combined with conventional treatment showed favourable outcomes, the authors appropriately caution that methodological limitations constrain the certainty of these findings. Clinical evidence is also represented in migraine and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). Zhang et al. (2026) synthesise 57 randomised controlled trials involving 6,005 participants and identify differences in the relative performance of Chinese botanical drug decoctions for migraine, while emphasising variability in study quality and the indirect nature of treatment comparisons. Shen et al. (2026) examine 35 randomised controlled trials of traditional Chinese medicine therapies for ALS. Although some interventions achieved favourable probability rankings, no significant differences in functional status were identified between traditional Chinese medicine therapies, integrated conventional treatment, Riluzole alone, and Riluzole with placebo. This distinction between treatment ranking and demonstrated superiority is important and illustrates the need for caution when translating comparative evidence into therapeutic claims. Even where clinical data exist, favourable rankings do not constitute demonstrated clinical efficacy. Deng et al. (2026) further broaden the scope of the Topic through their examination of natural products and traditional Chinese medicine formulations for ADHD. Their synthesis identifies potential mechanisms involving catecholamine neurotransmission, neurodevelopment and synaptic plasticity, neuroinflammation and the gut-brain axis, while highlighting reliance on individual animal models and insufficient pharmacokinetic and translational evidence. These limitations are not unique to ADHD but reflect wider challenges across the field. Indeed, the quality Indeed, the quality of the evidence base itself must be considered part of drug development. Wang et al. (2026) meta-epidemiological analysis provides an important critical perspective: among 79 systematic reviews and meta-analyses of natural product extracts for ischemic stroke, 86.1% were rated as critically low in methodological quality, and substantial publication redundancy was identified. Their findings show that increasing the volume of evidence does not necessarily strengthen confidence if methodological weaknesses are repeatedly reproduced. Taken together, the contributions suggest a useful framework for the next phase of traditional-medicine-inspired CNS drug development. Traditional knowledge and natural-product diversity provide candidate compounds and formulations, but these candidates require progressive filtering through phytochemical characterisation, mechanistic investigation, appropriate disease models, pharmacokinetics, toxicity and safety assessment, blood-brain barrier and brain-targeting considerations, and ultimately well-designed clinical studies.Traditional knowledge and naturalproduct diversity provide candidates, but each requires progressive filtering through phytochemical characterisation, mechanistic and model-based investigation, pharmacokinetic and safety assessment, and ultimately well-designed clinical studies. Computational approaches, including molecular docking, network pharmacology and machine learning, may increasingly assist in integrating these layers of evidence and prioritising candidates, but prediction cannot substitute for experimental validation.Across the 16 publications, the evidence converges around five interconnected research areas: stroke and neurovascular protection, Alzheimer's disease and neurodegeneration, neuropsychiatric and neurodevelopmental disorders, mechanisms of neuroprotection, and clinical and evidence synthesis.clinical evidence synthesis (Figure 1). The stroke studies examine Astragaloside IV, Fuzheng injections, Chunghyul-dan, natural-product extracts and traditional Chinese medicine for post-stroke cerebral edema, with recurring mechanisms involving neuroinflammation, oxidative stress, vascular protection and blood-brain barrier integrity. Alzheimer's-focused studies investigate Huang-Lian-Jie-Du Decoction, Kai-xin-san, cannabinoids and botanical metabolites, converging on Aβ and tau pathology, autophagy, programmed cell death, inflammation, oxidative stress and neuronal survival.The neuropsychiatric and neurodevelopmental studies extend these shared mechanisms to ADHD, depression and anxiety through neurotransmitter regulation, synaptic plasticity, the gut-brain axis, HPA-axis regulation and inflammatory pathways. Across these disease-specific areas, the papers repeatedly describe multi-target neuroprotective effects rather than isolated mechanisms, but they also converge on four major barriers to translation: safety and toxicity, bioavailability and brain targeting, the validity and translational relevance of experimental models, and the quality of the evidence supporting efficacy. These concerns become particularly important in the systematic reviews and network meta-analyses, where promising results are frequently qualified by risk of bias, methodological limitations, heterogeneity or uncertainty in comparative evidence; notably, the methodological analysis of ischemic-stroke reviews found 86.1% to be of critically low methodological quality. Overall, the network shows that although the 16 publications investigate different medicines and CNS disorders, they collectively describe the same translational problem: moving from multi-target biological and preclinical promise towards compounds or formulations that are sufficiently characterised, safe, brainaccessible, experimentally reproducible and supported by rigorous clinical evidence to justify development as CNS therapeutics (Figure 1).Recurring mechanisms include neuroinflammation, oxidative stress, blood-brain barrier integrity, programmed cell death and autophagy in stroke and Alzheimer's disease, and neurotransmitter regulation, synaptic plasticity, HPA-axis regulation and the gut-brain axis in neuropsychiatric and neurodevelopmental disorders. Most of this evidence is preclinical, whereas the clinical evidence derives from meta-analyses of randomised controlled trials in stroke, migraine and ALS. Across all areas, the contributions converge on four barriers to translation: safety and toxicity, bioavailability and brain targeting, the validity and translational relevance of experimental models, and the quality of the evidence supporting efficacy. The significance of this research topic therefore lies not only in demonstrating therapeutic potential. It also identifies where that potential can be lost between discovery and translation. Traditional medicine offers a rich starting point for CNS drug development, but historical use, mechanistic plausibility, preclinical efficacy and even favourable comparative rankings represent different levels of evidence.but historical use, mechanistic plausibility, preclinical efficacy and favourable comparative clinical rankings represent successively higher yet distinct levels of evidence, and none is equivalent to demonstrated clinical efficacy, which requires rigorous, adequately powered randomised trials. Progress will depend on connecting these levels through rigorous, reproducible and transparent translational pipelines. The future opportunity is not simply to identify more promising natural products, but to become better at determining which candidates are sufficiently characterised, safe, biologically plausible and evidence-supported to progress towards clinically meaningful CNS therapies.but to determine which candidates merit progression towards clinically meaningful CNS therapies.

titre: Chronic low-dose pharmacological amoxicillin exposure promotes depressive and anxious behavior in mice: Alterations in gut microbiota and local field potentials within the brain
resume: Abstract Mood and anxiety disorders are prevalent in contemporary society. Recent studies suggest a potential link between exposure to antibiotics and these disorders, with antibiotics potentially adversely affecting the gut microbiome, which in turn affects physiological and neurological processes, including mood and cognition. However, the underlying mechanisms have not been extensively studied. Two-month-old male ICR mice were randomized into three groups: (1) control group; (2) 2 mg/kg amoxicillin-treated group and (3) 4 mg/kg amoxicillin-treated group. After seven days of treatment with 2 mg/kg or 4 mg/kg amoxicillin or saline, mice were subjected to tests of anxiety- and depression-like behaviors, fear memory, and spatial recognition memory. At the end of the behavioral assessment, colon histopathology and gut microbiota composition were examined in each group of mice. In addition, local field potentials (LFPs) and auditory evoked potentials (AEPs) in the hippocampus (HPC), amygdala (AMY), and ventral tegmental area (VTA) of mice in different groups were recorded. The results showed that chronic administration of amoxicillin increased anxiety- and depressive- like behaviors, enhanced cue-induced fear memory, and slightly impaired spatial recognition memory in mice. The LFP study showed an increase in gamma oscillations in VTA and AMY. Late components of the AEP in these two brain regions were also affected by amoxicillin. After long-term administration of amoxicillin, the colon of mice in the 4 mg/kg group exhibited mucosal damage and reduced crypt structures with severe inflammatory cell infiltration. Amoxicillin greatly reduced the diversity of the microbiota and also altered the composition of the gut microbiota and its predicted function. Amoxicillin treatment significantly alters gut microbiota, leading to an increase in gamma oscillations and changes in auditory evoked potential (AEP) waves in the ventral tegmental area (VTA) and amygdala (AMY), which are indicative of altered neuronal activity in brain regions associated with emotional and reward processing. These alterations may underlie the observed increase in anxiety and depressive-like behaviors, indicating that greater attention should be paid to the impact of antibiotics on psychiatric disorders.

titre: Mechanisms of Traditional Chinese Medicine Enema Therapy in the Treatment of Atopic Dermatitis: A Gut–Skin Axis Perspective
resume: Atopic dermatitis (AD) is closely associated with dysbiosis of the gut microbiota. Based on the “gut–skin axis” theory, this review comprehensively examines the mechanisms underlying traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) enema therapy in AD. Gut dysbiosis, intestinal barrier disruption, and depletion of microbial metabolites can activate systemic immunity, driving Th2/Th17 polarization and elevated IgE levels. Integrated with TCM principles of “intestinal damp–heat” and “spleen deficiency with dampness excess,” TCM enema administration achieves high local rectal concentrations through rectal delivery, exerting therapeutic effects via multidimensional mechanisms: remodeling the gut microbiota, repairing the intestinal barrier (upregulating ZO-1/Occludin), inducing regulatory T cell (Treg) differentiation, suppressing systemic inflammation through TLR4/NF-κB and vagus nerve pathways, and modulating the neuro–endocrine–immune network to alleviate the itch–anxiety cycle. Compared with the limitations and adverse effects of conventional Western therapies, TCM enema represents a “treating the gut to modulate the skin” strategy that demonstrates unique advantages in moderate-to-severe and refractory AD, offering a novel integrated approach for the prevention and management of AD.

titre: Long-term outcomes of inferior mesenteric-to-ileocolic artery anastomosis in restorative proctocolectomy with ileal pouch–anal anastomosis
resume: The study aimed to evaluate the long-term feasibility (with up to 7 years of follow-up) of vascular augmentation via inferior mesenteric-to-ileocolic artery (IMA–ICA) anastomosis to resolve excessive pouch tension secondary to mesenteric restriction during total proctocolectomy with ileal pouch–anal anastomosis (IPAA). We retrospectively analyzed the clinical data of five patients (four with ulcerative colitis, one with familial adenomatous polyposis) who underwent IPAA combined with IMA–ICA anastomosis due to excessive mesenteric tension at Zhongnan Hospital of Wuhan University from April 2018 to September 2018. During a follow-up period of up to 7 years, pouch and vascular anastomotic patency were evaluated using spectral contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) enterography (spectral CTE) and endoscopy. Defecatory control and quality of life were assessed using the Wexner incontinence score and the Cleveland Global Quality of Life (CGQL) score, respectively. All five patients completed the follow-up, with a median follow-up duration of 91 months (interquartile range [IQR], 88–93). During the follow-up period, no pouch necrosis or severe anastomotic stricture secondary to ischemia was observed. The most recent CTE revealed complete patency of the IMA–ICA anastomosis, with no evidence of thrombosis or stenosis; endoscopy demonstrated a pink pouch mucosa with adequate perfusion. At the final follow-up, the median 24-h and nocturnal defecation frequencies were 6 (range, 5–7) and 1 (range, 0–2), respectively. The median Wexner incontinence score was 2 (range, 0–4), and the median CGQL score was 0.73 (range, 0.70–0.83). Three cases of mild pouchitis resolved following medical therapy. For patients with high mesenteric tension during IPAA, IMA–ICA anastomosis effectively resolves both the excessive mesenteric tension and distal pouch ischemia. As a feasible surgical approach, it can maintain long-term pouch perfusion and mucosal health, enabling patients to achieve acceptable long-term defecatory function and quality of life.

titre: Prevalence and factors associated with insomnia in patients with diabetes mellitus: A scoping review
resume: Insomnia is a significant concern in diabetes management, as it may worsen metabolic outcomes and negatively affect patients' quality of life. Determining the prevalence of insomnia and identifying its associated factors among patients with diabetes are essential. However, evidence syntheses in this area remain limited, with particularly few reviews addressing this topic. Therefore, the scoping review maps the existing literature on insomnia among patients with diabetes mellitus, focusing on its prevalence, associated factors, and potential management strategies. The review followed the five-stage framework proposed by Arksey and O’Malley. Six electronic databases (CINAHL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science) were searched for studies published between 2002 and 2025. A total of 1,638 records were identified, of which 21 studies met the inclusion criteria and were included in the review. Among patients with diabetes, the prevalence of insomnia ranged from 9.6% to 62%, with the highest prevalence reported in a study conducted in India. Five major categories of factors associated with insomnia were identified. These included: (1) demographic and social factors, such as female sex, older age, living alone, lower educational attainment, and longer diabetes duration; (2) psychological factors, including depression, anxiety, mood disturbances, neuroticism, and maladaptive coping styles; (3) diabetes-related clinical and metabolic factors, such as higher Body Mass Index (BMI) or obesity, poor glycaemic control (indicated by elevated HbA1c and fasting blood glucose levels), insulin resistance, diabetes-related complications, fatigue, gastrointestinal symptoms, and electrolyte imbalances, particularly abnormal magnesium and phosphorus levels; (4) lifestyle and behavioral factors, including low physical activity, lack of regular exercise, smoking, and the use of sleep aids or medication; and (5) comorbid physical conditions, such as bodily pain, other coexisting health conditions, and cardiovascular diseases, including hypertension and coronary artery disease. Future research should focus on gathering qualitative evidence to understand the mechanisms and experiences related to insomnia. Keywords: Associated factors, diabetes mellitus, insomnia, prevalence, scoping review

titre: 17q12 Microdeletion Syndrome Presenting With Refractory Hypomagnesemia and Diabetes: A Case Report
resume: The 17q12 microdeletion syndrome can be inherited in an autosomal dominant manner, although most cases of the syndrome are a result of a de novo mutation. Among the more common features associated with this chromosomal change are problems with the development or function of the kidneys and urinary system. These problems can range from severe malformations of the kidneys or kidney failure before birth to mild or no problems with the kidney or urinary bladder. Characteristic features include maturity-onset diabetes of the young 5 (MODY5), speech developmental delays, intellectual disability, and neuropsychiatric disorders like schizophrenia, anxiety, and bipolar disorder. We present a patient who had uncontrolled diabetes with hypomagnesemia. More common causes of hypomagnesemia are gastrointestinal losses, poor gastrointestinal absorption, proton-pump inhibitors, diuretics, and renal losses due to nephrotoxins or tubular dysfunction. Rarely, as in this case, hypomagnesemia was caused by renal magnesium wasting.

titre: Pengaruh terapi murottal al-quran terhadap kecemasan klien dispepsia
resume: Latar Belakang: Dispepsia merupakan kumpulan gejala gastrointestinal yang dapat menimbulkan ketidaknyamanan fisik dan masalah psikologis, salah satunya kecemasan. Terapi murottal Al-Qur’an merupakan intervensi nonfarmakologis yang berpotensi memberikan efek relaksasi dan membantu mengurangi kecemasan.Metode: Penelitian ini menggunakan pendekatan kuantitatif dengan desain quasi-experimental dan rancangan two-group pretest-posttest. Sebanyak 50 responden dipilih menggunakan teknik simple random sampling dan dibagi menjadi kelompok intervensi dan kontrol. Kelompok intervensi diberikan terapi murottal Al-Qur’an selama 15 menit, sedangkan kelompok kontrol tidak mendapatkan intervensi. Tingkat kecemasan diukur menggunakan kuesioner Zung Self-Rating Anxiety Scale (ZSAS) sebelum dan sesudah intervensi. Analisis data menggunakan uji Wilcoxon.Hasil: Hasil uji Wilcoxon menunjukkan nilai p < 0,001 (p < 0,05), yang berarti terdapat perbedaan tingkat kecemasan yang signifikan antara sebelum dan sesudah pemberian terapi murottal Al-Qur’an.Kesimpulan: Terapi murottal Al-Qur’an berpotensi menjadi intervensi nonfarmakologis pendamping dalam membantu mengelola kecemasan pada klien dispepsia.
