titre: Multimodal fMRI and DTI correlates of affective symptoms in diarrhea-predominant irritable bowel syndrome: a subtype-focused neuroimaging study
resume: Objective To investigate brain structural and functional alterations in diarrhea-predominant irritable bowel syndrome (IBS-D) and their associations with affective symptoms using multimodal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). Methods 53 IBS-D patients and 55 healthy controls (HCs) underwent resting-state functional MRI (rs-fMRI) and diffusion tensor imaging (DTI). Rs-fMRI data were analyzed using fractional amplitude of low-frequency fluctuation (fALFF), z-transformed regional homogeneity (zReHo), and functional connectivity (FC). For DTI data, we extracted fractional anisotropy (FA), mean diffusivity (MD), radial diffusivity (RD), and axial diffusivity (AD) under the tract-based spatial statistics (TBSS) framework. Inter-group comparisons of rs-fMRI metrics used FDR correction ( q < 0.05), whereas DTI metrics were compared using non-parametric permutation testing with TFCE correction ( p < 0.05). Abnormal imaging metrics were correlated with scale scores of symptoms, anxiety, depression and sleep quality. Results Compared with HCs, IBS-D patients showed increased fALFF in the left cuneus, left superior and middle occipital gyri, and left pericalcarine cortex; decreased fALFF in the right insula and bilateral precuneus/posterior cingulate cortex; and increased zReHo in the left thalamus/insula and sensorimotor regions. FC was altered, characterized by reduced insula-prefrontal connectivity, decreased sensorimotor-SMA connectivity, and enhanced thalamus/insula-hippocampal connectivity. DTI revealed lower FA in the left corticospinal tract, left cingulum bundle and right uncinate fasciculus with widespread MD and RD increases. Correlation analyses showed that fALFF in precuneus/posterior cingulate cortex was positively correlated with SAS ( r = 0.422, q = 0.045), zReHo in thalamus/insula with SDS ( r = 0.489, q = 0.013), and MD with PSQI ( r = 0.360, q = 0.047). Conclusion IBS-D is associated with multi-network, multi-level alterations involving the default mode network, thalamus-insula circuit, and sensorimotor network, with exploratory associations observed between select imaging dimensions and particular affective symptom dimensions. These findings provide subtype-focused, hypothesis-generating neuroimaging evidence for brain alterations in IBS-D.

titre: The Metabolic Syndrome and Microbiota-Gut-Brain Axis—Is There a Link?
resume: Metabolic syndrome (MetS), with obesity as its primary pathogenic driver, is a major public health concern and a leading risk factor for type 2 diabetes (T2D) and cardiovascular disease. Increasing evidence highlights the critical role of the microbiota-gut-brain axis (MGBA) in the pathogenesis of these disorders through its regulation of energy homeostasis, metabolic function, and immune responses. This review summarizes current evidence on the mechanisms by which disturbances in MGBA signaling contribute to the development and progression of MetS. Gut microbiome dysbiosis may increase intestinal permeability, facilitating the translocation of bacterial lipopolysaccharide into the systemic circulation. This process may contribute to metabolic endotoxemia and chronic low-grade inflammation, potentially promoting insulin resistance, adipose tissue dysfunction, and metabolic impairment. In addition, alterations in microbiome composition and function influence the secretion of gut-derived hormones, vagal signaling, hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal axis activity and bile acid metabolism, ultimately disrupting appetite regulation, glucose homeostasis, lipid metabolism and blood pressure control. Preclinical studies and limited clinical evidence suggest that gut microbiota-targeted interventions, including prebiotics and probiotics, may improve selected metabolic parameters. However, evidence demonstrating sustained clinical benefits or reductions in cardiometabolic events in patients with MetS remains insufficient. Although the MGBA represents a potential therapeutic target, further well-designed randomized controlled trials with predefined metabolic outcomes, direct assessment of microbial function, and adequate follow-up are needed to establish the clinical efficacy and long-term safety of microbiota-targeted interventions, including fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT).

titre: From Dysbiosis to Seizure Control: The Gut-brain Axis as an Emerging Therapeutic Frontier in Epilepsy
resume: Epilepsy is a chronic neurological disorder characterized by recurrent seizures resulting from abnormal and excessive neuronal activity.Although antiseizure medications (ASMs) remain the cornerstone of treatment, approximately one-third of patients develop drug-resistant epilepsy, highlighting the need for alternative therapeutic strategies.Increasing evidence suggests that gut microbiota play an important role in the pathophysiology of epilepsy through bidirectional communication along the gut-brain axis.Beyond cataloguing these associations, this review critically appraises the methodological quality and internal consistency of the existing evidence base, identifies recurring sources of contradiction across studies (sampling design, taxonomic resolution, confounding by diet, and ASM), and proposes an integrative framework in which dysbiosis is treated as a perturbation of a functionally interconnected gutimmune-neural network rather than an isolated biomarker.Experimental and clinical studies have demonstrated alterations in gut microbial composition in patients with epilepsy and in animal models, suggesting a potential disease-associated microbial signature.Moreover, interventions targeting gut microbiota, including ketogenic diet (KD), probiotics, prebiotics, antibiotics, and fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT), have shown promising anticonvulsant effects in preclinical studies, while clinical evidence remains limited and heterogeneous.Among these approaches, the KD currently has the strongest supporting evidence, whereas other microbiota-based therapies remain in the early stages of investigation.Despite substantial progress, causal relationships between alterations in the microbiota and epilepsy are not fully understood, and standardized clinical protocols are lacking.Rather than leaving this open-ended, we reach a graded conclusion: the KD and FMT are currently the only interventions supported by experiments that can distinguish causation from correlation and such evidence is confined to animal models; probiotic, prebiotic, short-chain fatty acid, and antibiotic data remain associative.Therefore, the priority for the field is not further cross-sectional taxonomic profiling-which cannot resolve causality by design-but rather longitudinal pre-diagnosis sampling, function-level multi-omics readouts, and donor-or strain-characterized interventional trials with prespecified microbiota endpoints.Until these are available, microbiota modulation should be positioned as an adjunctive, mechanistically stratified strategy under investigation for drug-resistant epilepsy, rather than as an established therapeutic option.

titre: The menopause–gut–brain axis in postoperative delirium and long-term cognitive outcomes after surgery: an immunometabolic perspective (scoping review)
resume: The article "The Menopause–Gut–Brain Axis in Postoperative Delirium and Long-term Postoperative Cognitive Outcomes: An Immunometabolic Perspective" provides a scoping review of the complex interplay between menopause, the gut microbiota, neuroinflammation, and postoperative neurocognitive outcomes—specifically postoperative delirium (POD) and cognitive decline. The review explores the menopause–gut–brain axis, examining the mechanisms involving estrogen signaling, gut microbiota dysbiosis, intestinal barrier permeability, immune response activation, and neuroinflammation. The authors suggest that these processes may increase the susceptibility of postmenopausal women to developing POD and postoperative neurocognitive disorders (PND) following surgical procedures. Based on an analysis of 124 publications, three primary themes were identified: gut microbiota dysbiosis as a common mechanism linking menopause and cognitive impairment; neuroinflammation as a key component in the pathogenesis of POD/PND; and interleukin-6 (IL-6) as a prominent biomarker for these risks. The review further discusses the potential impact of interventions targeting the gut microbiota, bacterial metabolites, immune responses, and estrogen signaling for the prevention and treatment of postoperative neurocognitive disorders. The objective of this work was to map the existing literature, identify the links between the menopause–gut–brain axis and postoperative cognitive outcomes, and highlight research gaps, potential biomarkers, and novel therapeutic avenues.

titre: Eating Behavior in Obesity: Integration of Cognitive, Emotional, and Interoceptive Factors
resume: This preprint presents an integrative literature review on the cognitive, emotional, and interoceptive factors that shape eating behavior in obesity.Obesity is a chronic and multifactorial condition whose understanding extends beyond the balance between energy intake and expenditure. This study aimed to analyze the influence of cognitive, emotional, and interoceptive factors on eating behavior and their relationship with obesity. An integrative literature review was conducted using national and international databases, focusing on studies addressing self-regulation, emotion regulation, interoception, intuitive eating, and mindful eating.Findings indicate that difficulties in self-regulation and inhibitory control may increase vulnerability to impulsive eating, whereas rigid dietary restraint may favor compensatory episodes. Emotional eating was associated with the use of food as a coping strategy for negative affective states, while impaired interoceptive perception may compromise the recognition of hunger and satiety. Conversely, strategies that promote body awareness, intuitive eating, and mindful eating may support a more adaptive relationship with food.It is concluded that multidimensional interventions integrating cognitive, emotional, and interoceptive components are more consistent with the complexity of obesity and may improve clinical and educational practices in Nutrition.This is the English version of the article originally published in Portuguese as “Comportamento Alimentar na Obesidade: Integração de Fatores Cognitivos, Emocionais e Interoceptivos” (DOI: 10.6084/m9.figshare.31229203).

titre: The Interoceptive Zeroing Hypothesis: A Neurocomputational Model for Suicidality in Autism Spectrum Disorder and the ZERO-I Protocol for Neuroaffirmative Intervention
resume: Objective: To reformulate the Interoceptive Zeroing Hypothesis as an exploratory and testable conceptual proposal concerning a possible pathway to suicidal distress in some autistic people. Method: A theoretical essay informed by a selective narrative synthesis of research on suicidality and autism, assessment measures, predictive processing, interoception, and official Brazilian data. This paper is not a systematic review and reports no original empirical data. Results: Meta-analyses indicate elevated prevalence of suicidal ideation and attempts in autistic samples, with substantial heterogeneity across studies. Evidence on interoception in autism also varies by dimension and measurement instrument. In Brazil, census data describe people who reported an autism diagnosis, whereas mortality records identify few autism diagnoses among suicide deaths, limiting autism-specific estimates. The paper proposes that, for some people and in particular contexts, intense sensory or interoceptive distress may shape the content and perceived function of suicidal thoughts. This possibility does not replace affective, social, clinical, or environmental explanations. Conclusion: The hypothesis should be treated as a research program. The IZS-A scale and ZERO-I protocol remain unvalidated proposals; cutoffs and clinical use are not recommended before participatory, psychometric, and longitudinal studies. Supplementary Material included: Methodological Research Sheets (Fichas de Pesquisa) for participatory content validity, psychometric feasibility (COSMIN guidelines), and ethical/safety safeguards (Brazilian Law No. 14.874/2024). PORTUGUÊS Objetivo: Reformular a Hipótese do Zeramento Interoceptivo como uma proposta conceitual exploratória e testável sobre uma possível via de sofrimento suicida em algumas pessoas autistas. Método: Ensaio teórico apoiado em síntese narrativa seletiva de estudos sobre suicidabilidade e autismo, medidas de avaliação, processamento preditivo, interocepção e dados oficiais brasileiros. O artigo não é revisão sistemática e não apresenta dados empíricos originais. Resultados: Meta-análises indicam prevalência elevada de ideação suicida e tentativas em amostras autistas, com heterogeneidade importante entre estudos. A evidência sobre interocepção no autismo também varia conforme dimensão e instrumento. No Brasil, dados censitários descrevem a população que declarou diagnóstico de transtorno do espectro autista, enquanto registros de mortalidade identificam poucos diagnósticos de autismo entre mortes por suicídio, limitando estimativas específicas. Propõe-se que, para algumas pessoas e em determinados contextos, sofrimento sensorial ou interoceptivo intenso possa influenciar o conteúdo e a função atribuída a pensamentos suicidas. Essa possibilidade não substitui explicações afetivas, sociais, clínicas ou ambientais. Conclusão: A hipótese deve ser tratada como um programa de pesquisa. A escala IZS-A e o Protocolo ZERO-I permanecem propostas não validadas; não se recomendam pontos de corte ou uso clínico antes de estudos participativos, psicométricos e longitudinais. Material Suplementar incluído: Fichas de Pesquisa metodológicas para validade de conteúdo participativa, viabilidade psicométrica (diretrizes COSMIN) e salvaguardas éticas e de segurança (Lei nº 14.874/2024).

titre: Weight Bias Internalization and Disordered Eating Behavior: The Indirect Effect of Body Trust
resume: Weight bias internalization (WBI) is associated with adverse outcomes, including disordered eating. The mechanisms linking WBI to disordered eating are not well understood. Two studies examined whether deficits in body trust, a facet of interoception, may play a role. Study 1 included 330 adults with a BMI over 30 (60.6% female; Mage = 40.81) recruited using Prolific’s representative sampling procedure. Study 2 sampled 482 undergraduates in the Southern U.S. with no BMI restrictions (70% female; Mage = 19.5). In both studies, participants completed the Modified Weight Bias Internalization Scale, the Multidimensional Assessment of Interoceptive Awareness-Trusting subscale, and the Eating Pathology Symptoms Inventory. In Study 1, WBI showed significant direct associations with binge eating (b = 1.96, p < .001) and body dissatisfaction (b = 2.85, p < .001), but not restriction (b = .12, p = .59). A significant indirect effect was found for body trust in the associations between WBI and binge eating and WBI and body dissatisfaction. Gender did not significantly moderate these paths. In Study 2, results were largely reproduced, except that a significant indirect path was observed with restriction as the outcome, but not binge eating. Findings provide preliminary evidence that body trust may play a role in the association between WBI and disordered eating among men and women, and across two populations: college students and community adults with obesity. Longitudinal research is needed to clarify temporal ordering, and to determine whether interventions that enhance body trust reduce disordered eating among individuals with elevated WBI.

titre: Soul Intelligence: From Artificial Intelligence to the Intelligence Beneath Fear
resume: The intelligence we build learns its states from us. This first-person essay proposes that we build and judge intelligence, our own first and the machine's second, by whether it serves the state in which fear resolves and care widens. I call the source of that state Universal Intelligence, and living from it Soul Intelligence. The essay draws on three sources: my own Life Between Lives regressions and my practice as a facilitator; three Guides' Collective Wisdom Sessions held with fellow facilitators of the Michael Newton Institute in 2026; and the research literature on hypnosis, self-transcendent experience, near-death experience and the behaviour of AI systems. It describes the soul state by five reported qualities, sets out what the evidence does and does not support across the Yoga Vāsiṣṭha, clinical hypnosis, spiritual regression and quantum approaches, and proposes Fundamental Peace as the measurable trace of the state in ordinary life. It then reads four sentences received in regression (be at peace; resolve fear into love; create with wisdom; you are never alone) as a specification for people and for AI systems, and names five studies that could show the proposal wrong. The essay makes no claim that souls, guides or a life between lives have been shown to exist, and no claim that machines are conscious. It claims that a describable human state has measurable consequences, and that the systems we build will carry whichever state we bring to them.

titre: Effects of a mindfulness intervention on pre-competition mental states in youth athletes: a randomized controlled trial
resume: Introduction Adolescent athletes face heightened pre-competition stress, yet evidence on mindfulness interventions for this population remains limited to isolated psychological outcomes. This study examined the effects of a mindfulness-based intervention on three pre-competition mental states–anxiety, sleep quality, and psychological resilience–while testing sport type and baseline anxiety as moderators. Methods A randomized controlled trial was conducted with 120 adolescent athletes (aged 14–18 years) recruited from three specialized sport schools. Participants were randomized to an 8-week multicomponent mindfulness program (weekly group sessions plus daily practices, n = 60) or to an active sport-psychology education control ( n = 60). Outcomes were assessed at baseline (T1), post-intervention (T2), and 4-week follow-up (T3). Results The intervention produced significant improvements across all three outcomes (anxiety: –14.45 points, η 2 p = 0.23; sleep quality: –3.11 points, η 2 p = 0.20; resilience: +15.92 points, η 2 p = 0.17), with no significant changes in the control group. Individual-sport athletes showed stronger responses than team-sport athletes (η 2 p = 0.20–0.25 vs 0.15–0.18), and moderation analyses indicated that athletes with higher baseline anxiety derived greater gains in sleep quality and resilience. Exploratory mediation suggested that increased mindfulness statistically accounted for approximately 28% of the intervention effect; however, mediator and outcomes were assessed at the same post-intervention time point, limiting causal inference. All gains were maintained at the 4-week follow-up. Discussion Findings identify sport type and baseline anxiety as key predictors of mindfulness intervention effectiveness in youth athletes, offering practical guidance for tailoring mindfulness training in youth sports contexts. Results should be interpreted in light of the multicomponent design, the short follow-up, reliance on.

titre: Efficacy and Safety of Acupuncture for Insomnia Accompanied by Subthreshold Anxiety Symptoms: Protocol for a Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials (Preprint)
resume: BACKGROUND Background: Insomnia accompanied by subthreshold anxiety symptoms is common in clinical practice, with high incidence, frequent recurrence, and a tendency toward refractoriness. Insomnia can induce anxiety, and anxiety is frequently accompanied by insomnia; the 2 conditions are mutually reinforcing and form a vicious circle, with hyperarousal proposed as a shared pathophysiological substrate. Conventional treatments, including cognitive behavioral therapy and pharmacological interventions, are limited by insufficient efficacy, potential adverse effects, and substantial costs. Acupuncture has gained increasing attention owing to its efficacy, cost-effectiveness, and favorable safety profile. OBJECTIVE Objective: This review aims to evaluate the efficacy and safety of acupuncture for insomnia accompanied by subthreshold anxiety symptoms compared with (1) sham or placebo acupuncture, (2) Western pharmacotherapy, and (3) waitlist or usual care; to appraise the methodological quality and certainty of the evidence; and to determine the optimal modality, intervention frequency, and treatment duration associated with the most favorable outcomes, thereby informing evidence-based clinical practice and decision-making. METHODS Methods: Electronic searches will be performed in English-language databases (PubMed, Cochrane Library, Web of Science, Embase, and Scopus) and Chinese-language databases (China National Knowledge Infrastructure, Wanfang Data, Chinese Biomedical Literature Database, and Chinese Scientific Journal Database) from database inception to October 31, 2026, Only studies published in English or Chinese will be eligible. ChiCTR and ClinicalTrials.gov will also be searched to assess selective reporting and publication bias; registry records without published results will not be included. Randomized controlled trials of acupuncture for insomnia accompanied by subthreshold anxiety symptoms will be eligible. Comparators will be grouped into sham or placebo acupuncture, Western pharmacotherapy, and waitlist or usual care, and will not be pooled across categories; other active comparators will be described narratively. Co-primary outcomes will be the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI) and anxiety severity, the latter measured by the Hamilton Anxiety Rating Scale (HAMA) or the Zung Self-Rating Anxiety Scale (SAS), analyzed separately by scale, with HAMA prioritized and SAS used in sensitivity analyses. Secondary outcomes will be the Insomnia Severity Index, the Generalized Anxiety Disorder 7-item scale, objective sleep parameters where reported, and the incidence of adverse events. Risk of bias will be assessed using the Cochrane Risk of Bias tool, version 2 (RoB 2), and the certainty of evidence using the Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development, and Evaluation (GRADE) approach. Random-effects models with restricted maximum likelihood estimation and the Hartung-Knapp adjustment will be used as the primary analysis. Study selection, data extraction, and quality assessment will be conducted independently by 2 reviewers, with disagreements adjudicated by a third reviewer. RESULTS Results: The findings will report the efficacy and safety of acupuncture for insomnia accompanied by subthreshold anxiety symptoms on the basis of the PSQI, HAMA, SAS, Insomnia Severity Index, Generalized Anxiety Disorder 7-item scale, and adverse event rates. CONCLUSIONS Conclusions: This systematic review will synthesize the current evidence on acupuncture for insomnia accompanied by subthreshold anxiety symptoms, inform clinical practice and decision-making, and identify research gaps and directions for future investigation. CLINICALTRIAL Trial Registration: PROSPERO CRD420261554592.

titre: Mental health monitoring and digital psychological interventions in competitive athletes: A systematic review and meta-analysis
resume: Purpose and Background: This systematic review and meta-analysis aims to evaluate the effectiveness of digital psychological interventions and the validity/responsiveness of active subjective mental health monitoring tools in competitive athletes. While competitive and elite athletes face substantial training demands and competitive stressors, recent sport psychology frameworks emphasize shifting from passive psychiatric screening to data-informed active mental health monitoring and positive psychological promotion. However, existing reviews remain largely qualitative or scoping in nature, and empirical trials of mobile/digital interventions report inconsistent findings regarding participant adherence and delivery modalities. Review Questions & Objectives: 1) To quantify the pooled effects (Hedges' g) of digital, mobile app-based (mHealth), blended, and mindfulness/self-compassion psychological interventions on positive mental health outcomes (mindfulness, self-efficacy, sport confidence, psychological resilience, subjective well-being) and competitive anxiety/stress reduction in competitive athletes. 2) To synthesize empirical evidence on longitudinal active subjective mental health monitoring tools (ecological momentary assessment [EMA], daily wellness questionnaires, SRSS, ARSS, RESTQ-Sport, SMHAT-1, and APSQ) in tracking athletes' stress-recovery states and psychological well-being. 3) To examine potential moderators of intervention efficacy through subgroup analyses and meta-regression, including delivery mode (self-guided standalone app vs. blended/practitioner-guided), content specificity (sport-tailored vs. generic), intervention duration, and objective participant adherence rate (%). Methods Overview (PICOS): - Population (P): Competitive, elite, professional, national, collegiate (e.g., NCAA), and youth academy athletes from any sport (healthy, sub-clinical, and symptomatic athletes are eligible). - Intervention/Exposure (I): Digital/online/app-based psychological interventions (mindfulness, CBT, ACT, self-compassion, psychological skills training) and longitudinal active subjective mental health monitoring. - Comparator (C): Waitlist control, treatment-as-usual (regular sport training), active control (for intervention trials); or within-participant repeated longitudinal measures (for monitoring studies). - Outcomes (O): Standardized measures of mindfulness (FFMQ, MAAS), self-efficacy/confidence (ASES, CSAI-2R), resilience/coping (CD-RISC, ACSI-28), psychological well-being (WEMWBS, WHO-5), perceived recovery/stress, and competitive anxiety. - Data Synthesis: Random-effects meta-analyses (REML estimator) will be conducted to pool standardized mean differences (Hedges' g) and correlation coefficients (r) with 95% confidence intervals. Heterogeneity will be assessed using Cochran's Q and I-squared statistics, methodological quality via Cochrane RoB 2.0 and JBI checklists, and overall evidence certainty via GRADE. Expected Outcomes: This project is expected to provide the first quantitative pooled effect estimates establishing how active subjective monitoring and digital psychological interventions promote mental health and resilience in competitive athletes, while identifying key adherence and design factors that optimize real-world implementation in elite sport settings.

titre: Self-guided digital intervention for depression symptoms during perinatal period: Results from a large-scale randomized controlled trial in the United States (Preprint)
resume: INTERNATIONAL REGISTERED REPORT RR2-10.1002/nur.22092 UNSTRUCTURED Background: Perinatal depression, occurring in pregnancy and throughout postpartum, is common and carries negative consequences for maternal, child, and family health. Self-guided digital (internet and/or app-based) interventions can reduce barriers and may prevent or address symptom development. Objective: The purpose of this study was to evaluate a self-guided digital intervention for use from pregnancy through six months postpartum, which has previously shown promise in non-US populations and has been adapted here for a US audience. Methods: We evaluated a self-guided digital intervention (Mamma Mia) in a three-arm parallel assignment randomized controlled trial with pregnant participants across the US, recruited using nationwide social media advertising and targeted local recruitment. All study activities were conducted remotely, and outcomes were collected via online self-report questionnaires. Participants were randomized in equal allocation to either: (a) Intervention Only (Mamma Mia; fully self-guided); (b) Intervention Plus Support (Mamma Mia+; self-guided plus 5 brief contacts from study nurses via phone or text); or (c) Usual Care Control. The 44-module intervention was used by pregnant participants from entrance into the study (approximately 25 weeks gestation) through 6 months postpartum, offering multi-modal content including psychoeducation about maternal mental health, infant development, and perinatal resources; self-monitoring of mental health symptoms; guided mindfulness and gratitude practices; and practices to enhance social support for mental health. Depression symptoms were assessed as the primary outcome and perinatal anxiety, stress, and subjective well-being as secondary outcomes, from enrollment to 6 months postpartum. A post-hoc analysis explored the effect of any exposure to the intervention, evaluating the trajectory of symptoms in participants of both intervention groups combined. Results: A total of 1757 individuals were randomized and included in this analysis. Those assigned to the Intervention Only (n=585) and Intervention Plus (n=586) groups showed persistently lower depression symptoms over time compared to the usual care controls (n=586) through the end of pregnancy and all postpartum assessments (e.g., at 6 months, control mean (M6.7 [SD4.88]) vs intervention (M5.8, [SD5.22]; Bonferroni adjusted p=0.04) and vs intervention plus (M5.8 [SD 5.76], Bonferroni adjusted p=0.02). There were no significant group differences in subjective well-being or perceived stress over time. The Intervention Only group differed from controls on perinatal-specific anxiety at end of pregnancy and early postpartum. In an exploratory post-hoc analysis, individuals with low baseline depression symptoms who had exposure to the intervention maintained low depression throughout the study; individuals with high baseline depression symptoms who had exposure to the intervention experienced decreased depression symptoms over time. Conclusions: This study demonstrates effects of a self-guided digital universal intervention program for perinatal depression and anxiety symptoms, but not subjective well-being or perceived stress. Exposure to the intervention in this study led to sustained improvements in depression symptoms from pregnancy through postpartum.

titre: Team-Based, Community–Delivered vs Office-Based Cognitive Behavior Therapy for Pediatric Anxiety and Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder: A Comparative Effectiveness Study
resume: Background: Anxiety disorders, including obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), are among the most common forms of psychopathology in youth. Cognitive behavior therapy (CBT) using exposure is a highly effective treatment, yet few youths receive it due in part to barriers attributable to the office-based manner in which it is often delivered. In 2017, our Parent Advisory Council identified 3 ways in which this treatment model did not meet the needs of all families with anxious children: (1) a shortage of appropriate providers delays treatment, (2) logistical problems (transportation, work schedules) impede ongoing participation in office-based care, and (3) families face difficulty executing treatment plans without direct support in the home. Objectives: The present study (1) compared the relative effectiveness of team-based, community-delivered CBT vs office-based CBT for anxiety/OCD for improving family treatment engagement/satisfaction, reducing anxiety symptoms, and reducing associated disability (quality of life and functional impairment); (2) examined predictors of treatment response, including severity of illness, caregiver burden, barriers to treatment access, and family accommodation; and (3) explored group differences in time course of response, durability of treatment gains, provider volume/capacity, and efficiency. Methods: This randomized trial compared team-based, community-delivered vs office-based delivery of up to 24 weeks of exposure-based CBT for 335 youth aged 5 to 18 years with anxiety and/or OCD. The intervention content was consistent across groups. In the team-based condition, treatment was delivered by a bachelor’s degree–level exposure coach and a PhD-level psychologist, with 3 visits a month taking place in the home or community (exposure coach) and 1 monthly visit in the office (PhD). In the office-based condition, PhD-level providers delivered all weekly sessions (4 visits a month) in the outpatient clinic setting. Participant symptoms were assessed by independent evaluators at baseline, weeks 6, 12, 18, and 24 (or end of treatment). Naturalistic follow-up assessments were conducted at 3 months (per protocol, week 36) and 6 months (per protocol week 48) post-treatment. The week-48 assessment point was the preregistered primary comparative effectiveness research (CER) outcome for the trial. Results: The final sample included 335 randomly assigned participants with a mean (SD) age of 11.2 (3.4) years. Most participants (61.8%) had multiple diagnoses, and 68.7% of participants were classified as “markedly” or “severely” ill. Most participants (66.6%) had received prior treatment, but only 28.4% had received prior exposure therapy. The primary CER result, the estimated percentage of responders at week-48 follow-up, was 81.4% (95% CI, 74.8%-86.9%) for participants randomly assigned to the team-based, community delivered condition and 69.3% (95% CI, 61.6%-76.3%) for those randomly assigned to the office-based condition. The discrete time survival analysis, with indicators for follow-up week, controlled for a priori specified covariates (age, race or ethnicity, stimulant, and serotonin reuptake inhibitor use) and showed a significant effect for treatment group (odds ratio, 1.34 [95% CI, 1.02-1.74]; P = .03). The team-based, community-delivered condition also had higher rates of session attendance than the office-based condition. Caregiver and participant engagement, satisfaction, and reduction in functional impairment were rated highly in both treatment conditions post-treatment, and there were no significant between-group differences. None of the moderators influenced participant response rate. Participants in the team-based, community-delivered condition responded better and faster to treatment than those in the office-based condition, although both treatment groups had similar durability of treatment gains. Licensed provider time was more efficiently used in the team-based, community-delivered condition; however, overall use of total provider time was less in the office-based condition. Conclusions: The results of this study provide important information on the effectiveness of a team-based, community-delivered treatment model with the potential to increase licensed provider capacity and reduce barriers to access to care. Both treatment arms led to very high rates of treatment response, engagement, and satisfaction across multiple independent evaluator-, caregiver-, and participant-rated measures; however, participants in the team-based, community-delivered arm had higher response rates throughout follow-up and responded more quickly. To our knowledge, this study is among the largest single-site effectiveness studies in pediatric anxiety/OCD and is especially notable in terms of the innovative service model, diagnostic complexity of the sample, use of empirically derived quality assurance and supervision strategies, and purposeful long-term engagement of a network of study stakeholders. Limitations: Primary limitations of this study include a lack of racial and ethnic diversity in the sample; the setting being in an academic medical center specialty clinic, which affected recruitment; use of highly experienced licensed providers as both clinicians and supervisors; the interruption caused by the COVID-19 pandemic; and the lack of opportunity to test a full telehealth model of team-based treatment as part of this study.

titre: Perfectionism vs. Excellencism: A Longitudinal Analysis of Clinical Outcomes
resume: Perfectionism has repeatedly been suggested as a risk and maintenance factor for mental health problems such as depression, anxiety, obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) and eating disorders (Shafran, & Mansell, 2001; Egan et al., 2010). Simultaneously, beneficial properties have been reported in association with higher levels of perfectionism, such as increased performance outcomes (Bellam & Curran, 2025) and greater perceived meaning in life, when differentiating between different facets of perfectionism (Suh et al., 2017; Park & Jeong, 2014). These findings emphasise the need for further research into the proposed dimensions of perfectionism as well as their potential effects on performance and mental health outcomes. To approach these inconsistencies, Gaudreau (2019) proposes the Model of Excellencism and Perfectionism (MEP), which suggests the potential need to review the degree of excellencism when investigating perfectionism and its impact on health-related outcomes. This study aims to replicate the conceptual distinction between perfectionism and excellencism as separate constructs, and examine their predictive value for clinically relevant outcomes such as levels of self-esteem and experienced psychological symptoms. For this purpose, this study conducts a secondary 4-week-longitudinal analysis of data provided by Müller et al. (2026). The data used in this study has been collected for validation purposes of an ultra-brief version of the Scale of Perfectionism and Excellencism (SCOPE; Gaudreau et al., 2022).

titre: LITTLE OWLS Children's Health Study
resume: The LITTLE OWLS study is a prospective, longitudinal birth cohort study investigating early-life microbiome development and its association with physical and mental health outcomes during childhood. Recruitment began in 2024, enrolling families from late pregnancy through the child's first 6 years of life, with a target of at least 1000- 1200 children and their families. The study characterizes longitudinal microbiome trajectories-including resilience and dysbiosis-and their relationship to common chronic diseases. Data are collected via online surveys, symptom and medication diaries, annual clinical exams, and repeated biological sampling of the child, mother, father/partner, siblings, and household environment. Findings are intended to support future diagnostics, prevention, and therapy for common chronic physical and mental diseases.

titre: Role of the Holdemanella Biformis-Related Amino Acid Metabolic Guild and Intestinal Barrier Injury in Cardiopulmonary Bypass-Associated Delayed Neurocognitive Recovery: A Prospective Observational Cohort Study
resume: Delayed neurocognitive recovery (dNCR) is a common neurological complication in adult patients undergoing cardiac surgery with cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB). Emerging evidence suggests that CPB-associated hypoperfusion and perioperative stress remodel the gut microbiome and impair intestinal barrier integrity, which may contribute to neuroinflammation and cognitive decline via the gut-brain axis. This prospective observational cohort study aims to investigate the longitudinal trajectories of the gut metagenome (specifically focusing on Holdemanella biformis and amino acid metabolic functions), fecal and plasma metabolites (L-lysine, L-tryptophan, tryptophanol, and short-chain fatty acids), and plasma markers of intestinal barrier injury (I-FABP) and endotoxin response (LBP) from pre-operation (T0) to post-operation (T2) in adult CPB patients, and to evaluate their associations with postoperative dNCR and domain-specific cognitive changes.

titre: Hyperbaric Oxygen Therapy (HBOT) for Refractory Crohn's Perianal Fistulae: a Prospective Interventional Pilot Study
resume: Background Perianal fistulae are among the most disabling complications of Crohn's disease, causing significant morbidity, impaired quality of life, and substantial healthcare utilisation. Despite advances in biologic and surgical therapies, many patients experience persistent fistula drainage and fail to achieve durable healing. Tissue hypoxia is a key regulator of intestinal inflammation and impaired wound healing in inflammatory bowel disease. Hyperbaric oxygen therapy (HBOT) increases tissue oxygenation, promotes angiogenesis, modulates inflammatory pathways, and may enhance fistula healing. Preliminary studies suggest that HBOT is a safe and effective adjunctive treatment for refractory perianal Crohn's fistulae, with reported clinical response rates of 75-87% and remission rates of 50-60%. However, current evidence is limited by small sample sizes and the absence of prospective studies within UK clinical practice. Aim To evaluate the preliminary efficacy of HBOT in patients with refractory perianal Crohn's fistulae treated in an outpatient setting. Methods This prospective pilot study will recruit ten adults with refractory perianal Crohn's fistulae from the Inflammatory Bowel Disease service at Barts Health NHS Trust. Refractory disease will be defined as persistent fistula drainage or failure to heal despite optimised medical therapy and appropriate surgical management. Participants will undergo HBOT 100% oxygen at 2.4 ATA for approximately 90 minutes per session, 40 sessions over 8 weeks. The primary outcome will be overall clinical response, defined as either clinical remission (complete cessation of fistula drainage) or partial response (clinically meaningful reduction in drainage and symptoms). Secondary outcomes will include treatment adherence, safety, tolerability, patient acceptability, and feasibility of recruitment and study completion. Expected Impact This pilot study will generate preliminary efficacy and feasibility data to inform the design, outcome measures, and sample size calculations of a larger clinical trial evaluating HBOT as a novel treatment strategy for refractory perianal Crohn's disease in the United Kingdom.

titre: Efficacy and Safety Exploration of Short Course Radiotherapy Followed by Surufatinib and Toripalimab in Neoadjuvant Treatment of Locally Advanced Rectal Cancer
resume: Why is this study conducted? The purpose of this study is to improve treatment efficacy, particularly the pathological complete response rate, in patients with high-risk/extremely high-risk locally advanced rectal cancer (LARC). While advances have been achieved with neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy combined with immunotherapy in recent years, regional recurrence and distant metastasis remain unresolved. New therapeutic strategies for this patient population are therefore urgently needed. Rectal cancer management typically includes surgery, radiation therapy and chemotherapy. Treatment paradigms are shifting toward neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy plus immunotherapy, which has demonstrated promising potential in several clinical trials. These data indicate that short-course radiotherapy combined with anti-angiogenic agents and immune checkpoint inhibitors may improve patient prognosis and tumor response. Nevertheless, the efficacy and safety of this regimen in high-risk patients require further validation. Against this background, the study evaluates a novel regimen of short-course radiotherapy followed by surufatinib and toripalimab (anti-PD-1) to raise the pathological complete response rate. The investigators also explore efficacy-related biomarkers including RAS/BRAF status and gene expression profiles to support personalized treatment. This study aims to optimize therapy for LARC patients and inform future treatment strategies. Why are participants invited to participate in this study? Participants are considered eligible for enrollment upon diagnosis of high-risk or extremely high-risk locally advanced rectal cancer consistent with study inclusion criteria. Eligibility requires confirmed pathological diagnosis, appropriate tumor location, and absence of severe comorbidities or exclusionary diseases (e.g., recurrent rectal cancer, cardiac dysfunction). Final enrollment decisions are made by study physicians based on individual clinical conditions. What do participants need to do to participate in this study? Study participation requires adherence to predefined procedures. Participants receive scheduled medical assessments including blood tests, imaging scans and anorectal function evaluation. During the study period, participants may complete questionnaires and provide biospecimens (e.g., blood samples) for efficacy analysis. The study team defines the frequency and content of each follow-up to maintain continuous monitoring throughout treatment. Compliance with study procedures supports evaluation of regimen efficacy. What are the risks of participating in this study? This study applies neoadjuvant short-course radiotherapy, anti-PD-1 monoclonal antibody (toripalimab), and anti-angiogenic therapy (surufatinib). Potential risks for participants are listed below: Risk of neoadjuvant short-course radiotherapy: Participants may develop grade ≥3 adverse events including, but not limited to, severe diarrhea, grade 3 neutropenia and grade 3 radiation dermatitis, which may impair quality of life. Risk of anti-PD-1 monoclonal antibody: Toripalimab may induce immune-related adverse events (irAEs) across organ systems. Common irAEs include skin toxicity (papules, pruritus; incidence 30%-40%), diarrhea/colitis (8%-19%), fatigue (16%-24%), immune-related hepatitis (5%), hypothyroidism (4%-10%), and hyperthyroidism (4%). Approximately two-thirds of patients receiving immune checkpoint inhibitors develop irAEs of varying severity, and serious adverse events are non-negligible. Risk of anti-angiogenic therapy: Surufatinib may trigger adverse events related to anti-angiogenic and immunomodulatory effects. Common adverse events (incidence \>20%) include proteinuria, hypertension, bleeding, liver dysfunction and diarrhea. Among grade ≥3 adverse events, hypertension (29.7%), proteinuria (14.5%), liver dysfunction (12.8%) and bleeding (4.5%) predominate. Rarely, treatment-related death may occur secondary to gastrointestinal hemorrhage or cerebral hemorrhage. Handling of research related injuries? This interventional study introduces no extra risks beyond standard clinical care. Any harm arising from study participation will be addressed for compensation and liability in accordance with applicable laws and regulations.

titre: The Analgesic Effects of Chest Orthosis Application in Costal Fractures in the Emergency Department and Its Effects on Quality of Life
resume: Rib fractures are a common cause of acute pain after blunt chest trauma. In the emergency department, pain is usually managed with a multimodal approach including nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), opioids, local anesthetic sprays, patches and nerve blocks. Systemic analgesics may cause gastrointestinal, renal and hepatic adverse effects, and opioids carry the risk of respiratory depression and dependence. External chest wall stabilization with a rib orthosis may reduce pain by stabilizing the fracture with fewer systemic adverse effects. This randomized, open-label, controlled trial compares the Chrisofix Chest Orthosis (CCO) combined with ibuprofen versus ibuprofen alone in adult patients presenting to the emergency department with fewer than three rib fractures. Pain intensity (Numeric Rating Scale), functional limitation, analgesic consumption and adverse events are assessed during emergency department observation and during a 7-day post-discharge follow-up.

titre: Effect of a Six-Week Mindfulness-Based Intervention on Glycemic Control, Cardiovascular Autonomic Function, Anxiety, and Depression in Adults With Type 2 Diabetes: A Randomized Controlled Trial
resume: The goal of this clinical trial was to learn whether a six-week mindfulness program, added to standard diabetes treatment, improves blood sugar control, heart rate variability (a measure of how the nervous system regulates the heart), anxiety, and depression in adults aged 18 to 60 years with type 2 diabetes. The main questions it aimed to answer were: * Does the mindfulness program lower glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c), fasting blood glucose, and 2-hour postprandial blood glucose? * Does it improve heart rate variability, cardiovascular autonomic dysfunction status, and anxiety and depression scores? Researchers compared participants who received standard therapy plus the mindfulness program with participants who received standard therapy alone. Participants in the mindfulness group listened to weekly audio-guided practices sent through WhatsApp (mindful eating, breathing exercise, body scan, mindful walking, dealing with unpleasant experiences, and loving-kindness meditation) and were asked to practice daily for six weeks. All participants had blood tests, a 3-minute heart rate variability recording, and the Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale questionnaire at the start of the study and after six weeks.

titre: Efficacy and Neural Mechanisms of Individualized Neuromodulation Combined With Thought Suppression Training in Individuals With Internalizing Disorders
resume: This study aims to investigate the therapeutic efficacy and neural mechanisms of individualized neuromodulation combined with autobiographical Think/No-Think (TNT) thought suppression training in individuals with internalizing disorders, including anxiety disorders, depressive disorders, obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), and post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), including complex PTSD (cPTSD). Internalizing disorders share common clinical features, including excessive negative emotional processing, impaired regulation of intrusive thoughts and memories, and difficulties in cognitive control. Increasing evidence suggests that impaired thought suppression is a transdiagnostic mechanism contributing to persistent negative thoughts, intrusive memories, rumination, and emotional dysregulation across different psychiatric conditions. However, effective interventions targeting this shared cognitive mechanism remain limited. This study is designed to examine whether individualized neuromodulation targeting abnormal neural circuits and oscillatory activity can enhance thought suppression ability and improve clinical symptoms. The study is based on the hypothesis that dysfunction of prefrontal-limbic and memory-related networks, including altered interactions between prefrontal cortex, hippocampal, and amygdala-related circuits, contributes to impaired cognitive control over unwanted thoughts and memories. Furthermore, individual differences in neural oscillatory characteristics may provide biomarkers for optimizing neuromodulation parameters. Eligible participants with internalizing disorders will undergo comprehensive clinical assessments, behavioral assessments, electroencephalography (EEG), and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) evaluations before intervention. Behavioral assessment will include an autobiographical Think/No-Think (TNT) paradigm designed to measure participants' ability to intentionally regulate retrieval of unwanted autobiographical memories. EEG and MRI assessments will be used to characterize individual neural oscillatory features and functional brain network characteristics associated with cognitive control, emotional regulation, and memory processing. Participants will be randomly assigned to one of five parallel intervention groups according to the study protocol: Individualized temporal interference stimulation (TIS) combined with autobiographical TNT thought suppression training; Individualized beta-frequency transcranial alternating current stimulation (tACS) combined with autobiographical TNT thought suppression training; Sham neuromodulation combined with autobiographical TNT thought suppression training; Individualized beta-frequency tACS alone; Individualized TIS alone. The first neuromodulation approach, individualized tACS, targets the right anterior dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (aDLPFC), a key region involved in cognitive control and thought suppression. The stimulation frequency will be individualized according to each participant's resting-state EEG beta-band peak characteristics. The second neuromodulation approach, individualized TIS, aims to modulate deep brain networks involved in emotional memory regulation and cognitive control. TIS stimulation parameters will be individualized according to participant-specific neurophysiological characteristics, with a focus on theta-related neural activity associated with limbic and memory-related circuits. During the combined intervention conditions, individualized tACS or TIS will be administered concurrently with autobiographical TNT training. Participants will practice intentionally retrieving autobiographical memories during Think trials and suppressing retrieval of unwanted autobiographical memories during No-Think trials. The tACS-only and TIS-only groups will receive the corresponding individualized neuromodulation intervention without TNT training, allowing evaluation of the independent effects of neuromodulation and comparison with combined neuromodulation-cognitive training approaches. Sham stimulation combined with TNT training will serve as a control condition for evaluating the specific contribution of active neuromodulation. The intervention period will last six days according to the study protocol. Clinical symptoms, thought suppression ability, emotional regulation, and behavioral performance will be assessed before and after intervention. Additional clinical follow-up assessments will be conducted at one month and six months after intervention to evaluate the durability of treatment effects.EEG and MRI assessments will be performed before and after intervention to investigate neurophysiological and neural network changes associated with treatment response.

titre: Different responses to hyoscine and bisacodyl in functional constipation and irritable bowel syndrome
Lactiplantibacillus plantarum alleviates Parkinson's disease progression by reducing enteroendocrine α-synuclein aggregation in a rotenone-induced mouse model
resume: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder driven by α-synuclein (α-syn) aggregation and accumulation. Recent evidence suggests that gut dysbiosis may trigger α-syn accumulation in the enteric nervous system, which spreads to the brain via the vagus nerve. Restoring the gut microbial balance through probiotic intervention offers a promising strategy to mitigate gut-origin pathology in PD. Lactiplantibacillus plantarum PS128 (PS128), a probiotic strain with neuroprotective properties, has shown neurotherapeutic benefits in PD models and patients; however, its mechanisms remain unclear. In a rotenone-induced PD mouse model, we found that PS128 supplementation significantly improved motor deficits and gastrointestinal dysfunction, reversed enteroendocrine cell (EEC) hyperplasia in the proximal colon (PC), and reduced α-syn accumulation in both intestinal and brain tissues. Notably, phosphorylated α-syn levels were significantly elevated in EECs, the myenteric plexus, and the substantia nigra, and these elevations were reversed by PS128. Furthermore, using real-time calcium imaging in a zebrafish model, we demonstrated that PS128 directly activates EECs. Transcriptomic profiling of the PC revealed calcium signaling and vitamin D metabolism as the major pathways modulated by PS128. Consistent with the transcriptomic findings, biochemical analyses demonstrated that PS128 increased serum calcium and 25-hydroxyvitamin D levels. Moreover, 16S rRNA sequencing and correlation analysis revealed that PS128 modulated gut microbiota composition in PD-like mice, with changes in specific taxa correlating with α-syn burden and calcium regulation. Taken together, our findings suggest that PS128 alleviates PD-like pathology through modulation of the gut-brain axis and provide mechanistic insights into the neuroprotective actions of probiotics.

titre: Comamonas aquatica diet inhibits TIR-1/SARM1-induced axon degeneration by providing vitamin B12
resume: Emerging evidence suggests the microbiome critically influences the onset and progression of neurodegenerative diseases; however, the identity of neuroprotective bacteria and the molecular mechanisms that respond within the host remain largely unknown. Here, we leverage Caenorhabditis elegans' well-characterized nervous system and ability to eat uni-bacterial diets to determine how metabolites and neuroprotective molecules from single species of bacteria suppress degeneration of motor neurons. We find that Comamonas aquatica significantly protects against degeneration induced by overexpressing a key regulator of axon degeneration, TIR-1/SARM1. Genetic analyses and metabolomics reveal Comamonas protects against neurodegeneration by providing sufficient vitamin B12 to activate METR-1/MTR methionine synthase in the intestine, which then lowers toxic levels of homocysteine in TIR-1-expressing animals. Defining a molecular pathway between Comamonas and neurodegeneration adds significantly to our understanding of gut-brain interactions and, given the prominent role of homocysteine in neurodegenerative disorders, reveals how such a bacterium could protect against disease.

titre: Effects of Lactiplantibacillus plantarum SG5 on anxiety, insomnia, and gut microbiota composition in college students
resume: Accumulating evidence suggests that the gut microbiota can significantly improve psychiatric symptoms such as insomnia and anxiety via the gut‑brain axis. However, current studies on probiotics for improving insomnia and anxiety in college students remain relatively scarce. In this study, Lactiplantibacillus plantarum SG5 was used to evaluate the potential therapeutic effect on insomnia and anxiety in college students by Hamilton Anxiety Scale (HAMA) and Athens Insomnia Scale (AIS). Subsequently, high-throughput sequencing was used to analyze the composition of the gut microbiota after the intervention. The results showed that 113 participants completed the clinical trial, with 56 in the placebo group (MP group) and 57 in the probiotic group (MB group). Compared to the MP, L. plantarum SG5 intervention significantly improved anxiety levels (MP vs. MB = 16.50 vs. 12.00, p = 0.0011) and insomnia severity (MP vs. MB = 11.00 vs. 8.00, p < 0.0001). Gut microbiota analysis after the intervention showed differences in microbiota composition and diversity between the two groups (35 participants per group). Specifically, after L. plantarum SG5 intervention, microbial diversity decreased, while the relative abundance of Bifidobacterium (p < 0.01) and Lactobacillus (p < 0.05) significantly increased. In contrast, the relative abundance of Bacteroides (p < 0.01) and Prevotella (p < 0.05) significantly decreased. These findings provide a possible idea supporting the development of SG5 may as a microbial agent for insomnia and anxiety in clinical settings ( https://www.chictr.org.cn/showproj.html?proj=213770 : ChiCTR2400083149, April 16, 2024).

titre: Diet-Driven Modulation of the Gut Microbiome to Enhance Neuroplasticity and Cognitive Recovery After Ischemic Stroke
resume: Cognitive impairment and limited neuroplastic recovery remain major contributors to long-term disability following ischemic stroke. Increasing evidence suggests that stroke-induced disruption of the gut-brain axis, characterized by microbiome dysbiosis and altered microbial metabolite signaling, may influence post-stroke inflammation, synaptic remodeling, and cognitive outcomes. Diet is a key modifiable determinant of gut microbiome composition and metabolic output, yet its role in post-stroke neuroplasticity has not been comprehensively synthesized. This narrative review examines dietary interventions with mechanistic or translational relevance to ischemic stroke recovery, including Mediterranean dietary patterns, ketogenic diets, high-fiber and prebiotic-enriched diets, probiotic and synbiotic supplementation, and intermittent fasting or caloric restriction. We summarize evidence linking diet-induced microbiome modulation to neuroinflammatory regulation, short-chain fatty acid signaling, microglial activity, mitochondrial function, and synaptic plasticity. Shared and diet-specific pathways are discussed, along with current limitations of the evidence base and barriers to clinical translation. Collectively, available data support a biologically plausible role for targeted dietary modulation of the gut microbiome as an adjunctive strategy to enhance cognitive recovery and neuroplasticity after ischemic stroke. Further well-designed clinical studies integrating microbiome profiling, neuroimaging, and cognitive outcomes are needed to define therapeutic potential and guide implementation in stroke rehabilitation. Among these dietary interventions, Mediterranean, high-fiber, and prebiotic-enriched diets currently have the strongest available evidence, while ketogenic and intermittent fasting approaches remain the least supported based on existing clinical and translational evidence.
revue: Journal of the American Heart Association

titre: Reply to correspondence: Gastrointestinal determinants of levodopa response in Parkinson's disease: An integrated perspective
resume: levodopa pharmacokinetic variability in Parkinson's disease, and we agree that gastrointestinal determinants of treatment response extend beyond gastric emptying. However, our review was deliberately focused on gastroparesis, while explicitly acknowledging that levodopa is absorbed in the duodenum and proximal jejunum and that gastrointestinal dysfunction in Parkinson's disease may involve more generalized transit abnormalities, small intestinal bacterial overgrowth, and gut microbiota-related mechanisms. Importantly, prolonged small bowel transit alone does not establish the direction or magnitude of its effect on levodopa bioavailability, nor does current evidence demonstrate that intestinal dysmotility is a more direct or predominant determinant than delayed gastric emptying. Rather than opposing gastric and intestinal mechanisms, we propose that gastric emptying, small bowel motility, and other pharmacokinetic, pharmacodynamic, and disease-related factors should be viewed as sequential, interdependent, and patient-specific determinants of levodopa response. Integrated studies combining gastrointestinal transit assessment, levodopa pharmacokinetics, and motor outcomes are therefore warranted.

titre: Plasma LBP and sCD14 levels in Parkinson's disease with Asian LRRK2 risk variants: Associations with systemic inflammation and clinical severity
resume: LRRK2 is implicated in the Parkinson's disease (PD) microbiome-gut-brain axis. We compared plasma lipopolysaccharide-binding protein (LBP) and soluble CD14 (sCD14), markers of gut permeability and endotoxin exposure, in PD patients with/without LRRK2 p.G2385R and/or p.R1628P and controls, and examined their associations with systemic inflammation and clinical severity. Neither marker differed between groups. Among PD patients, LBP correlated with higher IL-6, TNF-α, and worse motor function, while sCD14 correlated with higher IL-6, CCL5, and worse constipation, with no LRRK2 risk variant-specific associations. Further prospective longitudinal studies are warranted to determine the clinical significance of these associations.

titre: The hidden costs of stoma care in Canada: a primer for physicians and call to action
resume: SummaryOstomy surgery is a life-saving intervention for gastrointestinal, urologic, and gynecologic conditions. While the surgical procedure itself is publicly funded in Canada, patients often face substantial out-of-pocket postoperative expenses. Annual expenses can exceed $1000, with concerns such as peristomal skin complications and parastomal hernias further increasing the financial burden. Gaps in provincial and territorial funding models leave many people in Canada with inadequate insurance coverage, forcing difficult trade-offs between essential stoma care and basic living needs. This commentary highlights the important role that physicians play in recognizing these hidden costs, connecting patients with available resources, and advocating for more equitable access to specialized care and funding to improve the quality of life of people living with a stoma.
revue: Canadian journal of surgery. Journal canadien de chirurgie

titre: Efficacy and safety of deucravacitinib versus placebo in active psoriatic arthritis: a systematic review and meta-analysis
resume: BACKGROUND: Deucravacitinib is a first-in-class selective TYK2 inhibitor approved for plaque psoriasis. No comprehensive systematic review and meta-analysis (SRMA) has evaluated its multidomain efficacy and safety in psoriatic arthritis (PsA). METHODS: We conducted a PRISMA compliant SRMA comparing deucravacitinib 6 mg once daily versus placebo in adults with active PsA. Effect sizes were expressed as odds ratios (OR) or mean differences (MD) with 95% confidence intervals. Heterogeneity was assessed using the I2 statistic and the certainty of evidence was graded using the GRADE framework. RESULTS: Three RCTs (N = 1430) were included, all rated low risk of bias. Deucravacitinib significantly outperformed placebo across all ACR response thresholds (ACR20: OR 2.07 [1.68-2.56]; ACR50: OR 2.13 [1.63-2.79]; ACR70: OR 2.42 [1.61-3.63]). Significant benefits were observed across composite disease activity indices including DAS28-CRP remission (OR 2.14 [1.62-2.82]) and DAPSA remission (OR 3.50 [2.04-6.00]), as well as minimal disease activity. Dermatological outcomes showed large treatment effects though with substantial heterogeneity. Significant improvements were also demonstrated in physical function, dactylitis resolution, disease-specific quality of life, fatigue, pain interference, and all four WPAI domains. The safety profile was comparable to placebo, with no significant differences in total adverse events (OR 1.30 [0.79-2.16]), serious adverse events (OR 1.00 [0.45-2.20]), or gastrointestinal events (OR 0.73 [0.42-1.25]). CONCLUSIONS: Deucravacitinib 6 mg once daily demonstrates consistent, multidomain superiority over placebo in active PsA at 16 weeks without excess adverse event burden. Head-to-head trials and longer-term data are needed to define its position in the treatment algorithm.

titre: Impact of nutritional and nursing interventions on gastrointestinal function in elderly populations: A meta-analytic review
resume: BACKGROUND: Gastrointestinal (GI) dysfunction and malnutrition are prevalent health concerns among elderly populations, often resulting in diminished quality of life and increased morbidity. Nutritional and nursing interventions have been proposed as effective strategies to improve digestive health and nutritional status in older adults. This meta-analysis aimed to evaluate the combined impact of these interventions on gastrointestinal function and related nutritional outcomes in elderly individuals. METHODS: A systematic review and meta-analysis were conducted in accordance with the PRISMA 2020 guidelines. Comprehensive searches were performed in PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, ScienceDirect, Google Scholar, and the Consensus database for studies published between 2015 and 2025. Eligible studies included randomized controlled trials, quasi-experimental, and community-based interventions that assessed the effects of nutritional or nursing care on GI function in individuals aged 60 years and above. Data extraction and quality assessment were performed independently by two reviewers using the Cochrane RoB 2 and JBI tools. A random-effects model was used to calculate the pooled standardized mean differences (SMD) and mean differences (MD), along with 95% confidence intervals (CI). RESULTS: Nine studies with a total of 1875 elderly participants met the inclusion criteria. The pooled analysis demonstrated a significant improvement in gastrointestinal outcomes, with an SMD of 0.68 [95% CI: 0.41-0.95; p < 0.001], indicating a moderate-to-large effect. Nutritional biomarkers, including serum albumin and prealbumin, also improved significantly (MD = +3.25 g/L [95% CI: 1.84-4.66; p < 0.001]). Subgroup analyzes showed that both nutritional (SMD = 0.71) and nursing interventions (SMD = 0.62) were effective, with similar efficacy across community and hospital settings. Heterogeneity was moderate (I² = 47%), and no evidence of publication bias was detected (Egger's test p = 0.21). Sensitivity analyzes confirmed the robustness of the results. DISCUSSION: The findings indicate that integrated nutritional and nursing interventions significantly enhance GI function, improve nutrient absorption, and strengthen overall health among elderly populations. These results align with prior studies demonstrating the benefits of individualized dietary management, enteral nutrition, and nursing education in improving bowel motility and nutritional resilience. Mechanistically, these interventions likely exert their effects through improved gut microbiota balance, enhanced peristaltic activity, and increased patient engagement in dietary self-care. CONCLUSIONS: The available evidence suggests that nutritional and nursing interventions may improve gastrointestinal function and selected nutritional outcomes in older adults. However, given the limited number of included studies and variability in intervention approaches and study designs, these findings should be interpreted cautiously. Further well-designed, adequately powered studies with longer follow-up are needed to confirm the magnitude and durability of these effects across different geriatric care settings.

titre: Potentially Clinically Beneficial Interactions Between Biologically-Based Complementary Medicines and Cancer Treatment: A Systematic Scoping Review
resume: PurposeThis scoping review aimed to identify primary studies reporting potentially clinically beneficial interactions between biologically-based complementary medicines (BB-CMs) (e.g., herbs, vitamins, minerals, pre/probiotics etc.) and conventional cancer treatments.MethodsFollowing Joanna Briggs scoping review methodology, a comprehensive search was conducted across Scopus, MEDLINE, Web of Science Core Collection, CINAHL, Allied and Complementary Medicine, and Embase databases from their inception to September 20,2024. Two reviewers independently screened the citations. Data were extracted by a single reviewer and verified by another. Results were tabulated and narrated.ResultsFifty-five studies from 14 countries, involving 4,672 adults, adolescents and children, were included in the review. Study designs varied according to the patient characteristics, treatment types, dosages and durations of use, and comprehensiveness of reporting, including adverse events and declarations. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) (n=29) were most common, followed by non-RCTs (n=9). Studies mostly focused on digestive tract cancers (n=16), breast cancer (n=11) and lung cancer (n=8). The most frequently investigated conventional cancer treatments were chemotherapy (n=17) and chemotherapy with adjunctive medications (n=8), while the most common BB-CMs were traditional medicine multi-ingredient formulations (n=23), vitamins (n=10), and hormone products/pre/probiotics (n=4). The most frequent beneficial interactions evaluated were survival, treatment response, and symptom relief including side effects from conventional cancer treatment, and quality-of-life.ConclusionsA broad range of studies have evaluated beneficial interactions between BB-CMs and conventional oncological treatments. Further in-depth reviews of these beneficial interactions, along with more clinical trials are indicated to support evidence-informed decision-making by healthcare providers and people living with cancer.

titre: Pancreatic Exocrine Insufficiency Following Esophagectomy, Gastrectomy and Bariatric Surgery: A Systematic Review and Narrative Synthesis
resume: BACKGROUND: Pancreatic exocrine insufficiency (PEI) is an increasingly recognised consequence of esophagogastric surgery; however, its prevalence, burden across different surgical procedures, and optimal approaches to diagnosis and management remain incompletely characterized. This review aims to systematically evaluate the prevalence, diagnosis, clinical manifestations, nutritional consequences and management of PEI following esophagogastric surgery in adults. METHODS: A systematic review and meta-analysis was conducted according to Joanna Briggs Institute methodology and reported in accordance with PRISMA 2020. PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science and Embase were searched from January 2011 to May 2026. Eligible studies reported PEI following esophagectomy, gastrectomy, or bariatric surgery. Owing to substantial clinical and methodological heterogeneity, findings were synthesized narratively by surgical group and procedure. Risk of bias was evaluated using JBI critical appraisal tools. RESULTS: Seventeen studies comprising 1397 patients were included. Reported PEI prevalence varied substantially across surgical populations, ranging from 3.2% to 22.0% following esophagectomy, 25.0%-63.8% following gastrectomy, and 9.1%-32.6% in bariatric cohorts. Procedure-specific estimates varied considerably, with rates of 4.2%-17.2% following sleeve gastrectomy, 8.3%-10.3% following RYGB, 48.1% following distal RYGB and 75.0% following biliopancreatic diversion with duodenal switch. Fecal elastase-1 was the most frequently used diagnostic test, although diagnostic criteria and timing of assessment varied between studies. Gastrointestinal symptoms, weight loss, nutritional deficiencies and impaired quality of life were reported, while limited observational evidence suggested symptomatic improvement following pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy. CONCLUSIONS: PEI is an under-recognised consequence of esophagectomy, gastrectomy and bariatric surgery, with reported prevalence varying substantially between procedures and studies. Greater clinical awareness and standardised approaches to diagnosis are required, alongside prospective studies to better define postoperative screening and management. TRIAL REGISTRATION: This review was prospectively registered in PROSPERO (CRD420261369499).

titre: Role of Non-coding RNAs in radiation-induced digestive injury
resume: PURPOSE: Radiation therapy (RT) is a crucial treatment for malignant tumors. However, the digestive system contains radiation-sensitive organs, and adjacent normal tissues are susceptible to radiation-induced tissue injury (RITI), which, in severe cases, can impair the quality of life and disrupt treatment. Non-coding RNAs (ncRNAs) regulate tissue homeostasis and injury repair. They influence the onset, progression, and repair of RITI across multiple digestive organs by modulating DNA damage responses, mucosal epithelial regeneration, cell death, inflammatory signaling, and fibrotic remodeling. Ionizing radiation induces changes in ncRNA expression profiles and regulatory networks in various digestive organs. Elucidating the common regulatory mechanisms and tissue specificity of ncRNAs, as well as identifying key molecular targets, will provide new insights for the prevention and treatment of RITI. This article comprehensively reviews the research progress on ncRNAs in radiation-induced digestive injury according to the anatomical regions of the digestive system, summarizes their regulatory mechanisms and potential as biomarkers and therapeutic targets, and limitations of the current evidence. CONCLUSION: ncRNAs regulate the DNA damage response, epithelial regeneration, cell death, inflammatory response, and fibrosis throughout the occurrence, development, and repair of radiation-induced digestive injury. Current evidence, derived predominantly from cell and animal studies, supports regulatory roles for ncRNAs in radiation-induced digestive injury, with functional evidence comparatively more developed in intestinal and liver injury. ncRNA-based interventions also require further evaluation of causal mechanisms, selective delivery, therapeutic windows, and effects on tumor response to RT before clinical application.

titre: Cognitive impairment in metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease ‒ Clinical evidence, liver-brain mechanisms and research priorities
resume: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) is the most prevalent chronic liver disease worldwide and is increasingly recognized as a multisystem disorder with important extrahepatic manifestations. Among these, cognitive impairment and reduced health-related quality of life (HRQoL) have emerged as clinically relevant but under-recognized findings, although the extent to which cognitive impairment is independently associated with MASLD remains uncertain. This narrative review summarizes current evidence regarding cognitive impairment and HRQoL in MASLD, addressing clinical findings, potential underlying mechanisms, and therapeutic implications. Reported estimates of cognitive impairment vary substantially according to population characteristics, disease stage, and neuropsychological instruments, and should not be interpreted as a general population prevalence. Current evidence is predominantly observational, with some studies showing associations that persist after adjustment for cardiometabolic factors and others finding no independent association. Proposed mechanisms include systemic and neuroinflammation, insulin resistance, oxidative stress, and alterations in the gut-liver-brain axis, although direct human evidence remains limited for several pathways. Lifestyle and metabolic interventions may influence cognitive outcomes, but direct MASLD-specific evidence is limited. Future research should prioritize standardized cognitive assessment, longitudinal validation studies, careful control of confounding, integration of patient-reported outcomes, and prespecified cognitive endpoints in MASLD clinical trials.
