titre: From Brain Lesions to Treatment Targets: Converging on a Causal Circuit for OCD
Network structure of non-suicidal self-injury and multidomain psychiatric symptoms among adolescents with elevated depressive symptoms: a cross-sectional study
resume: Abstract Background Non-suicidal self-injury (NSSI) commonly co-occurs with depressive symptoms during adolescence, but its position within broader symptom-domain systems among adolescents with elevated depressive symptoms remains unclear. Examining this PHQ-defined subgroup may clarify whether NSSI is primarily linked with depressive symptoms or also connected with other domains relevant to follow-up assessment. This study examined how NSSI was embedded within a multidomain psychiatric symptom network among school-based adolescents with Patient Health Questionnaire (PHQ) module scores of 5 or higher. Methods This cross-sectional school-based screening study included 1,146 adolescents who met the Patient Health Questionnaire (PHQ) ≥ 5 inclusion criterion and had complete data on 10 symptom-domain nodes. A Spearman correlation matrix and EBICglasso were used to estimate the primary network. Signed-spinglass community detection with repeated seeds and 1,000 case-bootstrap networks was used to identify and validate data-driven communities. Node predictability, centrality, bridge expected influence, bootstrap stability, and relative importance analyses characterized symptom-domain organization and explained-variance patterns. Results The final network contained 43 nonzero edges among 45 possible edges. Signed-spinglass community detection identified a reproducible two-community organization: a core symptom community containing Ma, Pa, PTSD, GAD, PHQ, OCD, and NSSI, and a separation/social/school anxiety community containing SeP, SoP, and ScP. The two-community solution occurred in 999 of 1,000 case-bootstrap networks. Depressive symptoms showed the highest strength, one-step expected influence, two-step expected influence, and predictability. Bridge expected influence was highest for separation anxiety, school anxiety, and social anxiety symptoms, followed by depressive and obsessive-compulsive symptoms. NSSI showed moderate predictability (R² = 0.246), and depressive symptoms made the largest relative-importance contribution to NSSI explained variance. Conclusions Among adolescents with elevated depressive symptoms, NSSI was linked most closely with depressive, trauma-related, obsessive-compulsive, and generalized anxiety symptom domains. The findings suggest that NSSI in this subgroup was associated with depressive symptoms but was not limited to mood-related distress. Screening and follow-up assessment for adolescents with elevated depressive symptoms may benefit from considering trauma-related, repetitive/intrusive, and worry-related symptoms alongside depressive severity and NSSI. Because the data were cross-sectional and based on screening-domain scores, the findings should be interpreted as descriptive symptom-domain associations rather than causal pathways.

titre: Role of Probiotics in Improving Symptoms of Irritable Bowel Syndrome (Diarrhea-Predominant) By Assessing IBS-Qol (Quality of Life)
resume: Background: Irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) is a prevalent disorder of gut–brain interaction, and diarrhea-predominant IBS (IBS-D) is a common subtype associated with impaired health-related quality of life (HRQoL). Probiotics may improve symptoms through microbiome- and gut–brain–related mechanisms. Objective: To assess the effect of multi-strain probiotics on HRQoL and clinical outcomes in IBS-D. Methods: This prospective, open-label, non-randomized controlled study included 60 IBS-D patients allocated to probiotics plus standard therapy (n=30) or standard therapy alone (n=30). Probiotics contained Bacillus clausii, Lactobacillus acidophilus, Lactobacillus rhamnosus, and Bifidobacterium animalis at ≥1×10¹⁰ CFU/day for 8 weeks. IBS-D was diagnosed by Rome IV criteria and Bristol Stool Form Scale, and HRQoL was assessed using IBS-QoL. Results: Baseline characteristics and IBS-QoL scores were comparable between groups (p>0.05), except marital status (p=0.041). Post-treatment, the probiotic group achieved significantly greater improvement than controls in physical symptoms (p=0.004), social function (p=0.012), emotional function (p=0.018), work productivity (p=0.021), and total IBS-QoL (p=0.005). Clinical response was higher with probiotics (63.3% vs 23.3%; p=0.001), and ≥50% bowel frequency reduction was more frequent (56.7% vs 16.7%; p=0.001). Adverse events were low and similar between groups (p=0.246). Probiotic treatment independently predicted response (OR=5.47, 95% CI 1.82–16.43; p=0.002), and lower baseline IBS-QoL predicted response (OR=0.42, 95% CI 0.18–0.98; p=0.044). Conclusion: Multi-strain probiotics were associated with clinically meaningful improvements in HRQoL and symptom outcomes in IBS-D with good tolerability.
revue: Al-Azhar International Medical Journal /Al-Azhar International Medical Journal

titre: The prevalence of irritable bowel syndrome and its association with academic performance among medical students at Taibah University
resume: Objective: To determine the prevalence of irritable bowel syndrome among medical students, and to investigate its association with academic performance indicators. Method: The cross-sectional study was conducted at Taibah University, Madinah, Saudi Arabia, from February to October 2023, and comprised second- to sixth-year medical students aged at least 18 years. Data was collected using a self-administered online questionnaire that explored sociodemographic information, medical history, exercise history and irritable bowel syndrome symptoms as per the Rome IV criteria. The association of irritable bowel syndrome was assessed with academic achievement, extracurricular activities, lecture attendance, and attention during lectures. Data was analysed using SPSS 26. Results: Of the 1,020 students, 291(28.5%) completed the survey. Among them, 180(61.9%) were women, 69(23.7%) were in the third academic year and 260(89.3%) were non-smokers. Overall, 29(10%) subjects reported symptoms consistent with irritable bowel syndrome. Irritable bowel syndrome negatively affected extracurricular activities, lecture attendance, attention during lectures and study hours (p 0.05). Conclusion: Irritable bowel syndrome had a significant impact on academic performance, showing associations with decreased attention during lectures, increased absences, and fewer hours spent studying. Key Words: Irritable bowel syndrome, Prevalence, Academic success, Students, Medical.
revue: Journal of the Pakistan Medical Association

titre: Progress in treatment of irritable bowel syndrome with diarrhea by traditional Chinese medicine: An emphasis on microbiota-brain-gut axis
resume: Irritable bowel syndrome with diarrhea (IBS-D) is a common gastrointestinal disease distinguished by the presence of abdominal pain and diarrhea. However, the pathogenesis is still unclear. The gut microbiota consists of a wide variety of microorganisms that inhabit the gastrointestinal ecosystem. Modern medicine believes gut microbiota can form the microbiota-gut-brain (MGB) axis communication network with the brain and gut, thereby regulating the body’s gastrointestinal function. The disorder of MGB axis may be closely related to the occurrence of IBS-D. At present, the treatment of IBS-D mainly depends on chemical drugs. Unfortunately, this will produce adverse reactions and affect the gut microbiota, which is not conducive to the rehabilitation of patients. Traditional Chinese medicine (TCM), as a therapy used in China for thousands of years, has been proved to have a significant effect in the treatment of IBS-D, but the specific mechanism of action is still unclear. This article reviews the research progress of TCM in the treatment of IBS-D, focusing on the pathogenesis of MGB axis and IBS-D, as well as TCM therapy, including Chinese herbs, TCM prescriptions, acupuncture and moxibustion, integrative medicine therapy, which can regulate the MGB axis in the treatment of IBS-D, aiming to provide new ideas for the treatment of IBS-D in the future.

titre: Transcranial Direct Current Stimulation (tDCS) for Pain and Psychological Symptoms in Irritable Bowel Syndrome: A Scoping Review of Direct and Indirect Evidence
resume: This scoping review aims to map and synthesize the available evidence on the potential effects of transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) on pain and psychological symptoms in irritable bowel syndrome (IBS). The review considers both direct evidence from studies conducted in individuals or experimental models of IBS and indirect evidence from related conditions and mechanistic research relevant to the brain–gut axis. The review will examine the clinical and mechanistic findings concerning the potential effects of tDCS on pain-related outcomes and psychological symptoms, particularly anxiety and depression, as well as explore possible underlying neurophysiological mechanisms. By mapping the available evidence, this review seeks to identify current knowledge, highlight gaps in the literature, and provide directions for future clinical and experimental research on the application of tDCS in IBS. The review follows a scoping review approach, with study selection, data extraction, and evidence synthesis conducted according to the methodological framework for scoping reviews.

titre: Butyrate and Palmitoylethanolamide: Exploring Their Metabolic Potential in Explaining Clinical Improvement in Irritable Bowel Syndrome Patients, Data from A Randomised, Placebo-controlled Trial
resume: BACKGROUND: Irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) is a disorder of gut-brain interaction in which gut microbiome plays a major role. Butyrate and palmitoylethanolamide (PEA) exert anti-inflammatory and neuromodulator effects and may represent promising adjunctive treatments. We evaluated the clinical and microbiome-related effects of a combined formulation of sodium butyrate and PEA (BP 3:1) in patients with IBS. METHODS: In a randomized, double-blnd, placebo-controlled, 2 × 2 crossover trial, adults with diarrhoea-predominant or mixed IBS received BP 3:1 or placebo for two 6-week periods separated by washout. Gastrointestinal symptoms, IBS Severity Scoring System (IBS-SSS), intestinal permeability, and safety were assessed. Fecal microbiota composition and predicted functional potential were analyzed using 16S-rRNA sequencing and PICRUSt2. RESULTS: Forty-four patients completed the study. Alpha and beta diversity and taxonomic composition remained stable. In contrast, functional profiling revealed treatment-specific enrichment of microbial pathways involved in methionine and S-adenosyl-L-methionine biosynthesis, while placebo was associated with pathways related to complex carbohydrate degradation. BP 3:1 significantly improved abdominal bloating (p = 0.020), stomach gurgling (p = 0.014) and nausea (p = 0.030) compared with placebo, with consistent estimates in mixed-effects models adjusting for period and sequence effects, while IBS-SSS showed a clinically relevant but non-significant numerical reduction (p = 0.070). No effects were observed on intestinal permeability. Among clinically improving patients, BP 3:1 was associated with modulation of polyphenol-degrading, biosynthetic and proteolytic microbial pathways. BP 3:1 was well tolerated, with a safety profile comparable to placebo. CONCLUSIONS: BP 3:1 significantly improves IBS symptoms and modulates microbial metabolic potential without inducing a quantitative and/or qualitative alteration in the taxonomic composition of the microbiota. These findings support a functional microbiome-mediated effect in IBS. CLINICALTRIAL: gov NCT06432569 (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06432569).

titre: Development of a Core Outcome Set for Inflammatory Bowel Disease With Irritable Bowel Syndrome‐Like Symptoms for Use in Clinical Trials and Clinical Practice: A Study Protocol
resume: ABSTRACT Background Up to one‐third of patients with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) in remission experience residual symptoms including irritable bowel syndrome (IBS)‐like symptoms, which impair quality of life and psychological well‐being. Evidence supporting therapeutic interventions remains limited. Furthermore, considerable heterogeneity in definitions of residual symptoms and reported outcomes hampers comparison between studies and limits translation into clinical practice and guidelines. We therefore aim to develop an international core outcome set (COS) for residual symptoms in patients with IBD in remission including IBS‐like symptoms for use in clinical trials and routine care. Methods The COS will be developed in accordance with the Core Outcome Measures in Effectiveness Trials (COMET) Handbook. Potential residual symptoms and outcomes will be identified through qualitative patient interviews and a systematic review of the literature and categorised according to the COMET taxonomy. Identified outcomes will subsequently be prioritised through an international Delphi consensus exercise of up to three rounds involving patients and healthcare professionals (e.g., gastroenterologists, IBD nurse specialists/physician assistants, dieticians, psychiatrists). Finally, a consensus meeting with representatives from all stakeholder groups will be held to discuss and vote on the final COS. Discussion The development of a COS for IBD with residual symptoms including IBS‐like symptoms will improve consistency of outcome measurement and reporting, facilitate comparability and synthesis of evidence and ensure that relevant outcomes for both patients and healthcare professionals are measured. Trial Registration The study is registered in the COMET database ( https://www.comet‐initiative.org/Studies/Details/4119 )

titre: Functional constipation in paediatric populations: A clinical review and homoeopathic repertory
resume: Functional constipation, also known as chronic idiopathic constipation, is a prevalent condition in paediatric medicine. Characterised by the absence of structural, anatomical, or physiological (such as metabolic or hormonal) causes, its etiology is primarily rooted in neurological, psychological, or psychosomatic factors. This article explores the physiological milestones associated with childhood constipation, the pathophysiology of stool withholding, and introduces a specialised clinical regional repertory designed to streamline homoeopathic remedy selection based on stool characteristics, causation, and concomitant symptoms.

titre: Therapeutic management of chronic functional constipation using Cascara sagrada: The gentle bowel regulator: A case series
resume: Introduction : Constipation is a common gastrointestinal complaint characterized by persistent, difficult, infrequent or seemingly incomplete defecation. Chronic constipation can significantly affect the quality of life and may result from inadequate fibre intake or fluid intake or from disordered colonic transit or anorectal function. Cascara sagrada, a well-known Homoeopathic Mother Tincture prepared from Rhamnus purshiana, acts as a natural stimulant of the bowel, enhancing peristalsis and promoting regular defecation without dependency. Case summary : Three cases of chronic functional constipation was successfully therapeutically managed with Cascara Sagrada mother tincture. No secondary cause of constipation was identified after clinical evaluation in these cases. Diagnosis was established according to the Rome IV criteria for chronic functional constipation after exclusion of secondary causes. The patients were given cascara sagrada mother tincture in all these cases. Cascara sagrada was selected based on its clinical affinity for chronic atonic constipation with habitual laxative dependence, difficult evacuation, and sluggish intestinal peristalsis as described by Boericke and Clarke. The first patient showed easy passage of stool the next of giving medicine and within 10 days easier passage of stools was noticed. The second patient achieved daily bowel movements without laxatives after four weeks of treatment. The third patient demonstrated gradual improvement in bowel regularity and complete relief of constipation during follow-up.

titre: Psychosocial and Environmental Determinants of Nausea in Patients with Functional Dyspepsia: An Exploratory Experience Sampling Method (ESM) Study
resume: Background and Aims Nausea is a frequently reported symptom in functional dyspepsia (FD). However, its pathophysiology remains poorly understood, with daily life factors influencing its dynamic nature. This study aimed to identify psychosocial and environmental triggers of nausea in FD using the experience sampling method (ESM). Methods In this prospective observational study conducted at a secondary and tertiary academic hospital, 35 Rome IV FD patients (71.4% female, mean age 44.7 years) and 34 healthy controls (HCs; 70.6% female, mean age 44.1 years) completed ESM assessments over seven consecutive days (10 assessments/day). Symptoms and contextual factors were rated on an 11-point Numeric Rating Scale. Data were analyzed using linear mixed-effects models. Results Among completers (>24/70 questionnaires), c ompletion rates were 62.2% in FD and 69.7% in HCs. Mean seven-day nausea scores were 1.35 (SE 0.32) in FD and 0.10 (SE 0.06) in HCs ( P <.001). In FD, a 1-point increase in positive affect was associated with a 0.29 decrease in nausea ( P < .001), while negative affect was associated with a 0.24 increase in nausea ( P < .001). Comfort in a situation ( P < .001) and pleasantness in company ( P = .037) were negatively associated with nausea. Lagged scores for psychosocial factors were not associated with nausea. No association was found between food intake and nausea ( P = .177). In secondary analysis, concurrent upper abdominal pain was positively associated with nausea ( P < .001). Conclusion Real-time affect, comfort, and pleasantness were associated with concurrent nausea in FD, whereas temporal relationships remain uncertain. ESM-based monitoring may offer a promising approach for characterizing individual symptom variability in daily life. ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT04204421.

titre: BRIDGING AUTOMATION AND ROBOTICS IN INDUSTRIALIZED BUILDING SYSTEM (IBS): CHALLENGES, IMPACTS, AND STRATEGIES OF ADOPTIONS
resume: The Industrialised Building System (IBS) was introduced in Malaysia in the early 1960s to address the growing demand for affordable housing, reduce reliance on foreign labour, and enhance the overall quality and productivity of the construction sector. Recently, the construction industry has begun integrating automation and robotics, aligning with the global shift towards the Fourth Industrial Revolution (IR 4.0). The Construction 4.0 Strategic Plan (2021–2025) further emphasises digitalisation, robotics, and automation to improve industry efficiency and sustainability. However, the construction industry has been slow to adopt these advancements, limiting the full benefits of automation in IBS. Persistent challenges, including resistance to change, high initial investment costs, a shortage of skilled personnel, and technical complexities, hinder widespread adoption. This research examines the integration of automation and robotics in IBS to enhance construction productivity. A questionnaire survey was used for the data collection exercise. The data collected were analysed using descriptive statistical methods utilising the Statistical Package for the Social Sciences (SPSS) software. The study is guided by three (3) objectives: (1) To identify barriers to the integration of automation and robotics in IBS, (2) To analyse the impact of automation and robotics on construction productivity compared to conventional IBS, and (3)To propose strategies to improve the adoption of these technologies.Findings reveal that the integration of automation and robotics in (IBS) facessignificant barriers, primarily due to the high costs of investment. titre: AN REVIEW ARTICLE ON EFFECT OF DIET AND LIFESTYLE MODIFICATIONS IN THE MANAGEMENT OF GRAHANI ROG
resume: Grahani Roga is a well-established functional gastrointestinal disorder in Ayurvedic medicine, characterised by impairment of the intestinal seat of digestion and absorption, designated Grahani. The condition bears significant clinical overlap with what contemporary gastroenterology describes as Irritable Bowel Syndrome (IBS). Classical treatises identify disturbed Agni (digestive fire) as the central pathological event, precipitated primarily by faulty dietary practices, irregular lifestyle, and psychosocial stress. To synthesise classical Ayurvedic textual evidence and contemporary scientific literature in elucidating the role of diet and lifestyle in the aetiopathogenesis and management of Grahani Roga. A narrative review was conducted drawing from primary Ayurvedic classical texts — Charaka Samhita, Sushruta Samhita, Ashtanga Hridaya, Madhava Nidana, Bhavaprakasha, Chakradatta, and Yoga Ratnakara — and from peer-reviewed modern gastroenterological literature retrieved through PubMed, Scopus, and AYUSH-affiliated databases. Pathya Ahara (wholesome diet), Dinacharya (regulated daily regimen), Sansarjana Krama (graduated dietary rehabilitation), and psychosomatic interventions collectively constitute the foundation of Grahani Roga management, corroborated by contemporary evidence on gut-brain axis modulation and microbiota regulation.

titre: PANCHAKARMA IN THE MANAGEMENT OF GRAHANI ROGA: A NARRATIVE REVIEW OF CLINICAL EVIDENCE
resume: Grahani Roga is described in Ayurveda in relation to impaired Agni and altered gastrointestinal function. Some clinical presentations overlap with irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), although the diagnostic constructs are not synonymous. This narrative review discusses published clinical reports on Panchakarma interventions used for Grahani Roga and clinically correlated IBS, with particular attention to Basti procedures. The available literature includes small clinical studies, comparative investigations and case reports. Takra Basti and Erandamooladi Niruha Basti have been associated with symptomatic improvement in small studies, while Piccha Basti reports describe improvements in bowel frequency, mucus, bloating and, in some recent cases, validated IBS outcome scores. Evidence for Vamana is limited, and no efficacy conclusion can be drawn from a registered Virechana trial without an available outcome report. Interpretation is constrained by small samples, heterogeneous diagnostic criteria and treatment protocols, concomitant therapies, and inconsistent outcome reporting. Reports involving inflammatory bowel disease or ulcerative colitis are considered separately from functional IBS/Grahani evidence. Current findings are hypothesis-generating rather than definitive; well-designed prospective studies with standardized interventions, validated outcomes, systematic safety reporting and longer follow-up are needed.
auteurs: Isha Roat1*, Rajeev Kumar Pandey2, Divya Gupta3, Yashwant Chaudhary4

titre: THE ROLE OF THE GUT-BRAIN AXIS IN THE PATHOPHYSIOLOGY OF PARKINSON’S DISEASE: A CURRENT LITERATURE REVIEW
resume: Parkinson’s Disease (PD) is a chronic neurodegenerative disorder characterized by the progressive loss of dopaminergic neurons. Recent scientific paradigms have shifted focus from the central nervous system to the bidirectional communication between the gastrointestinal tract and the brain, known as the gut-brain axis. This literature review aims to explore the mechanisms by which intestinal microbiota imbalance (dysbiosis) and gut inflammation contribute to PD pathogenesis through the spread of misfolded alpha-synuclein protein. Key factors such as immune responses, intestinal permeability, and microbial metabolites are identified as crucial elements in disease progression. A deeper understanding of this axis highlights the potential for novel microbiota-based therapeutic interventions to improve patient prognosis and mitigate the global burden of Parkinson's Disease.

titre: Organoid-based gut-brain axis models as an evaluation framework for functional food bioactives: opportunities and challenges
resume: Functional food bioactives affect the gut–brain axis (GBA) via intestinal, microbial, immune, endocrine, metabolic, and neural pathways. Although traditional cell and animal models are able to show only a part of these processes, human studies offer little information about the mechanisms at the tissue level. This review offers a question-driven approach to the use of intestinal organoids, brain organoids, co-culture systems, and interconnected gut–brain organ-on-a-chip systems when assessing functional foods. The choice of model is determined by the particular biological questions being asked, the routes of exposure, the measurable endpoints, and the translational goals. The review looks at how these systems can be used to study intestinal barrier function, immune and inflammatory regulation, neuroprotective responses, microbiota–host interactions, and interindividual variability. At present, the direct evidence is mainly derived from research on the intestinal barrier and the microbiota, while work involving brain organoids, interconnected gut–brain systems, and donor-specific nutrition is still in its early stages or depends on findings from other fields. The promise of new technologies such as multi-omics, real-time sensing, and the use of artificial intelligence (AI) to assist in analysis is highlighted as a way to improve dynamic phenotyping and to enable integration with biomarkers from human cohorts and from studies on dietary interventions. Nevertheless, problems such as incomplete tissue maturation, limited vascular and immune integration, batch-to-batch variability, low throughput, high cost, and the absence of standardisation continue to act as major obstacles to wider acceptance. Organoid-based systems are seen as something that can complement, not replace, digestion and fermentation models, conventional cell and animal studies, and human intervention trials. When used in a clearly defined context, these platforms can connect physiologically relevant dietary exposures with the underlying tissue mechanisms and human evidence, thus helping to prioritise functional food bioactives and mechanistic biomarkers for human validation and for future nutritional research.

titre: The Gut–Brain Axis Mechanism in Alzheimer’s Disease: From Animal Models to Clinical Translation and Emerging Treatment Strategies
resume: Research on gut microbiota in Alzheimer’s disease (AD) has progressed from observational correlation studies toward investigation of causal relationships in preclinical models. Human observational studies have reported associations between alterations in gut microbiota and the entire spectrum of AD, from the preclinical stage to dementia, and are associated with Amyloid-beta (Aβ) deposition, phosphorylated Tau (p-tau) positivity, dysregulation of bile acid and short-chain fatty acid (SCFA) metabolism, as well as impaired intestinal barrier function. The strongest causal evidence currently derives from germ-free or antibiotic-treated animal models, fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) between healthy controls and AD patients, and colonization by specific bacterial strains or metabolites—interventions that have been shown to modulate Aβ load, tau phosphorylation, microglial activation, synaptic pruning, and cognitive behavior in animal models. Mechanistically, the gut–brain axis in AD has been proposed to integrate four interconnected pathways, with the strength of evidence and the extent of human validation varying considerably across them: (1) reduced production of SCFA-producing bacteria accompanied by upregulation of pro-inflammatory pathways; (2) disruption of intestinal epithelial tight junctions, allowing lipopolysaccharide (LPS) and bacterial toxins to enter the systemic circulation; (3) reprogramming of peripheral and central innate immune systems, leading to hyperactivation of microglia and complement-mediated synaptic clearance; and (4) global rearrangement of microbial metabolite networks (including SCFAs, bile acids, tryptophan metabolites, and LPS), has been proposed to collectively regulate Aβ homeostasis, tau pathology, microglial activation, and blood–brain barrier (BBB) integrity. Clinically, the evidence base remains uneven: probiotics have been associated with some improvements in some inflammatory markers and cognitive measures in small randomized controlled trials (RCTs); FMT has been reported in case studies in human AD; modified ketogenic diets have been associated with cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) biomarkers; and molecules such as GV-971 (Sodium Oligomannate) provide proof-of-concept for microbiota-targeted strategies, though independent validation is needed. Overall, gut microbiota research in AD has advanced considerably, with animal and human studies suggesting that dysbiosis may contribute to AD pathology through immune, metabolic, and barrier-related pathways, although clinical intervention evidence remains preliminary and requires further validation.

titre: Coarse cereal bioactives and the gut-brain axis: from multi-omics dissection to targeted delivery—a critical review
DEPRESSION: ETIOLOGY, PATHOPHYSIOLOGY, CLINICAL ASSESSMENT AND THERAPEUTIC APPROACHES IN VIEW OF RECENT STUDIES UPDATED REVIEW
resume: Depression is a common and disabling psychiatric disorder characterized by persistent low mood, loss of interest or pleasure, cognitive and emotional disturbances, and a range of somatic symptoms. Major depressive disorder (MDD) is a heterogeneous condition arising from complex interactions among genetic vulnerability, environmental stress, psychological factors, neurobiological abnormalities and social determinants. Contemporary research has moved beyond a simple monoamine-deficiency model toward an integrated understanding involving altered neural circuits, impaired neuroplasticity, hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal-axis dysfunction, inflammation, immune signaling, metabolic abnormalities and the microbiota-gut-brain axis. Diagnosis remains primarily clinical, although standardized instruments such as the Patient Health Questionnaire-9 can support screening. Treatment includes pharmacotherapy, psychotherapy, exercise and other psychosocial interventions. Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors and other antidepressants remain important pharmacological options. Cognitive behavioral therapy is an established psychological intervention, while digital psychological interventions and exercise have increasing evidence. Treatment-resistant depression remains a major challenge and has stimulated development of rapid-acting and mechanistically novel interventions, particularly ketamine and esketamine, together with neuromodulation approaches. Emerging research is investigating neuroplasticity, inflammatory mechanisms, metabolic pathways and gut-brain interactions as potential therapeutic targets. An integrated, individualized and biopsychosocial approach is therefore central to contemporary depression research and management.

titre: Synergistic effects of Lactobacillus rhamnosus and tryptophan on gut microbiota, 5-hydroxytryptamine metabolism, and feather-pecking behavior in laying hens with antibiotic-induced dysbiosis
resume: Feather pecking (FP), a common behavioral disorder in laying hens, poses significant challenges to both animal welfare and the economic sustainability of commercial egg production. Increasing evidence links gut dysbiosis to the development of FP through the microbiota-gut-brain (MGB) axis, particularly via disruptions in tryptophan (Trp) metabolism and serotonin (5-HT) signaling. In this study, the effects of Lactobacillus rhamnosus LR-32 (LR-32) and Trp, administered individually or in combination, were investigated in laying hens with antibiotic-induced dysbiosis, a model previously established to provoke FP behavior. A total of 240 Hy-Line Brown hens (70 wk of age; initial body weight: 2.02 ± 0.13 kg) were allocated to four dietary groups ( n = 60 per group, with four replicates of 15 hens each): control (Con), LR (1×10 11 colony-forming units [CFU]/kg LR-32), TRY (0.8 g/kg Trp), and LR + TRY, for 12 wk. The results showed that compared with the Con group, LR-32 supplementation significantly increased laying rate, improved feather condition, and reduced the incidence of severe feather pecking (SFP) ( P < 0.05). The combined LR + TRY treatment further lowered SFP incidence and produced a synergistic improvement in eggshell strength ( P < 0.05). Compared with the Con group, both LR-32 and Trp supplementation elevated serum Trp, 5-HT, and interleukin-10 (IL-10) levels, while reducing serum levels of lipopolysaccharide (LPS), diamine oxidase (DAO), tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α), and interleukin-6 (IL-6) ( P < 0.05), with the combined treatment exerting more pronounced anti-inflammatory and serotonergic effects. Moreover, both treatments raised 5-HT concentrations in the hypothalamus and ileum, with LR-32 upregulating the mRNA expression of TPH1 , TPH2 , and 5-HTR1A ( P < 0.05). Western blot analysis further demonstrated that the combined LR + TRY treatment synergistically suppressed protein expression in the TLR4/NF-κB pathway along the gut-brain axis. Microbiota analysis indicated that both interventions helped restore microbial diversity and increased the abundance of Lactobacillus , while decreasing the abundance of Proteobacteria and Desulfovibrio . Correlations analysis showed that Lactobacillus was positively associated with 5-HT levels but negatively with TLR4/NF-κB pathway protein expression, consistent with reduced SFP incidence. In summary, LR-32 and Trp acted additively to alleviate FP behavior by restoring gut microbial balance, reducing systemic inflammation, and enhancing serotonergic signaling through the MGB axis. These findings highlight the potential of targeted nutritional interventions to improve behavioral welfare in laying hens.

Plasma ASCA, CD14, and LBP Levels in Individuals with Mood, Anxiety, and Personality Disorders: Relationships with Aggression, Depression, and Anxiety
resume: ABSTRACT Background Immune dysregulation and low-grade systemic inflammation are implicated across psychiatric disorders, yet the biological sources and specificity of these processes remain unclear. Gastrointestinal (GI)–associated immune activation and microbial translocation have been linked to psychotic disorders, but their relevance to non-psychotic conditions and dimensional psychopathology is less well defined. We examined plasma markers indexing distinct immune pathways—antibodies to Saccharomyces cerevisiae (ASCA), soluble CD14 (sCD14), and lipopolysaccharide-binding protein (LBP)—in relation to aggression, impulsivity, depression, and anxiety. Methods Plasma ASCA, CD14, and LBP levels were measured in physically healthy, medication-free adults with intermittent explosive disorder (IED), psychiatric controls with mood, anxiety, and personality disorders, and healthy controls. Participants completed standardized diagnostic interviews and validated dimensional assessments. Group differences and symptom associations were examined using multivariable models. Results ASCA levels were elevated in individuals with IED compared with both psychiatric and healthy controls and were positively associated with aggression, trait depression, and trait anxiety. CD14 levels were strongly associated with aggression and impulsivity and, also, to state depression and anxiety. In contrast, LBP levels were most consistently associated with depressive and anxiety symptoms rather than aggression or impulsivity, indicating dissociable immune pathways. Conclusions GI-associated immune activation and innate immune signaling markers show distinct, dimension-specific associations with psychopathology in a medically healthy, medication-free sample. The dissociation among ASCA, CD14, and LBP highlights the heterogeneity of immune correlates of psychiatric symptoms. Given the cross-sectional design, these findings are hypothesis-generating and do not establish temporal or causal relationships between immune signaling and behavioral dysregulation.

titre: Natural orange extract supplementation and its effects on gastrointestinal discomfort and gut microbiota in healthy adults: a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled clinical trial
resume: Natural orange extract rich in citrus flavanones was evaluated for its effects on gastrointestinal discomfort and gut health in a 90-day randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial. Sixty-four healthy adults aged 18–65 years with gastrointestinal discomfort received either natural orange extract (500 mg/day) or placebo once daily. Supplementation significantly improved digestive and total Gastrointestinal Quality of Life Index (GIQLI) scores compared with placebo at Days 45 and 90 (both p < 0.0001), with a greater proportion of participants achieving normal stool consistency by Day 45 (89.3%; p = 0.0210). No significant between-group differences were observed in inflammatory biomarkers, although trends toward increased short-chain fatty acid production and improved gut microbial diversity were noted with supplementation. These findings suggest that natural orange extract may improve gastrointestinal symptoms, quality of life, and stool consistency while supporting gut microbiome health. Larger studies are needed to confirm these effects.

titre: Continuous Glucose Monitoring, Chronic Abdominal Pain and Dumping Symptoms 10–15 Years After Roux-en-Y Gastric Bypass: A Cross-Sectional Analysis
resume: Background Chronic abdominal pain after Roux-en-Y gastric bypass (RYGB) negatively impacts quality of life and healthcare resources. Improved understanding of its underlying mechanisms may enable new therapeutic strategies. Continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) in individuals after RYGB demonstrates increased glycemic variability and a high prevalence of hypoglycemia. Emerging evidence suggests an association between glycemic variability, gut hormone alterations and gastrointestinal symptoms, including abdominal pain. Objectives To explore 14-day CGM profiles in patients with and without chronic abdominal pain after RYGB and examine the relationship between abdominal pain and symptoms of early and late dumping syndrome. Setting University hospital, Norway Methods A cross-sectional study of patients 10 – 15 years post-RYGB, monitored with CGM for 14 days and answering the Dumping Severity Scale questionnaire (DSS). Results In total 142 individuals were included, 75 of them reported chronic abdominal pain and 67 reported no pain. The median (IQR) follow-up time was 12.9 (12.2 – 13.3) years after RYGB. CGM confirmed hypoglycemia in 77 (54%) participants, but no significant differences in CGM-derived metrics were observed between the groups. The median (IQR) DSS subscores were significantly higher in the abdominal pain group, even after exclusion of gastrointestinal symptom items (early dumping: 9.0 (7.0–11.0) vs 7.0 (5.0–9.0); late dumping: 11.0 (9.0–13.0) vs 7.0 (6.0–10.0), p<0.001). Conclusions CGM profiles were similar in patients with and without abdominal pain after RYGB. However, chronic abdominal pain was associated with a higher burden of early and late dumping symptoms.
revue: Surgery for Obesity and Related Diseases

titre: (ID: 284) Age-related changes in serotonin and lower bowel dysfunction: potential future preventative strategies
resume: Abstract Introduction Age-related lower bowel dysfunction is a significant clinical and economic challenge, affecting approximately 10% of adults over the age of 60 in the UK and costing the NHS an estimated £1.7 billion annually [1]. Conditions such as chronic constipation and faecal incontinence contribute substantially to reduced quality of life, increased hospital admissions, and long-term care requirements. Current management strategies are largely reactive, focusing on symptom control after dysfunction has developed rather than preventing disease progression. Serotonin (5-hydroxytryptamine; 5-HT), is a key pharmacological mediator of bowel function, released from enterochromaffin cells within the mucosal epithelium. Acting through receptors including 5-HT₃ and 5-HT₄, serotonin initiates and modulates secondary messenger systems and enteric reflexes that regulate propulsion and defecation. Despite its established role throughout the gastrointestinal tract, the effects of ageing on serotonergic signalling and continence have not been fully characterised [2]. Aim To investigate age-related changes in serotonin and determine the contribution to lower bowel dysfunction. Method A longitudinal preclinical study was undertaken in 20 male C57BL/6J mice assessed at 12, 14, 16 and 18 months of age to investigate age-related changes in lower bowel serotonin availability. Serotonin was measured in vivo using 3D-printed electrochemical sensors, with electrochemical techniques used to quantify serotonin release. Measures of bowel function, including faecal pellet output and faecal water content, were assessed alongside serotonin signalling to evaluate age-associated functional changes. All procedures complied with the UK Animals (Scientific Procedures) Act 1986 and were conducted under Home Office project licence PP1472338. Results Anodic peak current increased significantly with age, showing an enhanced serotonin availability in older age groups (one-way ANOVA, p < 0.0001, n = 14). In contrast, faecal pellet output and faecal water content decreased with age (one-way ANOVA, p < 0.001, n = 20), indicating the development of an age-associated constipation phenotype. The coexistence of elevated serotonin release and a constipation phenotype suggests that age-related dysfunction may arise from dysregulation of serotonergic signalling pathways. Discussion This study demonstrates that ageing is associated with a significant increase in serotonin alongside lower bowel dysfunction. When combined with previous ex vivo pharmacological studies a consistent picture emerges: ageing enhances mucosal transmitter availability but disrupts synchronised motor coordination. Elevated 5-HT appeared linked to altered epithelial handling, including increased synthesis, reduced uptake via the serotonin reuptake transporter (SERT), or impaired clearance. Prolonged 5-HT exposure has previously been shown to desensitise 5-HT₃ receptors on sensory neurons and reduce 5-HT₄ receptor efficacy on motor neurons. This may reflect age-related changes in function of SERT, leading to altered 5-HT3 receptor responsiveness and changes in 5-HT-dependent secondary messenger mechanisms resulting in uncoordinated motility responses [2,3]. Collectively, these findings identify several potential targets for future investigation. Modulation of serotonin clearance pathways, including SERT, and modulation of 5-HT₃- and 5-HT₄-mediated signalling pathways may represent potential strategies for improving gastrointestinal motility in ageing populations. Limitations include the exclusion of female animals due to insufficient data and the use of a preclinical model, requiring validation in human populations. These findings highlight the value of mechanistic pharmacological research in identifying future diagnostic, preventative, and therapeutic strategies. Keywords Ageing, Serotonin (5-HT), Lower bowel dysfunction, Constipation, Gastrointestinal motility, Serotonergic signalling, Electrochemical sensing, Preventative medicine, Pharmacology

titre: Immuno-Metabolic Depression: From Immune–Metabolic Dysregulation to Biomarker-Guided Precision Psychiatry
resume: Immuno-metabolic depression (IMD) describes the clustering of atypical energy-related symptoms, low-grade inflammation, and metabolic dysregulation within major depressive disorder. This structured narrative review evaluates its biological basis and potential utility for patient stratification and treatment selection. PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Library were searched through July 2026 without a lower publication-date restriction. Clinical, genetic, multi-omics, and neuroimaging evidence links energy-related symptom profiles with inflammatory and metabolic abnormalities. Human observations and preclinical experiments implicate interacting immune, metabolic, endocrine, kynurenine, dopaminergic, and gut–brain pathways, although an IMD-specific causal sequence remains uncertain. C-reactive protein, symptom profiles, and metabolic indices may support research stratification; their ability to predict differential treatment benefit requires validation. Anti-inflammatory and dopaminergic studies report preliminary mechanistic or symptom-related findings in selected samples, while exercise has shown favorable effects on immunometabolic indices. The reviewed semaglutide trial did not demonstrate benefit for the primary executive-function outcome or depressive symptoms, despite favorable secondary findings for global cognition and weight. IMD therefore remains a research framework with potential clinical relevance. Standardized definitions, longitudinal studies, and adequately powered randomized trials are needed to establish whether biomarker-guided treatment selection improves depressive, functional, and cardiometabolic outcomes beyond standard care.

titre: ALEXITHYMIA AND PARENTAL BONDING AMONG FIRST-VISIT ADOLESCENT PATIENTS IN SPECIALIZED MENTAL OR MEDICAL HEALTHCARE
resume: ABSTRACT Background: Alexithymia is a personality trait characterized by difficulties in identifying and describing emotions. In adults, it has been associated with several psychiatric conditions and medical illnesses. Although similar associations appear to exist in adolescents, alexithymia has been studied only rarely in adolescent patient populations. Furthermore, experienced parental bonding has not previously been studied in relation to alexithymia in clinical adolescent samples. Therefore, our aim was to investigate the prevalence of alexithymia and its association with parental bonding among adolescents entering specialized mental or medical healthcare. Methods: The study samples comprised first-visit patients attending an adolescent psychiatry clinic (n=176, aged 13-22 years) or a paediatric clinic (n=117, aged 12-15 years). Alexithymia was assessed using the Toronto Alexithymia scale (TAS-20) and perceived parental bonding with the Parental Bonding Instrument (PBI). The psychometric properties of the TAS-20 were assessed using confirmatory factor analysis and the main analyses were carried out using general linear models. Results: High levels of alexithymic features were prevalent in both samples, with rates of 48.3% in the adolescent psychiatry sample and 19.7% in the paediatric sample. Median TAS-20 scores were significantly higher in the former (60.0 vs. 51.0, p<0.001). Low parental care was significantly related to alexithymic features in both samples. High maternal overprotection had a significant association with alexithymic features only in the adolescent psychiatry sample. Conclusions: Alexithymic features are common among adolescents entering specialized healthcare, particularly among those referred to adolescent psychiatry. Perceived parental bonding is significantly related to alexithymia also among patients referred to paediatric care. Further research is needed to clarify the role of alexithymia in somatic complaints and medical illnesses during adolescence.
revue: DOAJ (DOAJ: Directory of Open Access Journals)

resume: This study is about validating the TAS-20 IF in French language and further invetisgating how alexithymia influences one's rating of other's alexithymia. To do so, we recruited dyads of participants that have known each other for at least one year. Participants were invited to the lab and simultaneously completed an online Qualtrics survey on the lab computers. Participants completed the following questionnaires: Toronto Alexithymia Scale (TAS-20, Bagby et al., 1994; French translation from Loas et al., 1996), the Toronto Alexithymia Scale Informant Form (TAS-20 IF, Bagby et al., 2021) and the Positive And Negative Affect Schedule (PANAS, Watson et al., 1988, French translation from Gaudreau et al., 2006). The order of TAS-20 and TAS-20 IF were counterbalanced across participants. We additionally recorded sociodemographic information, and data about the dyad's relationship (familiarity, closeness, liking, nature the relationship).

titre: The Upaniṣads and modern mental health: A scientific and metacognitive exploration of consciousness, selfhood, emotional regulation, and psychological well-being
resume: The Upaniṣads contain sophisticated reflections on consciousness, the self, desire, attention and suffering that are highly relevant to contemporary mental health. This conceptual narrative review examines eleven principal Upaniṣads (Bṛhadāraṇyaka, Chāndogya, Kaṭha, Taittirīya, Māṇḍūkya, Īśā, Muṇḍaka, Kena, Praśna, Aitareya and Śvetāśvatara) in the light of psychological and psychiatric constructs, including metacognition, decentering, emotional regulation, psychological flexibility, interoception and mindfulness. The comparisons are interpretive and hypothesis-generating, and philosophical claims are kept separate from empirically testable ones. This paper proposes an integrative five-dimension framework, discusses clinical implications and safeguards, and suggests a pilot study design. The Upaniṣads may contribute to culturally informed formulation and psychoeducation without displacing evidence-based treatment; their specific applications require empirical testing.

titre: P073 Double vision and a difficult diagnosis
resume: Abstract Introduction Giant cell arteritis (GCA) is the commonest systemic vasculitis in older adults and is classically characterised by new-onset headache, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication and visual symptoms. However, atypical presentations and negative cranial investigations can delay diagnosis and treatment. We describe a 63-year-old man presenting with sequential bilateral sixth cranial nerve palsies and headache without classical cranial symptoms. Temporal artery biopsy was negative off steroids. Extensive investigation excluded infective, malignant and autoimmune mimics before PET-CT demonstrated large-vessel vasculitis supporting a diagnosis of atypical GCA. This case highlights the diagnostic value of multimodal imaging and multidisciplinary assessment. Case description A 63-year-old man with hypertension presented with a four-day history of severe left-sided headache associated with nausea, vomiting and peri-orbital pain in November 2024. CT brain was unremarkable and he was initially managed as presumed migraine. He subsequently developed a left sixth cranial nerve palsy causing diplopia prompting neurological assessment. MRI brain and vascular imaging were normal, while inflammatory markers were modestly elevated (ESR 44 mm/hr, CRP 9 mg/L). Given concern for vasculitis, temporal artery biopsy was performed but showed no evidence of giant cell arteritis. Despite negative investigations, empirical treatment with intravenous methylprednisolone followed by 60 mg oral prednisolone was commenced because of high clinical suspicion. Temporal artery ultrasound performed after almost 11-days on steroids was negative. One month later, whilst receiving prednisolone 60 mg daily, he re-presented with worsening headache and developed a contralateral sixth cranial nerve palsy. He denied jaw claudication, scalp tenderness or visual loss. Repeat inflammatory markers were only mildly elevated and the progression of symptoms despite corticosteroids prompted extensive investigation. Multiple lumbar punctures demonstrated non-specific inflammatory cerebrospinal fluid changes. Comprehensive autoimmune, infective and malignant screening, including haematological and ENT assessment, failed to identify an alternative diagnosis. Repeated attempts to taper corticosteroids resulted in recurrent headaches, constitutional symptoms and marked rises in inflammatory markers (ESR 110, CRP 108). Severe claustrophobia delayed MRI and PET-CT imaging, necessitating hypnotherapy, while corticosteroids were rapidly tapered in the interim. PET-CT performed off steroids, in August 2025 demonstrated faint FDG uptake involving the ascending aorta and aortic arch consistent with aortitis and large-vessel vasculitis. Following multidisciplinary review, a diagnosis of atypical large-vessel giant cell arteritis was made. Tocilizumab was commenced in October 2025, with methotrexate added five months later for ongoing steroid sparing. Diplopia resolved completely, headaches improved substantially and inflammatory markers normalised, allowing gradual corticosteroid reduction. Discussion This case demonstrates the diagnostic challenges posed by atypical giant cell arteritis. Sequential bilateral sixth cranial nerve palsies are an uncommon manifestation of GCA and, combined with the absence of jaw claudication, scalp tenderness and visual loss, initially favoured neurological rather than vasculitic diagnoses. A further challenge was the negative temporal artery biopsy off steroids and ultrasound after 11-days on steroids. Temporal artery biopsy is susceptible to skip lesions and therefore cannot exclude GCA in patients with a convincing clinical presentation. This case reinforces that negative cranial investigations should not provide false reassurance when suspicion remains high. The relapsing clinical course proved equally informative. Symptom recurrence during corticosteroid tapering, accompanied by progressively rising inflammatory markers, suggested ongoing inflammatory disease despite treatment. Extensive investigation excluded infective, malignant and alternative autoimmune disorders, while repeated multidisciplinary discussion ensured the differential diagnosis continued to evolve. PET-CT proved pivotal by demonstrating inflammation within the ascending aorta and aortic arch, supporting a diagnosis of large-vessel GCA that had not been identified by cranial investigations. This highlights the complementary role of whole-body vascular imaging in patients with suspected GCA and inconclusive temporal artery assessment, particularly when large-vessel disease is suspected. The case also illustrates the practical challenges encountered during investigation. Severe claustrophobia delayed MRI and PET-CT, prolonging diagnostic uncertainty and emphasising the importance of adapting investigations to individual patient circumstances. This case reinforces the point that when patients have persistent clinical suspicion for giant cell arteritis despite negative temporal artery ultrasound and biopsy, earlier PET-CT or alternative large-vessel imaging should be incorporated into the diagnostic pathway. Key learning points • This case reinforced that giant cell arteritis should remain an important differential diagnosis in patients over 50 years presenting with new headache and cranial neuropathies, even in the absence of classical cranial symptoms. Sequential bilateral sixth cranial nerve palsies, although rare, may represent an atypical manifestation of GCA. • Negative temporal artery ultrasound and biopsy do not exclude giant cell arteritis. Prior corticosteroid exposure, skip lesions and isolated large-vessel involvement may all reduce the diagnostic yield of cranial investigations. Clinical judgement should therefore remain central when investigations and presentation appear discordant. • A further learning point was the importance of reassessing the diagnosis throughout the disease course. Relapsing symptoms during corticosteroid tapering, rising inflammatory markers and failure to identify an alternative diagnosis all supported ongoing inflammatory disease despite initially inconclusive investigations. • This case also highlighted the value of multidisciplinary collaboration and multimodal imaging. PET-CT ultimately identified large-vessel inflammation and established the diagnosis after extensive neurological, infectious, malignant and autoimmune investigations had proved non-diagnostic. • The principal learning objective from the conference would be to better understand the investigation of suspected large-vessel giant cell arteritis when temporal artery ultrasound and biopsy are negative. In particular, I would welcome discussion regarding the optimal timing of PET-CT, the influence of corticosteroid exposure on imaging sensitivity, and strategies for balancing clinical judgement with negative investigations to minimise diagnostic delay and prevent irreversible complications.

titre: Managing insomnia: An evaluation of cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia in clinical and preventive contexts
resume: Insomnia is a highly prevalent and often persistent disorder that remains under-recognized and undertreated in routine care. This thesis examined the relationship between insomnia and mental health symptoms, the effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of insomnia interventions, and opportunities to improve access to and optimize insomnia treatment. Although cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) is the first-line treatment and has been shown to improve sleep and potentially reduce mental health symptoms, access to CBT-I in routine care remains limited, resulting in a substantial treatment gap. In Chapter 2, we examined the relationship between insomnia and symptoms of major depressive disorder (MDD), social anxiety disorder (SAD), panic disorder (PD), generalized anxiety disorder (GAD), post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), and borderline personality disorder (BPD), using cross-sectional online data. Insomnia was highly prevalent across all symptom domains. Network analyses showed that insomnia severity was directly associated with symptom severity of MDD, GAD, and BPD, whereas associations with SAD, PD, and PTSD were no longer direct when accounting for other comorbid symptoms. In Chapter 3, we presented the study protocol for a series of randomized controlled trials evaluating therapist-guided internet-delivered CBT-I (iCBT-I) in adults with insomnia and co-occurring symptoms of SAD, PD, GAD, PTSD, or BPD. The studies were conducted across three levels of mental healthcare, ranging from individuals not currently receiving or awaiting mental health care to individuals awaiting general or specialized secondary care. In Chapter 4, we evaluated the clinical effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of guided iCBT-I among individuals not currently receiving or awaiting mental health care. Guided iCBT-I yielded large and sustained reductions in insomnia severity and improvements in sleep diary outcomes. Small improvements were observed in symptoms of SAD, PD, GAD, and BPD, but were not maintained at six-month follow-up. No effects were found for PTSD symptoms. The economic evaluation showed no differences in societal costs between groups. Although iCBT-I had a high probability of being cost-effective in reducing insomnia severity from a societal perspective, these improvements did not translate into similar improvements in quality-adjusted life years (QALYs). In Chapter 5, we conducted a mixed-methods process evaluation of participants' and therapists' experiences with guided iCBT-I across all three levels of care. Overall, the intervention was well accepted, with most participants reporting improvements in sleep and high satisfaction. However, optimizing its impact may require more flexible guidance and adaptable treatment content to better align with individual needs. In Chapter 6, we investigated the long-term preventive effects of CBT-I, circadian rhythm support (CRS), and their combination on depression incidence over four years. Only combined CBT-I and CRS reduced the risk of incident depressive disorders, and this effect was limited to individuals with unspecified insomnia rather than those with the subtype associated with an increased lifetime risk of mental disorders. These findings highlight the potential value of combined or more intensive interventions and treatment approaches tailored to insomnia subtypes. Building on these findings, we identified five key levers for optimizing insomnia treatment: guidance, treatment content, treatment dose, engagement and adherence, and next-step options for individuals who do not respond to initial treatment. Primary care emerged as the central entry point for reducing the treatment gap, while secondary care should focus on integrating insomnia interventions into existing treatment pathways. Future research should inform how insomnia care can be effectively implemented and tailored across settings to improve access and treatment outcomes.

titre: Long-Term Acquisition and Maintenance of Cognitive Behavioral Therapy Skills Through a Smartphone-Based Intervention: A Secondary Analysis of the RESiLIENT Trial
resume: Background Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) is assumed to confer longer-term benefit partly through the acquisition and maintenance of therapeutic skills, but evidence on these processes after smartphone-based CBT remains limited in subthreshold depression. This exploratory secondary analysis of the RESiLIENT randomized controlled trial examined 50-week changes in five CBT skill domains: behavioral activation (BA), cognitive restructuring (CR), problem solving (PS), assertion training (AT), and behavioral therapy for insomnia (BI). Methods The reported comparisons involved 3,280 participants with baseline PHQ-9 scores of 5 or higher assigned to nine CBT intervention arms or the weekly self-check control arm. Self-reported skill enactment was assessed at baseline and weeks 6, 26, and 50. Standardized mean differences versus self-check were reported for 135 CBT contrasts. P-values and confidence intervals used a Dunnett approximation within each domain and visit. Results Estimated changes in CR skill scores favored several intervention arms over self-check, whereas changes in BA skill scores favored the intervention in some comparisons. Estimated between-group differences in PS, AT, and BI skill scores were generally small. At week 50, standardized mean differences for BA+CR versus self-check were 0.26 (95% CI 0.07–0.46) for BA and 0.27 (0.07–0.47) for CR. The corresponding CR estimate in the CR arm was 0.21 (0.01–0.41). These estimates illustrate exploratory patterns and do not establish superiority of one intervention or skill domain. Conclusions This exploratory study describes varying patterns of change across self-reported CBT skill domains over 50 weeks following a brief smartphone-based intervention. These findings may inform future research on the persistence of CBT skill use and its relationship with longer-term clinical outcomes.

titre: Combination of cognitive behavioral therapy and antidepressant medication versus the monotherapies for obsessive compulsive disorder: A systematic review and meta-analysis
resume: Cognitive behavior therapy (CBT) and antidepressive medication (ADM) are recommended as first-line treatments for patients with obsessive compulsive disorder (OCD) of mild to moderate severity, whereas the Combination of CBT and ADM is recommended for patients with severe OCD. A systematic review and meta-analysis was conducted of randomized controlled trials with adults or children in which the Combination was compared with the monotherapies, or CBT with ADM. Four databases were systematically searched for studies published until August 2026. Twenty-three studies were included, comprising 1381 participants, 820 adults and 561 children. CBT had a drop-out rate of 14.7%, ADM 18.9%, and the Combination 21.2%, with no significant difference between treatments. There was no significant difference in OCD scores between Combination and CBT ( g = 0.05), but both the Combination and CBT were significantly better than ADM ( g = 0.75 and 0.38, respectively). Average response rate was significantly higher for the Combination (73%) and CBT (64%) compared to ADM (40%). Moderator analyses indicated that pre-treatment OCD severity was not a significant moderator of outcome. The results of the present meta-analysis suggest that current recommendations regarding concurrent Combination treatment may warrant refinement, particularly given the lack of added benefit over CBT alone. Prospero registration id: CRD420261300204.

titre: Reaction-time changes around rule shifts on the Wisconsin card sorting test in obsessive–compulsive disorder and treatment-resistant depression
resume: Conventional Wisconsin Card Sorting Test (WCST) indices quantify errors and categorization performance, whereas reaction-time measures may provide complementary information about performance surrounding rule shifts. This study compared conventional WCST performance and rule-shift-related reaction-time patterns among patients with obsessive–compulsive disorder (OCD), patients with treatment-resistant depression (TRD), and healthy controls (HCs). This retrospective study included 181 participants: 38 with OCD, 67 with TRD, and 76 HCs. Reaction times before and after each of five WCST rule shifts were analyzed using generalized estimating equations (GEE), adjusting for age, sex, and education. Four conventional WCST indices were compared using Kruskal–Wallis tests, with Holm correction across the four omnibus tests. An additional exploratory analysis examined 19 conventional WCST indices, with Holm correction across these 19 tests. In the full GEE model, planned contrasts averaged equally across the five rule shifts showed a greater pre-to-post change in log-transformed reaction time in OCD than in HCs (β = 0.146, 95% CI 0.064–0.228; Holm-adjusted p = 0.00149) and in TRD than in HCs (β = 0.107, 95% CI 0.037–0.177; Holm-adjusted p = 0.00538). The OCD–TRD contrast was not statistically significant (β = 0.039, 95% CI − 0.046 to 0.123; Holm-adjusted p = 0.370). The group-by-phase-by-shift interaction was not statistically significant. None of the four primary conventional WCST omnibus tests or the 19 exploratory omnibus tests remained statistically significant after their respective Holm corrections. Both clinical-group differences remained significant in full-model sensitivity analyses addressing extreme reaction times, although the OCD–HC estimate was attenuated when very long reaction times were excluded; a contribution of medication to the TRD findings could not be excluded. Patients with OCD and TRD showed greater pre-to-post rule-shift reaction-time changes than HCs when estimates were averaged across five rule shifts. Robust group differences in conventional WCST indices were not established after correction for multiple testing. Reaction-time measures may complement conventional WCST indices, but independent replication is needed before clinical or mechanistic conclusions can be drawn.

titre: Feeding and eating disorders in adults: Systematic review and meta-analysis
resume: Aims Avoidant/Restrictive Food Intake Disorder (ARFID) in adults is less studied than in younger populations, and prevalence estimates vary across populations and assessment methods. This systematic review and meta-analysis estimated the prevalence of positive ARFID screens or study-defined ARFID in adults and examined variation by geographical location, population characteristics, and assessment approach. Food neophobia and food selectivity were secondary narrative outcomes. Methods The review was registered in PROSPERO (CRD420251267471), conducted according to Joanna Briggs Institute guidance, and reported following PRISMA. PubMed, Embase, and the Virtual Health Library were searched without language or date restrictions. Observational studies of adults aged 18–65 years reporting prevalence of ARFID, food neophobia, or food selectivity were eligible. Two reviewers independently screened studies and extracted data. Risk of bias was assessed using JBI tools. Random-effects meta-analyses were conducted. Results Twenty-three studies (370,230 adults) were included; 20 (368,494 participants) contributed to the ARFID meta-analysis. The exploratory pooled prevalence was 19.5% (95% CI: 7.6%–41.9%; prediction interval: 0.2%–97.2%; I 2 = 99.8%). The pooled point estimate was 24.8% in clinical samples and 4.1% in non-clinical samples, although population type was not a significant moderator ( p = .170). Studies using the Nine Item ARFID Screen (NIAS) yielded 33.7% versus 5.8% for non-NIAS studies, but moderation remained inconclusive. Conclusion Positive ARFID screens and study-defined ARFID are frequently identified in the adult samples studied to date, but the pooled estimate should not be interpreted as general-population prevalence. Substantial clinical and methodological heterogeneity limits comparability and supports stratified interpretation and diagnostic confirmation.

titre: Michel de Goedt, Éveiller aux choses de Dieu. Théologie de la vie chrétienne,avant-propos du Fr. Marie-Didier Golay (ocd) et présentation de Bruno Charmet, Toulouse, Éditions du Carmel, « Recherches carmélitaines », 2025, 241 p.,
Recurrent Angular and Exfoliative Cheilitis with Mixed Anxiety and Depression Disorder: A Case Report of Psychodermatology
resume: Introduction: Cheilitis is defined as inflammation of the lip area. The factors that affect cheilitis include infection, mechanical factors, poor oral hygiene, factitious activity like lip licking or picking, psychological stress, nutritional deficiencies, and others. Cheilitis is also related to psychiatric disorders, such as anxiety, depression, eating disorders, obsessive-compulsive disorder, and personality disorder. Case: This case report is about a 20-year-old female with recurrent angular and exfoliative cheilitis and a history of mixed anxiety and depression disorders. Psychological stress fluctuation influenced the symptoms. The patient got hydrocortisone topical, urea topical, escitalopram, and cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) and showed clinical improvement. Discussion: Cheilitis could be related to or triggered by psychiatric diseases, psychological conditions, patients’ habits, or self-injurious behavior. Other risk factors such as immune defects and B vitamin deficiencies are also considered to affect that psychodermatological condition. Conclusion: Cheilitis is one of the common cases in clinical practice. It’s important to explore psycho-dermatologic interactions. Physicians must consider patients’ psychological condition in recurrent cheilitis cases and provide proper treatment.

titre: Systems Biology and Machine Learning Reveal Oxidative Stress Hubs and Therapeutic Targets in Diarrhea-Predominant Irritable Bowel Syndrome
resume: BACKGROUND: Diarrhea-predominant irritable bowel syndrome (IBS-D) is a common functional gastrointestinal disorder, and accumulating evidence suggests that oxidative stress is involved in its pathophysiology. This study explored oxidative stress-related mechanisms in IBS-D and screened potential diagnostic biomarkers and therapeutic targets through integrative bioinformatics analysis. METHODS: Transcriptomic datasets from the National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI)-Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) database were analyzed using integrative bioinformatics approaches to identify oxidative stress-related core genes in IBS-D. Eight potential biomarkers were identified and evaluated for diagnostic performance via receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis. Among these, the key gene ACO2 was further investigated using Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG)-based gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) and immune correlation analyses to explore the association between ACO2 expression and disease-related biological processes. In addition, the eight target proteins were used for reverse screening of potentially therapeutic traditional Chinese medicines and their active compounds. RESULTS: In total, 206 oxidative stress-related genes were identified, with predominant enrichment observed in mitochondrial energy metabolism and cellular stress-response pathways, including oxidative phosphorylation and hypoxia-inducible factor 1 (HIF-1) signaling. The eight potential diagnostic biomarkers demonstrated robust diagnostic performance (area under the ROC curve (AUC) = 0.896) in distinguishing IBS-D patients from healthy controls. Notably, ACO2 emerged as a key hub gene associated with distinct metabolic and immune-related pathway enrichment profiles. In parallel, a competing endogenous RNA (ceRNA) regulatory network centered on ACO2 was established, providing additional insight into its potential post-transcriptional regulatory mechanisms. Furthermore, reverse screening based on the eight target proteins identified luteolin, phillygenin, quercetin, and wogonin as candidate active compounds from Forsythia suspensa. Molecular docking further indicated favorable binding affinity between these compounds and the biomarker proteins. CONCLUSIONS: This integrative bioinformatics study identifies oxidative stress-related molecular signatures and potential biomarkers in IBS-D. Reverse screening and molecular docking further suggest that luteolin, phillygenin, quercetin, and wogonin from Forsythia suspensa may represent potential candidate compounds targeting these biomarkers. These findings provide a theoretical basis for further experimental validation.

titre: Efficacy of Lactose Reduction in Irritable Bowel Syndrome and Recurrent Abdominal Pain: A Systematic Review
resume: BACKGROUND/OBJECTIVES: Lactose intolerance (LI), irritable bowel syndrome in adults (IBS) and recurrent abdominal pain (RAP) in children are frequently diagnosed worldwide. This systematic review aimed to assess the effects of dietary reduction in lactose on symptoms, quality of life and healthcare visits in IBS and children with recurrent abdominal pain. METHODS: PubMed, Cochrane Library, Embase and Lilacs were searched for studies on IBS and RAP investigating the effect of a reduction of dietary intake of lactose for at least 4 weeks on abdominal pain, stool characteristics, bloating and distension, and quality of life published up to 15 August 2026. No restriction in language, publication type or data limit was applied. Four reviewers independently screened the abstracts for eligibility, and risk of bias was assessed by two reviewers with ROBINS-2. Disagreements were resolved by consensus or consulting with a senior investigator. Results were summarised in tabular form. The systematic review was registered on PROSPERO (CRD42024617161). RESULTS: Eighteen studies met eligibility criteria based on the title and abstract. Upon review of full-text articles, three studies in adults and six studies in children were retained for data extraction. Lactose breath tests (LBTs) were performed in all studies. All but one study prospectively compared patient cohorts. IBS was defined by Manning criteria in two studies and Rome II criteria in one study. Only patients with a positive LBT were subjected to dietary intervention in eight of nine studies. No control group was included in one of three and three of six of the studies in adults and children, respectively. None of the studies compared symptomatic evolution based on validated questionnaires. Improvement in pain was reported by two of three and five of six of the studies on IBS and RAP, respectively. The risk of bias was high for all studies. No study assessed quality of life. CONCLUSIONS: Current evidence in support of dietary lactose reduction in patients with IBS and RAP is limited due to a high risk of bias, the use of old criteria, the absence of a valid comparator group and poorly defined outcomes. A positive LBT was associated with improvement in pain after a lactose-free diet. Future studies on the role of lactose restriction in IBS and RAP should recruit patients based on current diagnostic criteria and assess outcome by validated measures, preferentially applying a randomised controlled design.

titre: Family Risk and Resilience Patterns Differentiate Early Childhood Vulnerability to Intergenerational Transmission of Abdominal Pain
resume: Children are at increased risk of developing chronic abdominal pain if a parent has an abdominal pain-related disorder of brain-gut interaction such as irritable bowel syndrome, suggesting family mechanisms of intergenerational pain transmission. However, patterns of family risk and resilience factors that predict children's vulnerability for developing chronic abdominal pain remain unknown. In a sample of parents with an abdominal pain-related disorder of brain-gut interaction and their young child without chronic pain, this cross-sectional study identified subgroups representing different constellations of family risk and resilience factors. It also tested subgroup differences on two vulnerability markers for children's future development of chronic abdominal pain: child emotional functioning and parental protective behavior. Baseline data from 212 parents and their 4-7-year-old child, participating in a randomized controlled trial testing a preventative intervention were included. Latent mixture modeling indicated a 3-group solution: (1) "High Socioeconomic Status, High Functioning" (55%) characterized by lower anxiety and depression and higher family resilience, (2) "Low Socioeconomic Status, High Pain Burden" (13%) characterized by higher pain catastrophizing and gastrointestinal symptoms, and (3) "High Socioeconomic Status, High Distress" (32%) characterized by higher parenting stress. Two of the three groups ("Low Socioeconomic Status, High Pain Burden" and "High Socioeconomic Status, High Distress" groups) showed lower child emotional functioning, and the "Low Socioeconomic Status, High Pain Burden" group also showed higher parental protective behavior, than the "High Socioeconomic Status, High Functioning" group. Results contribute to theoretical models of intergenerational pain transmission and help identify families who could benefit from preventative interventions. PERSPECTIVE: Among families of parents with chronic abdominal pain, low family resilience, low socioeconomic status, high parent pain burden, and high parent psychological distress may make young children more vulnerable to developing chronic abdominal pain in the future. These findings inform targeted interventions to prevent intergenerational transmission of abdominal pain.

titre: Diffuse Uterine and Extrauterine Leiomyomatosis Presenting as a Large Abdominopelvic Mass Mimicking Malignancy
resume: Diffuse uterine and extrauterine leiomyomatosis is an uncommon benign condition that can mimic malignancy on imaging. We report a 48-year-old multiparous woman presenting with abdominal pain and abnormal uterine bleeding. Imaging revealed a large heterogeneous uterine mass with peritoneal involvement. Total abdominal hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy was performed. Histopathology confirmed diffuse leiomyomatosis. This rare entity poses diagnostic challenges and may lead to unnecessary aggressive treatment if misdiagnosed. Histopathology and immunohistochemistry are essential for accurate diagnosis. Awareness of this condition is crucial for appropriate management and avoidance of overtreatment.

fiche.verdict: Une léiomyomatose utérine et extra-utérine diffuse rare imite une malignité pelvienne, nécessitant une histologie rigoureuse pour éviter l'surtraitement.
