titre: ВАРЬИРОВАНИЕ ПРЕДЛОЖНО-ПАДЕЖНЫХ ФОРМ В СИСТЕМЕ РУССКИХ КОМПАРАТИВНЫХ ФРАЗЕОЛОГИЗМОВ (КОММУНИКАТИВНО-ПРАГМАТИЧЕСКИЙ АСПЕКТ)
resume: Статья посвящена проблеме формально-грамматического (морфологического) варьирования в системе компаративных фразеологизмов русского языка. Вариативность компонентов в составе устойчивого сравнения рассматривается автором как неотъемлемое свойство этой языковой единицы, расшатывающее ее структурно-семантический «каркас», но не разрушающее актуальное образно-компаративное значение. В качестве предмета исследования выбраны падежные формы компонента В – образа устойчивого сравнения: как под венец – как к венцу; как под гипнозом – как в гипнозе. Ставится вопрос о специфике слов-сопроводителей, которые употребляются с каждым из вариантов. Для подтверждения семантического единства устойчивых сравнений привлекаются лексикографические сведения и текстовые фрагменты, извлеченные из Национального корпуса русского языка [8] и авторской картотеки Словаря устойчивых сравнений русского языка В. М. Огольцева [9]. Особое внимание уделено нюансам семантики и употребления вариантных форм устойчивых сравнений, которые определяются следующими основными факторами: общее и частное значение падежной формы в целом; семантика предлога; сдвиги в компаративном значении, связанные с изменением грамматических характеристик слов-сопроводителей; коммуникативная ситуация. Сформулирован критерий, отличающий случаи формально-грамматического варьирования образа В от более радикальных «грамматических модификаций», которые влекут за собой изменение признака-основания, а значит, приводят к формированию новой компаративной единицы. The article is devoted to the problem of formal-grammatical (morphological) variation in the system of comparative phraseological units of the Russian language. The author considers the variability of components in the composition of a stable comparison as an integral property of this linguistic unit, which destabilizes its structural-semantic “frame” but does not destroy its actual figurative-comparative meaning. The article focuses on the case forms of the component B, which represents the image of a stable comparison: kak pod venets (as if for the wedding) – kak k ventsu (as if to the wedding); kak pod gipnozom (as if under hypnosis) – kak v gipnoze (as if in hypnosis). The article raises the question of the specificity of the accompanying words that are used with each of the variants. To confirm the semantic unity of stable comparisons, lexicographic information and text fragments extracted from the National Corpus of the Russian Language [8] and the author’s card index of the Dictionary of Stable Comparisons of the Russian Language by V. M. Ogoltseva [9] are used. Special attention is paid to the nuances of the semantics and usage of variant forms of stable comparisons, which are determined by the following main factors: the general and specific meaning of the case form in general; the semantics of the preposition; shifts in the comparative meaning associated with changes in the grammatical characteristics of the accompanying words; and the communicative situation. A criterion is formulated that distinguishes cases of formal and grammatical variation of the image B from more radical “grammatical modifications” that entail a change in the base feature and thus lead to the formation of a new comparative unit.
revue: Bulletin of the Chuvash State Pedagogical University named after I Y Yakovlev

titre: Architecture of the Mind: Volume II: The Illusion Regarding What We Call Reality, from Plato to Algorithms (Sample)
resume: Summary: Arquitetura da Mente, Volume II This volume examines illusion as a foundational, adaptive mechanism rather than a perceptual error. The central argument positions illusion as the "zero term"—the structural condition that makes other mental states intelligible. The work is organized into five sections. The first establishes philosophical and neuroscientific foundations, reinterpreting Plato's allegory and Kant's transcendental architecture through the framework of predictive processing, in which perception operates as a "controlled hallucination." The second section traces historical shifts in institutional authority over the real, from medieval ecclesiastical control—contrasting the validation of Hildegard of Bingen with the condemnation of Marguerite Porete—through Galileo's telescopic observations to Robertson's phantasmagorias. The third analyzes literary works—Os Lusíadas, Dom Quixote, and The Tempest—as early explorations of reality construction, collective memory, and performative belief. The fourth section examines perceptual engineering across art, photography, hypnosis, cinema, psychedelics, virtual reality, and deepfakes, demonstrating the progressive technical mediation of experience. The fifth addresses contemporary algorithmic mediation of identity, the erosion of factual evidence, and the digital transformation of spiritual meaning. The conclusion proposes an ethical distinction between necessary illusions—art, hope, spirituality—that organize experience, and toxic illusions—conspiracies, malicious deepfakes—that erode shared reality. The work ultimately reframes the central question from an epistemological one ("What is real?") to an ethical and pragmatic one ("What kind of reality should be constructed?"), arguing for critical algorithmic literacy and a disciplined approach to perception. Keywords: Illusions; Perception; Artificial Intelligence; Information Literacy; Philosophy; Books.
revue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

titre: Sexual disorders in people with post-traumatic stress disorder
resume: Background. The article addresses key aspects of sexual dysfunctions in patients with post traumatic stress disorder, covering epidemiology, clinical patterns, diagnosis, and treatment approaches. Results. The prevalence of sexual dysfunction in individuals with post traumatic stress disorder is notably high, reaching up to 88.6% in some studies. Specific types of dysfunction show distinct frequency ranges: erectile dysfunction is reported in 43-58% of men with post traumatic stress disorder, rising to 85% in certain studies; decreased libido is found in 32-40% of men and 35% of women; premature ejaculation occurs in 27-41.8% of men; anorgasmia affects 18-22% of men; dyspareunia is diagnosed in approximately 20% of female veterans. The wide range of reported rates (from 8.4 to 88.6%) is largely due to methodological differences across studies, including variations in sample selection, diagnostic criteria, and data collection methods. Sexual dysfunctions in post traumatic stress disorder are multifactorial. Key contributing factors include psychogenic elements, comorbid mental health conditions, as well as organic, iatrogenic, and interpersonal factors. Clinical manifestations are diverse and encompass decreased libido, erectile dysfunction, premature ejaculation, anorgasmia, vaginismus, dyspareunia, and, in some cases, hypersexuality and compulsive sexual behavior. Two main clinical patterns are identified: one characterized by a predominance of anxiety depressive fixation on the sexual problem, and another marked by significant partner conflicts that can both intensify and perpetuate symptoms. Treatment and rehabilitation are implemented in stages. The initial stage focuses on psychoeducation, correction of distorted beliefs about sexual norms, sexual resocialization, and reduction of tension in partner relationships. The second stage includes targeted psychotherapy and, when necessary, pharmacotherapy. Psychotherapeutic methods used include cognitive behavioral therapy, eye movement desensitization and reprocessing, Gestalt therapy, Ericksonian hypnosis, integrative sex therapy, and family therapy. An important component is the restoration of temporal perspective, which involves the ZTPI questionnaire, structured interviews, techniques such as "Life Line Beyond Trauma" and "Letter from the Future", goal setting along a time line, and mindfulness practices within the framework of sensate focus exercises. Pharmacotherapy is regarded as a supportive intervention, with efforts made to minimize its negative impact on sexual function. The third stage of rehabilitation aims at readapting couple relationships and preventing relapses. The article concludes that sexological support should be integrated into the overall rehabilitation system for patients with post traumatic stress disorder. The proposed management algorithm enables early identification of sexual dysfunctions and implementation of comprehensive interventions that improve quality of life and treatment adherence.

titre: Effect of Mind-Body Therapies on Mental Health Outcomes in Bipolar Disorder: Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials
resume: The aim of this study was to examine the effectiveness of mind–body therapies on mental health outcomes (depressive symptoms, manic symptoms, anxiety, quality of life, and mindfulness) in individuals with bipolar disorder. Randomized controlled trials published in English without year restriction and comparing mind–body therapies with an active control group or a wait-list control were included. Scopus, PubMed (MEDLINE), Wiley, ScienceDirect, and Web of Science (WOS) databases were searched up to April 2024. Nine studies including a total of 1,205 participants were included in the meta-analysis. Mind–body therapies were not associated with significant effects on depressive symptoms, manic symptoms, or quality of life. However, these therapies were associated with a significant reduction in anxiety and a significant increase in mindfulness scores. Future studies should aim to develop and implement mind–body therapy programs specific to bipolar disorder and design studies to evaluate whether these interventions are applicable in individuals with bipolar disorder. Given their potential to reduce anxiety and increase mindfulness, mind–body therapies may be considered as a complementary approach to pharmacological and psychosocial treatments in bipolar disorder.
revue: Psikiyatride Guncel Yaklasimlar - Current Approaches in Psychiatry

titre: Effect of Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction Combined With Family Support on Depressive Symptoms and Sleep Quality in Patients With Postpartum Depression: A Retrospective Cohort Study Based on Propensity Score Matching
resume: Background: To explore the association between mindfulness-based stress reduction nursing combined with family support nursing and depressive symptoms, sleep quality, related physiological indicators in patients with postpartum depression using a retrospective propensity score-matched design. Methods: A total of 472 patients with postpartum depression admitted to Nanjing Medical University Affiliated Women’s and Children’s Hospital between October 2022 and October 2025 were included. After propensity score matching, 106 patients who received family support nursing alone (control group) and 106 who received mindfulnessbased stress reduction nursing combined with family support nursing (observation group) were analysed. Outcomes were assessed before nursing, at 4 and 8 weeks after nursing. Repeated measures analysis of variance (ANOVA) and post-hoc tests with Bonferroni correction were applied. The primary outcome was the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS) score. Secondary outcomes included Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI) scores, sleep architecture parameters, inflammatory markers (IL-1β, TNF-α, IL-6), salivary cortisol, heart rate variability (HRV) parameters, and nursing satisfaction rate. Results: Repeated measures ANOVA revealed significant time, group, and time × group interaction effects for EPDS scores, PSQI scores, and sleep architecture (p < 0.001). At 4 and 8 weeks, EPDS and PSQI scores were lower than baseline values in both group (p < 0.0167, Bonferroni corrected), and scores at week 8 were further reduced compared with those at week 4 (p < 0.0167). The observation group showed significantly lower EPDS and PSQI scores than the control group (p < 0.0167). Similar patterns were observed for inflammatory markers, salivary cortisol, and HRV parameters. The observation group also had a higher satisfaction rate (86.79% vs. 73.58%, p = 0.016). Conclusions: In this retrospective matched cohort, mindfulness-based stress reduction nursing combined with family support nursing was associated with greater improvements in depressive symptoms, sleep quality, and stress-related physiological parameters compared with family support nursing alone. These associations warrant confirmation in prospective randomised controlled trials.

titre: Recognition of Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder by Non-Specialist Health Workers in India: Treatment Delay as a Modifiable Outcome : A Narrative Review
resume: Background: Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) is a treatable mental health condition frequently recognised late. Patients often first present to general health settings, where non-specialist health workers play a crucial role in early identification. Objective: To synthesise evidence on treatment delay in OCD, examine barriers to recognition in non-specialist settings, and assess the potential role of the general health workforce in reducing delays in the Indian context. Methods: A narrative review was conducted using PubMed, Scopus, and Google Scholar to identify literature published between 2005 and 2025. Search terms included OCD, duration of untreated illness, help-seeking, recognition, misdiagnosis, mental health literacy, health workers, nurses, and India. Relevant national survey reports were also reviewed. Studies were selected based on relevance rather than systematic eligibility criteria. Findings: Pooled estimates indicate a mean age at help-seeking of 28.66 years, compared with an onset age of approximately 19.5 years, with a pooled duration of untreated illness of 80.23 months. Prolonged untreated illness is associated with poorer treatment response. Under-recognition, symptom concealment, and professional misdiagnosis contribute to delays. In India, an estimated 84.5% treatment gap for mental disorders and psychiatrist availability of approximately 0.3 per 100,000 population highlight the importance of non-specialist healthcare providers. Mental compulsions, scrupulosity, and intrusive postnatal aggressive thoughts may be particularly difficult to recognise. Conclusion: Evidence on OCD knowledge among Indian non-specialist health workers remains limited. Integrating symptom recognition, brief screening, and cadre-specific training into general healthcare may improve early identification. Descriptive research is urgently needed to establish baseline knowledge and inform targeted interventions.
revue: International Journal of Health Care and Biological Sciences

titre: Do people perceive mental disorders as a part of the true self? Implications and variation across seven disorders
resume: Abstract We investigated public beliefs about the extent to which mental disorders are perceived to be part of the true self, that is, the set of traits and behaviors that compose one’s core character. We conducted three quantitative vignette-based studies (total n = 601) in UK general public samples, considering seven disorders (attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), anorexia nervosa, autism spectrum disorder (ASD), bipolar disorder, major depressive disorder, schizophrenia, and obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD)). For each disorder, participants rated how much the disorder reflects the vignette character’s true self, along with perceived causes of the disorders (studies 1 and 2), perceived severity, age of onset, duration, probability of recovery (study 2), and stigmatization (study 3). Disorders differed sharply in the extent to which they were judged to be part of the true self: ADHD, ASD, and OCD received higher true self ratings than major depressive disorder, anorexia nervosa, and schizophrenia, with bipolar disorder intermediate. A disorder was rated more ‘true self’ when it was: perceived as more “biologically” caused; less “psychologically” caused; less severe; and recovery was perceived as less likely. Although the extent of stigmatization also varied across disorders, true self ratings did not predict stigmatization. Our results show that the public thinks about different mental disorders in quite different ways, suggesting that different disorders should not be lumped together when considering attitudes and their consequences.

titre: Introduction: Facing Eating Disorder Fears
resume: Abstract This introductory chapter presents Facing Eating Disorder Fears (FEDF), an evidence-based exposure therapy program that targets anxiety underlying anorexia nervosa, bulimia nervosa, binge eating disorder, and other specified feeding and eating disorders. It outlines the guide’s 10-chapter structure, emphasizing psychoeducation, skill development, in vivo exposure and imaginal exposure, emotional processing, habituation, inhibitory learning, and relapse prevention. The chapter establishes the clinical rationale for applying exposure therapy to eating disorders by highlighting functional similarities with anxiety disorders, post-traumatic stress disorder, and obsessive–compulsive disorder and referencing supporting research. It describes the program’s active treatment framework, including structured sessions, therapist guidance, individualized fear hierarchies, systematic exposure practice, and homework that promotes skill generalization and self-efficacy. Finally, the chapter explains the theoretical foundations of habituation and inhibitory learning and positions FEDF as a comprehensive clinical guide that prepares therapists to address eating disorder fears and facilitate sustained recovery.

titre: A Clinical Trial to Examine the Effects of Gut Health Supplements to Improve Gut and Digestive Health and Function
resume: This is a double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trial evaluating the efficacy of JSHealth's Debloat \& Detox supplement, used alone or in combination with their Probiotics supplement, on gut and digestive health and function in 60 female participants aged 18-45 with self-reported bloating and digestive discomfort. Participants will be randomly assigned to either the intervention or placebo group for eight weeks. During the first four weeks, intervention participants will take the Debloat \& Detox supplement and placebo participants will take a corresponding placebo. During weeks five through eight, intervention participants will add the Probiotic supplement and placebo participants will add a probiotic placebo. Outcomes will be assessed via study-specific questionnaires and abdominal circumference measurements at Baseline, Day 1 (after first use), and at the end of Weeks 2, 4, 6, and 8.

titre: Recovery Time With the Application of ALDRETE Score in Patients Undergoing Gastrointestinal Endoscopy: a Randomized Controlled Trial
resume: Over the past decades, the volume and complexity of gastrointestinal endoscopy (GI) interventions have increased due to the progress in diagnostic and therapeutic procedures along worldwide implementation of colorectal cancer screening and surveillance programs. Nowadays, the first line for procedural sedation is either propofol or midazolam, in combination with opiates when analgesia is required, depending on the country's human resources, service framework, and legislation. Provision of sedation has been shown to decrease patient's anxiety, discomfort and pain improving at the same time procedure efficiency. However, administration of sedative and/or analgesic medications is not risk-free, as a variety of serious adverse effects i.e. respiratory depression, arrhythmia or hypotension may occur. In this regard, optimal discharge management after a procedure with sedation/analgesia, until the patient returns to a fully conscious, clinically stable, and ideally cognitively functional state can be challenging for both endoscopists and nursing personnel\[6\]. In an effort to address this, international endoscopy societies suggest the use of standardized discharge criteria and scoring systems such as the Post Anesthesia Recovery (PAR), or Aldrete, score, Aldrete scoring system and the modified post-anesthesia discharge scoring system (mPADSS), combined with clinical assessment to ensure patient safe discharge and readiness for discharge. Still, data supporting the use of Aldrete score derive mainly from studies evaluating patients discharge post-surgery, while evidence for model use in the setting of GI endoscopic procedures remain scant\[8,9\]. In this context, the investigators conducted a randomized controlled trial (RCT) aiming to explore the impact of Aldrete scoring system on safe discharge of participants who have undergone GI procedures under analgesia/sedation.

titre: Efficacy and safety of a fixed-dose papain and alpha-amylase combination in patients with functional dyspepsia: a real-world study
resume: BACKGROUND: Functional dyspepsia (FD) is highly prevalent and often inadequately managed because conventional therapies may have limited efficacy or tolerability. Enzyme-based therapies offer a physiologically relevant alternative by supporting digestion. This study evaluated the real-world effectiveness and safety of a fixed-dose combination (FDC) of papain and alpha-amylase in patients with FD. METHODOLOGY: This prospective, multicenter, single-arm intervention study enrolled adults with FD (Rome IV criteria) across four Indian centers. Patients received the FDC for 12 days. The primary endpoint was a ≥50% reduction in composite symptom score. Secondary endpoints included symptom resolution, time to relief, safety, and subgroup outcomes. Assessments were conducted at baseline, Day 7, and Day 12. RESULTS: Of 160 enrolled patients, 144 (90%) completed the study. Mean symptom scores declined significantly from 9.35 ± 1.42 (baseline) to 0.15 ± 0.35 (Day 12; p< 0.0001), indicating 98.4% improvement. Clinical response was achieved in all patients by Day 7 and sustained on Day 12, with 85.4% achieving excellent response. The arithmetic mean (unweighted) of domain-specific resolution percentages reached 98.7% by Day 12. Median time to initial relief was approximately 4 hours. Adverse events were mild and reported in 12.5% of patients. CONCLUSION: The FDC demonstrated short-term rapid, substantial, and consistent symptom relief with favorable tolerability in patients with FD.

titre: Ameliorative Effects of Casein Peptides on Constipation-Predominant Irritable Bowel Syndrome: Involvement of the GC-C/cGMP Signaling Pathway
resume: This study investigated the effects of casein peptides on constipation-predominant irritable bowel syndrome (IBS-C) in mice. Results revealed that oral administration of casein hydrolyzate significantly attenuated constipation symptoms, reduced visceral hypersensitivity, improved intestinal barrier integrity, suppressed inflammatory responses, and restored serum neurotransmitter balance in IBS-C mice. Casein hydrolyzate did not alter guanylyl cyclase C (GC-C) mRNA levels but significantly increased cyclic guanosine-3',5'-monophosphate (cGMP) levels in the colon of IBS-C mice, suggesting the possible involvement of the GC-C/cGMP signaling pathway in the above effects. Additionally, nine casein peptides with potential GC-C agonistic activity were identified through an integrated in silico screening and ex vivo functional evaluation, among which PFPGPIPN showed the highest activity. Moreover, in vivo experiments confirmed that PFPGPIPN significantly ameliorated IBS-C symptoms and elevated colonic cGMP levels in mice. These findings highlight the potential of casein peptides as bioactive ingredients in functional foods for the management of IBS-C.
revue: Journal of agricultural and food chemistry

titre: Parental Interpretation Biases as a Transdiagnostic Risk Factor for Adolescent Anxiety and Depressive Symptoms
resume: INTRODUCTION: Anxiety and depressive symptoms often emerge during adolescence. Although parents play an important role in shaping adolescent mental health, the prospective association between parental cognitive biases and adolescents' mental health remains underexplored. This longitudinal study examined whether parental interpretation biases (IBs) were prospectively associated with changes in adolescents' anxiety and depressive symptoms, and whether adolescents' own IBs statistically mediated these associations. METHODS: A community sample of 88 adolescents (Mage = 12.85 years; 51% boys) and their parents (Mage = 45.66 years; 83% mothers) living in Canada completed a computer-based Scrambled Sentences Task (SST) to assess interpretation biases. Both parents and adolescents self-reported anxiety and depressive symptoms at baseline, and adolescents provided follow-up data 1 year later. RESULTS: Path analysis indicated that more negative parental IBs were significantly associated with increases in adolescents' anxiety and depressive symptoms over 1 year, even after controlling for parental internalizing symptoms. The magnitude of effects did not significantly differ between anxiety and depression, and a Bayesian informative hypothesis test provided evidence that the effects were comparable. Unexpectedly, the analyses did not support adolescents' IBs as a statistical mediator of the association between parental IBs and adolescents' symptom changes. However, parental IBs remained significant predictors above and beyond adolescents' own IBs and parental internalizing symptoms. CONCLUSION: This work provides preliminary evidence for parental cognitive biases as a transdiagnostic predictor of adolescents' emotional outcomes, operating above and beyond the effects of parental symptomatology and adolescents' own IBs. As such, parental IBs may be a valuable target in interventions aimed at fostering healthier emotional development in adolescents.

titre: Integrated gut microbiome and fecal metabolome profiling identifies taurine-associated microbial dysbiosis across the Alzheimer's disease clinical spectrum
resume: BACKGROUND: Gut microbiome alterations have been associated with Alzheimer's disease (AD), but how microbial composition, fecal metabolites, and cognitive function relate across the cognitive impairment spectrum-from subjective cognitive decline (SCD) through mild cognitive impairment (MCI) to AD-remains unclear. We integrated microbiome and metabolome profiles across this clinical spectrum. METHODS: Fecal samples from 84 participants [10 healthy controls (HC), 22 SCD, 23 MCI, 29 AD] underwent 16S rRNA V3-V4 sequencing and untargeted LC-MS metabolomics. Profiles were integrated via Procrustes analysis, sparse canonical correlation, MIMOSA2 community-metabolism modeling, and mediation analysis. Differential abundance was assessed by Kruskal-Wallis, ANCOM-BC2, and LinDA. RESULTS: Microbial composition differed across groups (ANOSIM R = 0.111, p = 0.001; Adonis R 2 = 0.070, p = 0.002). Cross-method validation confirmed 8 differentially abundant genera in AD vs. HC with 100% directional concordance between ANCOM-BC2 and LinDA, including depletion of butyrate-producing Lachnospiraceae (Blautia, Dorea, Fusicatenibacter) and enrichment of opportunistic pathobionts (Klebsiella, Escherichia-Shigella). Taurine showed the highest MIMOSA2 community-prediction R 2 (0.129; n = 62) and was positively associated with MMSE scores (r = 0.45, BH-FDR Q = 0.0005). A multi-omic random forest model (5 genera + 5 metabolites + age + sex) discriminated AD-clinical spectrum participants from HC with AUC = 0.86 (95% CI 0.82-0.90), although pairwise differences from the age + sex baseline (AUC = 0.75) did not reach statistical significance. Statistical mediation analysis was consistent with a Blautia → taurine → MMSE statistical mediation [ACME = 0.21, p = 0.008; 54% proportion mediated, bootstrap 95% CI (9%, 58%)]. CONCLUSION: Integrated multi-omic profiling reveals coordinated microbiome-metabolome dysregulation across the AD clinical spectrum, with taurine as a candidate microbial-metabolic node linking gut dysbiosis to cognitive performance. Microbial and metabolic alterations are detectable at the SCD stage, before objective cognitive impairment. These findings warrant validation in larger, age-matched cohorts and higher-resolution metagenomic studies.

titre: Beyond the lungs and heart: a possible association between digestive disease and exercise intolerance in 10 dogs
resume: INTRODUCTION: Exercise intolerance and panting are classically attributed to cardiac, respiratory, or other diseases. In some cases, the underlying etiology remains undetermined despite a comprehensive diagnostic workup. While fatigue is one of the most common symptoms in humans with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), chronic enteropathy is not currently recognized as a primary cause of exercise intolerance in dogs. METHODS: A retrospective review was conducted on the medical records of 10 dogs presenting with exercise intolerance lacking overt digestive or respiratory signs. All dogs underwent empirical gastrointestinal-directed medical and dietary therapies with subsequent owner-perceived clinical resolution. RESULTS: Ten dogs presenting with chronic exercise intolerance were evaluated. Six of these dogs also exhibited unexplained panting at rest (6/10). Subtle gastrointestinal signs and abdominal discomfort on palpation were present in four and five cases, respectively. Standard cardiopulmonary and metabolic investigations were largely unremarkable. Notably, half of the cohort (5/10) exhibited cobalamin insufficiency or deficiency. Dogs were managed with gastrointestinal-directed medical therapies (e.g., prokinetics, acid suppressants, tylosin) and/or dietary modifications (predominantly low-fat, single-protein (monoprotein), or hydrolyzed diets). Following these targeted interventions, all dogs achieved complete clinical resolution per owners within a median of 21 days. CONCLUSION: A gastrointestinal etiology may be considered in dogs presenting with unexplained exercise intolerance and excessive panting. Subtle physical exam findings, serum cobalamin and folate concentrations, and empirical dietary/medical trials can be used to support clinical suspicion. This case series suggests a potential canine equivalent of human IBD-related fatigue, highlighting the need for further research into the gut-brain axis, intestinal dysbiosis, and delayed gastric emptying in veterinary medicine.

titre: Mediterranean-ketogenic vs. medium-chain triglyceride supplemented Mediterranean diet: Effects on the gut-brain-immune axis in Parkinson's disease
resume: Ketogenic diets have been proposed as potential neuroprotective interventions for Parkinson's disease (PD), but concerns remain regarding their effects on the gut microbiome and gut-brain-immune axis. We conducted a randomized crossover trial comparing 8-week Mediterranean-ketogenic (MeDi-KD) versus medium-chain triglyceride-supplemented Mediterranean (MeDi-MCT) diets, separated by an 8-week washout (NCT05469997). Primary outcomes included changes in gut microbiome taxonomic and functional profiles, fecal short-chain fatty acid (SCFA) production, and biomarkers of intestinal permeability and inflammation. Neither intervention significantly altered microbiome diversity or functional gene abundance, established features of PD-associated dysbiosis, nor fecal or plasma biomarkers of intestinal permeability (zonulin) or inflammation (calprotectin). The MeDi-KD modestly reduced total fecal SCFAs, while both interventions increased the relative abundance of Roseburia hominis, and the MeDi-MCT was associated with decreases in plasma IL-1β and IL-8. No severe adverse events were reported, supporting further investigation of MeDi-KD strategies in larger, longer-duration PD trials.

titre: Targeted Colostrum Bioactive Proteins Improve Gastrointestinal Symptoms and Modulate the Gut Microbiome: A Randomised Double-Blind Placebo-Controlled Trial
resume: BACKGROUND: Gastrointestinal (GI) symptoms such as indigestion, bloating and reflux are common and can negatively affect quality of life. Bovine colostrum is a rich source of nutrients and other bioactive constituents that has been shown to be beneficial for gut health. METHODS: This 12-week, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, 3-arm study aimed to evaluate the effects of MaolactinGI™, a proprietary bovine colostrum supplement, on upper GI symptoms and gut microbiome composition in healthy adults aged 18 years and older experiencing moderate GI discomfort. Participants completed a 4-week run-in period followed by an 8-week intervention period. Outcomes measured included changes in upper GI symptoms via the Gastrointestinal Symptom Rating Scale (GSRS), Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease Questionnaire (GerdQ), Bloating Symptoms Visual Analogue Scale (BSVAS), Digestion-associated Quality of Life Questionnaire (DQLQ), Bristol Stool Chart, intestinal permeability, faecal calprotectin, serum inflammatory markers, gut microbiome analyses, blood safety markers and adverse events. RESULTS: Ninety eligible participants were allocated to either the high-dose (500 mg/day), low-dose (250 mg/day), or placebo groups, and data from 83 participants were analysed. The high-dose MaolactinGI™ group demonstrated statistically significant improvements in the total GSRS score and DQLQ score compared with placebo, suggesting a meaningful reduction in total symptom burden and improved quality of life. The improvements in GSRS were clinically meaningful in size, supporting the practical relevance of MaolactinGI™ for adults experiencing everyday upper GI discomfort. High-dose supplementation also preserved microbial richness relative to placebo (Chao1); exploratory within-group analyses further indicated enrichment of SCFA-associated commensal taxa. The intervention was well tolerated and demonstrated an acceptable safety profile. CONCLUSIONS: These findings support the potential of targeted colostrum-derived bioactive protein fractions as a novel nutritional strategy for supporting GI health and microbiome balance.

Préservation de la richesse microbienne intestinale (Chao1) et enrichissement de taxons producteurs d'AGCV.
Bonne tolérance et profil de sécurité acceptable de l'intervention.
fiche.conclusion: Les protéines bioactives de colostrum ciblées constituent une stratégie nutritionnelle prometteuse pour soutenir la santé digestive et l'équilibre du microbiote.

fiche.conclusion_simple: Le colostrum bovin réduit les symptômes digestifs hauts et module positivement le microbiote chez l'adulte.

titre: Construction and application of a transitional health management program for children with Hirschsprung disease undergoing colonic irrigation based on the intervention mapping framework
resume: OBJECTIVE: To develop an Intervention Mapping (IM) theory-based transitional health management program for children with Hirschsprung disease (HD) undergoing retrograde enema and evaluate its effectiveness. METHODS: Guided by IM theory, the intervention was developed through semi-structured interviews, literature review, expert consultation, and a pilot study. From April 2024 to June 2025, 94 children with HD and their primary caregivers were recruited from a tertiary pediatric hospital in Fujian Province and randomly assigned to an intervention group (n = 47) or control group (n = 47). The intervention group received multidisciplinary transitional health management based on IM theory, while the control group received routine care. Bowel preparation, enema-related complications, nutritional and growth outcomes, and caregivers' caregiving ability, anxiety, and depression were assessed. RESULTS: Eighty-three participants completed follow-up (intervention, n = 42; control, n = 41). Compared with the control group, the intervention group had better bowel preparation, lower incidences of enterocolitis and overall complications, and more favorable preoperative nutritional and growth outcomes. Caregivers in the intervention group showed significantly greater caregiving ability and greater improvements in anxiety and depression at 1 week and 1 month after discharge (all P 0.05). Repeated-measures analyses demonstrated significant group-by-time interactions for caregiving ability, anxiety, and depression (P < 0.05). CONCLUSION: The IM theory-based transitional health management program is feasible and effective in improving clinical and caregiver-related outcomes in children with HD receiving retrograde enema and their families.

titre: Feasibility and acceptability of a mindfulness-based vitality promotion program in a lifelong learning setting: a single-arm mixed-methods study
resume: BACKGROUND: As global aging accelerates, age-related psychophysiological conditions have emerged as major public health concerns. Promoting and sustaining vitality, an inherent human capacity, is essential for healthy aging and long-term well-being. The Mindfulness-based Vitality Promotion (MVP) program is a mindfulness-based behavioral intervention designed to enhance physical and psychological vitality and support sustainable well-being. This study evaluated the feasibility and acceptability of the MVP program and explored preliminary pre-post changes in health-related outcomes among community-dwelling individuals in a lifelong learning setting. METHODS: This study employed a single-arm mixed-methods design. A total of 35 participants were recruited for this study. The MVP program was delivered over 8 weeks, with each session lasting 90 min. Quantitative data were collected through self-report questionnaires, and qualitative data were obtained via semi-structured interviews. Feasibility and acceptability were assessed based on program retention, session attendance, and participant satisfaction. RESULTS: Quantitative analysis revealed significant pre-post increases in integrative vitality and well-being, along with significant reductions in depression, fatigue, and anxiety. No statistically significant changes were observed in pain, sleep disturbance, digestive symptoms, anger, or mindfulness. Of the 35 enrolled participants, 31 completed the program (88.6%), with a mean attendance of 6.37 of eight sessions. Among the 30 satisfaction survey respondents, 28 (93.3%) indicated willingness to participate again and 30 (100%) indicated willingness to recommend the program to others. The qualitative analysis identified four major themes: (i) diverse life challenges and self-care needs, (ii) learning through experience, connection, and application, (iii) regaining balance and agency in life, and (iv) sustaining practice requires continued support. CONCLUSION: Mixed-methods findings provide preliminary information regarding the feasibility and acceptability of the MVP program and indicate favorable pre-post changes in several self-reported health-related outcomes. The MVP program may represent a practical lifelong learning intervention with potential relevance for public health promotion. Further controlled studies are warranted to establish its efficacy. TRIAL REGISTRATION: The trial was first submitted to the Clinical Research Information Service, Republic of Korea (KCT0009961, https://cris.nih.go.kr/cris/search/detailSearch.do?seq=28524&search_page=L), on October 8, 2024, before participant enrollment began, and registration was finalized on November 28, 2024.

titre: Study on Gardeniae Fructus for treating depression with combination of network pharmacology, metabolomics and gut microbiota
resume: BACKGROUND: Depression is a prevalent and disabling mental disorder with limited therapeutic efficacy and delayed response to conventional antidepressants, highlighting the urgent need for safe and effective alternatives. Gardeniae Fructus (GF), a traditional Chinese medicine with documented neuroprotective properties, has shown rapid antidepressant-like effects, yet its mechanisms remain incompletely understood. METHODS: Depression-like behaviors were induced by reserpine in adult Sprague-Dawley rats. Thirty-five rats were randomly and evenly divided into five groups: control (CON), Model, low-dose GF (GFL, 1.2 g/kg·d), high-dose GF (GFH, 2.4 g/kg·d), and fluoxetine (FLU, 10 mg/kg·d). Depressive behaviors were assessed by sucrose preference test, forced swimming test, open field test, body temperature, and eyelid ptosis tests. Differential metabolites were identified through serum untargeted metabolomics, and metabolic pathways were analyzed using MetaboAnalyst. The anti-depression targets of GF were determined by network pharmacology. A network pharmacology-metabolomics network was constructed in Cytoscape, and interactions between key components and key targets were verified by molecular docking. Gut microbiota of rats in different groups was analyzed by 16S rDNA sequencing, and multi-omics integration analysis was performed. RESULTS: 11 active components of GF and 140 potential targets associated with depression were identified, with quercetin emerging as a key compound. Protein-protein interaction analysis highlighted AKT1, TNF, IL6, VEGFA, and TP53 as core targets. In reserpine-induced depressive rats, GF treatment significantly ameliorated depressive-like behaviors, involving shortened immobility time and enhanced sucrose preference, improved body temperature, and alleviated eyelid ptosis. 16S rRNA sequencing revealed that GF modulated gut microbiota composition, and altering functional pathways including thiamine, butanoate, and fatty acid metabolism. Untargeted metabolomics identified 28 differentially expressed metabolites between GF-treated and model groups, predominantly involving lipids and amino acids. Integrated network and metabolomic analyses pinpointed glycosphingolipid metabolism as a critical pathway, with PTEN as a key target and sphinganine and phytosphingosine as principal metabolites. Molecular docking confirmed stable binding between quercetin and PTEN (binding energy: -7.2 kcal/mol). Correlation analyses demonstrated that Bifidobacterium and Turicibacter exhibited pronounced associations with multiple metabolic alterations. CONCLUSION: This integrative approach reveals that GF alleviates depression through multi-target, multi-pathway mechanisms involving regulation of gut microbiota, modulation of glycosphingolipid metabolism, and targeting of PTEN, providing a comprehensive basis for its neuroprotective effects and offering novel insights into Traditional Chinese Medicine-based antidepressant strategies.

titre: Mind-body reprogramming therapy: development, theoretical foundation, and clinical application for Long COVID
resume: This paper presents the development and clinical rationale for Mind-Body Reprogramming Therapy (MBRT), a novel, theory-based intervention for patients with Long COVID experiencing persistent symptoms. Rooted in predictive processing, classical and operant conditioning, and Relational Frame Theory (RFT), MBRT targets maladaptive brain-based alarm responses believed to underlie symptoms such as fatigue, pain, and cognitive dysfunction. We argue that the chronicity of these alarms in patients reflects not only inferential biases and conditioned responses, but verbal relational networks that bind symptoms to identity, anticipated futures, and rule-governed avoidance, which become primary targets of treatment. The intervention combines personalized education, stress regulation techniques, and experiential learning delivered by an interdisciplinary team over a 7-10-day hybrid format. We describe the theoretical foundation of MBRT and outline its core components, including psychoeducation, values clarification, interoceptive exposure, and behavior change strategies. A detailed case study illustrates the therapeutic process and potential for recovery. We argue that persistent symptoms in Long COVID may reflect learned brain patterns rather than ongoing physical injury, and that targeted interdisciplinary interventions can help patients reverse these patterns. MBRT is currently under evaluation in a randomized controlled trial.

titre: Insula abnormalities in anxiety disorders: An ALE meta-analysis of cross-diagnostic convergence and subtype dissociation
resume: BACKGROUND: Insula abnormalities have been widely documented across anxiety disorders. However, the identification of convergent spatial patterns, effect direction gradients, and cross-subtype differences within the insula has proven challenging due to inconsistent findings across individual studies. METHODS: Whole-brain voxel-wise MRI studies reporting insula coordinates in anxiety disorders vs. healthy controls were collected from PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, PsycINFO, and Scopus. Activation likelihood estimation identified convergent insula abnormalities, separated increase and decrease foci, and compared panic disorder, generalized anxiety disorder, social anxiety disorder, and specific phobia. RESULTS: Forty-one experiments (1249 individuals) were included. Cross-diagnostic convergence was found in left anterior insula (MNI -36,14,-6; Z = 7.78) and right putamen/posterior insula (MNI 38,-16,12; Z = 5.09). A dorsal-ventral gradient (ventral decrease, dorsal increase) and an anterior-posterior gradient (anterior increase, posterior decrease) emerged. In exploratory subgroup analyses, PD and SAD predominantly involved left anterior insula. For GAD (k = 8, below threshold) and SP (k = 6, below threshold), preliminary findings suggested putamen-dominant pattern in GAD and segregated putamen/insula clusters in SP. These subtype-related patterns require replication. CONCLUSIONS: These findings are consistent with a preliminary insula-putamen axis model of anxiety disorders that may involve differential engagement of insula-based emotional-interoceptive and putamen-based sensorimotor circuits across subtypes, with the left anterior insula (MNI -36, 14, -6) emerging as the most robust cross-diagnostic locus identified empirically.

Gradients d'activation : ventral (baisse), dorsal (hausse), antérieur (hausse), postérieur (baisse)

titre: Breathing-evoked potentials in humans during wakefulness and sleep
resume: Breathing modulates cortical activities and cognitive functions, but the neurophysiological basis of the brain-breathing relationship is incompletely understood. We aimed to determine whether breathing at rest evokes scalp EEG-detectable potentials (as inspiratory occlusions do in the respiratory-related evoked potential model), whether these signatures persist during sleep and whether they are linked to sleep-organizing processes. We examined recordings from 729 participants in the Cleveland Family Study to identify cortical activity time-locked to inspiration during wakefulness and sleep, with a median of 7871 respiratory cycles analysed per participant. Breathing-related cortical responses were assessed in the time and frequency domains. Quiet breathing evoked a reproducible sequence of cortical potentials during wakefulness, including a pre-inspiratory component ∼300 ms before inspiration and several post-inspiratory peaks ≤3 s after. These responses persisted during non-rapid eye movement stages 2 and 3 (N2 and N3) and rapid eye movement (REM) sleep, in which they showed simplified morphology resembling K-complexes and co-occurred with increased spindle-range activity. The pattern was present irrespective of body mass index and was qualitatively unchanged in the 203 participants free of sleep-disordered breathing, arguing against obesity or sleep apnoea as its origin. Scalp EEG can detect breathing-evoked potentials during quiet breathing in awake humans. These potentials persist during sleep with a morphology that resembles cortical activities previously associated with sleep stabilization. Further studies are needed to determine the physiological and clinical significance of these observations in health and disease. KEY POINTS: Spontaneous breathing at rest evokes reproducible breathing-related cortical potentials detectable with scalp EEG. These potentials persist during sleep. They are associated with time-locked modulation of cortical oscillatory activity.

titre: Words under the skin: Physiological responses to interoceptive metaphors
resume: Embodied accounts of language propose that linguistic meaning is grounded in sensorimotor systems. While previous research has focused on the central nervous system, the involvement of the autonomic nervous system (ANS) in language comprehension remains underexplored. To fill this gap, we investigated whether processing interoceptive metaphors, namely figurative expressions referring to internal bodily sensations (e.g., 'I feel butterflies in my stomach'), modulates the ANS. Forty-five healthy participants read interoceptive metaphors and non-bodily-related literal sentences while cardiac, electrodermal, and respiratory signals were continuously recorded. We further distinguished between two types of interoceptive metaphors, depending on whether the interoceptive element served as the target (INT-target, e.g., 'I feel butterflies in my stomach') or source domain (INT-source, e.g., 'I thirst for success' to convey ambition) of the metaphor. Results revealed subtle but measurable effects: compared to non-bodily-related literal sentences, interoceptive metaphors were associated with higher heart rate variability and longer inspiratory duration. No significant differences emerged between INT-target and INT-source metaphors. These findings provide the first evidence that language grounded in internal bodily experience is associated with subtle differences in selected autonomic indices relative to non-bodily-related literal sentences.

titre: Alexithymia in Chronic Lumbar Radicular Pain: A Comparative Study of Failed Back Surgery Syndrome and Lumbar Disc Herniation
resume: BACKGROUND Failed back surgery syndrome (FBSS) involves persistent pain after surgery, with psychosocial factors contributing to symptom burden. Alexithymia is associated with chronic pain, but whether it is surgery-related or a broader feature of chronic lumbar radicular pain is unclear. We compared alexithymia between FBSS and non-surgical lumbar disc herniation (LDH). MATERIAL AND METHODS This cross-sectional study included 150 patients: FBSS after 1 surgery (n=64), FBSS after multiple surgeries (n=42), and magnetic resonance imaging-confirmed non-surgical LDH (n=44). Pain, disability, alexithymia, anxiety, and depression were assessed using the visual analog scale, Oswestry Disability Index, 20-item Toronto Alexithymia Scale, and Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale. The primary analysis compared combined FBSS (n=106) with LDH (n=44); secondary analyses examined surgery-related variables. Correlation analyses and exploratory logistic regression were performed. RESULTS Patients with FBSS had greater disability and more frequent neurological and functional impairments than patients with LDH. Alexithymia prevalence did not differ significantly between groups and was unrelated to number of surgeries, fixation material, or time since first operation. Alexithymia scores correlated with pain, disability, anxiety, depressive symptoms, and sociodemographic factors. In exploratory logistic regression, HADS total score was independently associated with definite alexithymia; however, this finding warrants caution because events were limited and no predictive or causal inference can be made. CONCLUSIONS Alexithymia showed no surgery-specific difference between FBSS and LDH and may represent a broader psychosocial correlate of chronic lumbar radicular pain. Psychosocial assessment should be considered in surgical and non-surgical populations, although outcome benefits require further study.
revue: Medical science monitor : international medical journal of experimental and clinical research

titre: A Telemedicine Strategy for Hypnosis in the Management of Chronic Neuropathic Pain: A Randomized Exploratory Study
resume: Hypnosis is recommended for the management of chronic neuropathic pain, but access to this intervention remains limited due to travel distances and difficulties. This single-center, prospective, randomized exploratory study evaluated the feasibility of a hypnosis program carried out partly via telemedicine, compared with a full face-to-face program. A total of 30 eligible patients were randomized into a group of 15 patients who received three of five sessions via telemedicine and a control group of 15 patients who received all sessions in person. Primary outcomes were feasibility of the telemedicine-based hypnosis, secondary outcomes included pain score, anxiety and depressive symptoms, frequency of self-hypnosis practice, and qualitative subjective experience. Most patients (80%) completed the telemedicine program, suggesting a good feasibility. Preliminary efficacy results indicated a mean reduction of pain intensity of 2.7 (±2.0) points in the telemedicine group compared with 2.2 (±1.8) in the control group with an average difference of 0.5, 95% CI [-1.1; 2.0]. Our exploratory study suggests that the telemedicine hypnosis program is feasible for managing neuropathic pain.
revue: The International journal of clinical and experimental hypnosis

titre: Feasibility, acceptability, and tolerability of operation calm: a mixed-methods evaluation with children, parents, and clinicians
resume: BACKGROUND: Anxiety related to medical and dental procedures is common in childhood. Brief, portable interventions that combine immersive virtual reality (VR), mindfulness, and nature exposure may help children practice self-regulation, but the feasibility, acceptability, and tolerability of Operation Calm require evaluation before clinical efficacy testing. METHODS: This protocol describes a community-based, single-arm, dynamic mixed-methods pre-post feasibility study. Approximately 50 children and adolescents aged 6-17 years, up to 50 parents or legal guardians, and 50 pediatric clinicians or supervised trainees will be recruited across Canada. Children will complete one approximately 10-minute self-guided Operation Calm session using a smartphone-compatible VR headset and one of five 360° nature scenes paired with standardized mindfulness narration. Parents and clinicians will review one scene in an approved web-based format. Primary domains are recruitment and procedural feasibility, acceptability, engagement, usability, appropriateness, perceived usefulness, implementation feasibility, and child tolerability. Children will complete the Children's Anxiety Meter-State and a current calmness rating immediately before and after VR, the Pediatric Simulator Sickness Questionnaire after VR, and a child evaluation. Parents and clinicians will complete group-specific evaluations with quantitative and open-ended items. RESULTS: Feasibility and evaluation outcomes will be summarized descriptively with transparent denominators and confidence intervals where informative. Exploratory paired pre-post changes in child anxiety and calmness will be analyzed using paired-samples t tests or Wilcoxon signed-rank tests, with effect sizes and confidence intervals. Open-ended responses will undergo qualitative content analysis, and quantitative and qualitative findings will be integrated using a convergent mixed-methods approach. Scene-level profiles will be descriptive rather than confirmatory. CONCLUSIONS: This early-stage study will determine whether Operation Calm can be delivered safely and consistently outside hospital care and identify refinements needed before a clinical feasibility study or randomized trial. Immediate pre-post changes will be interpreted as exploratory and will not establish efficacy. CLINICAL TRIAL REGISTRATION: https://clinicaltrials.gov, ClinicalTrials.gov NCT07694934.

titre: Effects of acceptance and commitment therapy on psychological and health-related outcomes in stroke patients: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
resume: BACKGROUND: Stroke is a leading cause of disability worldwide and is frequently accompanied by psychological and functional impairments. Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT), a third-wave behavioral intervention focusing on psychological flexibility, has been increasingly applied in stroke rehabilitation. Although previous reviews have suggested beneficial effects of ACT in stroke patients, whether these benefits persist in the short term after the intervention ends, and the certainty of the evidence, remain unclear. METHODS: A systematic review and meta-analysis was conducted according to PRISMA guidelines and registered in PROSPERO (CRD420261325108). Randomized controlled trials evaluating ACT in stroke patients were included. Pooled effects were calculated using random-effects models, with separate analyses for post-intervention and follow-up outcomes. Sources of heterogeneity were explored using subgroup analyses and meta-regression. Risk of bias was assessed using the Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 tool, and certainty of evidence was evaluated using the GRADE framework. RESULTS: Twenty-two RCTs involving 1,975 participants were included. ACT may be associated with reductions in depressive symptoms (post-intervention: SMD = -1.32, 95% CI: -1.80 to -0.84; follow-up: SMD = -0.76, 95% CI: -1.07 to -0.45) and anxiety symptoms (post-intervention: SMD = -1.36, 95% CI: -1.90 to -0.82; follow-up: SMD = -0.51, 95% CI: -1.42 to 0.40, not significant); depressive symptoms remained statistically significant at follow-up. Heterogeneity was considerable for both outcomes at post-intervention (I2 = 93.68% for depression and 93.60% for anxiety), so the pooled estimates represent average effects across studies. ACT may also be associated with improvements in psychological flexibility, quality of life, and sleep quality; however, these outcomes were based on a limited number of studies and showed considerable heterogeneity (I2 = 74.68 to 92.26%), so they should be interpreted cautiously. However, no statistically significant effects were observed for activities of daily living, neurological function, or hope. ACT did not appear to increase dropout rates in the available studies (K = 16; RR = 0.99, 95% CI: 0.58-1.69). Meta-regression analyses indicated that intervention duration may not be a significant moderator of treatment effects. The certainty of evidence ranged from very low to moderate, mainly due to risk of bias and inconsistency. CONCLUSION: Acceptance and Commitment Therapy may be a useful adjunctive intervention for improving psychological outcomes in people with stroke. However, evidence for functional recovery remains insufficient. Future high-quality RCTs with standardized protocols, larger samples, and longer follow-up are needed to confirm the long-term effectiveness of ACT. SYSTEMATIC REVIEW REGISTRATION: https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/, identifer CRD420261325108.

titre: The treatment efficacy of mindfulness-based cognitive therapy combined with medication on obsessive-compulsive disorder: evidence from effective connectivity of the triple network
resume: OBJECTIVES: To evaluate the clinical efficacy of mindfulness-based cognitive therapy (MBCT) plus SSRIs on obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), and explore its underlying neural mechanisms. METHODS: A non-randomized controlled trial enrolled 53 OCD patients (medication group, n = 30; MBCT+medication group, n = 23) and 23 healthy controls (HCs). Patients received a 10-week intervention, with clinical assessments conducted at baseline, week 4 and 10, and fMRI acquired at baseline and week 10. Repeated-measures ANOVA, Granger causality analysis, elastic-net logistic regression and bayesian ridge regression were used for clinical efficacy, effective connectivity (EC), diagnostic classification and treatment-response prediction. RESULTS: The MBCT+medication group showed greater improvements in obsessive-compulsive symptoms, depression, mindfulness and quality of life than the medication group (P < 0.050), but not in anxiety (P = 0.082). At baseline, OCD showed abnormal EC within and between the frontoparietal (FPN) and salience networks (SN) versus HCs (P < 0.050). Post-intervention, the MBCT+medication group showed increased inhibitory EC within the SN (P = 0.040) and excitatory EC from the SN to the FPN (P = 0.021). Aberrant EC achieved moderate diagnostic performance (accuracy = 0.726, specificity = 0.740, sensitivity = 0.711), whereas treatment response was not predicted (cross-validated R2 = -0.100). CONCLUSION: MBCT combined with medication significantly improved clinical efficacy in OCD, accompanied by altered EC within the SN and from the SN to the FPN as concurrent neurobiological changes.

titre: Bouldering-Psychotherapy for treating depression in adolescents (BooSt): study protocol for a randomized controlled trial
resume: BACKGROUND: Currently, there are hardly any validated group therapy programs for depressed adolescents in Germany. A recent meta-analysis confirmed a moderate antidepressant effect of exercise in adolescents with depressive symptoms. In addition, four recent systematic reviews reported positive effects of exercise interventions on psychological well-being, mood, and quality of life in adolescents with depression or depressive symptoms. We developed a manualized behavioral-therapy-based group program involving Bouldering-Psychotherapy (BPT) for adolescents (BPT-J) based on the adult version of BPT, which has already demonstrated its efficacy. The aim of the study is to evaluate the efficacy of BPT-J. METHODS: The study is designed as a randomized, controlled, prospective, longitudinal, single-blind trial with two arms (BPT-J intervention group [IG], waitlist-control group [CG]). The primary aim is to investigate the efficacy of the BPT-J group therapy for adolescents for treating depressiveness. Eligible participants are adolescents with subclinical and clinical depressive symptoms between 13 and 18 years of age. The adolescents in the CG are offered participation in an identical intervention after t1. The 10-week intervention is accompanied by four data collection points for all participants: participants and their legal guardians fill out online questionnaires at the start of therapy (t0), immediately after IG therapy (t1), after CG therapy (t2), and 12 months after finalizing the intervention (follow-up, t3). In addition, structured video interviews are conducted at t0 and t1. DISCUSSION: BooSt trial addresses the limited availability of evidence-based group interventions for adolescents with depressive symptoms in routine care. If efficacy is confirmed, BPT-J may represent a scalable, manualized, and potentially well-accepted treatment approach that could complement existing psychotherapeutic services for adolescents. Given the increasing demand and limited access to psychotherapy, the intervention may contribute to improving accessibility of mental health care. The group-based format may additionally support cost-effective implementation, reduce waiting times, facilitate peer support, and help reduce stigmatization associated with mental health treatment. Findings from the BooSt trial may further inform dissemination and implementation strategies in child and adolescent mental health care. TRIAL REGISTRATION: ISRCTN, ISRCTN79659949, prospectively registered 19/02/2025, DOI: https://doi.org/10.1186/ISRCTN79659949 , URL: https://www.isrctn.com/ISRCTN79659949 .

titre: Time for psychiatry to seriously consider broad-spectrum micronutrients
resume: Broad-spectrum micronutrients (BSM) are shown to improve mental health in randomised controlled trials. Robust positive effects are reported for emotional regulation, irritability and aggression. The effect sizes are modest, but comparable to cognitive-behavioural therapy and antidepressants. It is time to consider BSM as an informed choice when treating psychological distress.

titre: Neuroscience-informed psychoeducation for stuttering and other speech disorders
resume: Speech and communication disorders have historically been framed as behavioral habits or peripheral motor problems, an interpretation that obscures their neurobiological complexity, contributes to stigma, and may discourage people from seeking treatment. This chapter applies the framework of Neuroscience-Informed Psychoeducation (NIPE) to speech disorders, focusing on developmental stuttering as the primary exemplar, childhood apraxia of speech as a second speech disorder, and Tourette syndrome with vocal tics as a neurodevelopmental condition with prominent vocal manifestations, while drawing on obsessive-compulsive disorder, attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, and autism spectrum disorder as mechanistically informative comparators. We integrate evidence suggesting that speech symptoms emerge from interactions among distributed cortico-basal ganglia-thalamo-cortical loops, cerebellar timing and prediction networks, auditory-motor integration pathways, executive and limbic systems, and, as a working hypothesis, glial mechanisms that may regulate circuit stability. Within this framework, symptom variability and heterogeneous treatment response are reframed as expected features of state-dependent neural systems rather than failures of effort, motivation, or character. We describe how NIPE can translate these mechanisms into accessible, non-reductionist explanations that complement speech therapy, pharmacotherapy, neuromodulation, and multidisciplinary care by aligning expectations, reducing stigma, and supporting engagement during the gradual process of neuroplastic change, which we frame as support for adaptation, participation, and self-efficacy rather than as normalization of brain circuitry. We also consider precision NIPE tailored to dominant mechanism profiles, the promise and ethical risks of digital delivery, and key limitations, including neurobiological oversimplification and limited direct trial evidence, that define priorities for establishing NIPE as a rigorously tested, person-centered component of care.

titre: [Roles of growth factor-mediated brain-gut axis crosstalk in neurorepair following ischemic stroke]
resume: In recent years, the brain-gut axis, a critical bidirectional signaling pathway between the central nervous system and the gut microbiota, has attracted increasing attention for its role in the pathological progression of ischemic stroke (IS). Cell growth factors, including brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF), nerve growth factor (NGF), insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1), and vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF), are not only classical neuroprotective molecules but may also act as key signaling mediators of brain-gut axis communication because of their multifaceted roles in intestinal barrier regulation, peripheral immune remodeling, and central-peripheral crosstalk. Gut microbiota metabolites, such as short-chain fatty acids, tryptophan metabolites, and bile acid derivatives, can regulate BDNF, NGF, IGF-1, and VEGF through the PI3K/Akt and MAPK/ERK pathways, thereby affecting synaptic plasticity, neuronal survival, angiogenesis, and neural repair. The downstream signals of these factors converge on shared core pathways, producing functional additivity and synergistic effects. Based on these mechanisms, intervention strategies such as probiotic supplementation (e.g., Bifidobacterium bifidum ), prebiotics or dietary fiber (e.g., inulin and arabinoxylan), natural product modulation (e.g., diosmetin, rhubarb extract, and cornuside), and fecal microbiota transplantation can reshape the gut microbiota, increase metabolites such as short-chain fatty acids, regulate tryptophan metabolism, and inhibit inflammatory pathways such as TLR4/NF-κB. These interventions indirectly upregulate endogenous growth factors, including BDNF, IGF-1, and FGF, and activate signaling pathways such as PI3K/Akt, MAPK/ERK, and BDNF/TrkB/CREB, thereby reducing cerebral infarct volume, improving neurological and cognitive function, alleviating post-stroke depression, and promoting hippocampal neurogenesis, thus demonstrating considerable neuroprotective potential. This review focuses on the interrelationships among cell growth factors, the brain-gut axis, and IS, explores how growth factors act as messengers of the brain-gut axis and play a bridging role in the pathological progression of IS, and discusses novel therapeutic strategies targeting this axis.
revue: Zhejiang da xue xue bao. Yi xue ban = Journal of Zhejiang University. Medical sciences

titre: Involvement of PGE<sub>2</sub> in intestinal immunity of heat-stressed broilers with a potential link to the brain-gut axis
resume: Heat stress severely impairs broiler intestinal health and production, and prostaglandin E2 (PGE 2 ) plays a crucial role in body thermoregulation. However, the regulatory mechanism linking PGE 2 to intestinal inflammation through the brain-gut axis has not been fully elucidated in broilers. Here, we integrated in vivo and in vitro experiments to explore how PGE 2 mediates heat stress-induced intestinal immune dysfunction in broilers. Heat stress increased brain and rectal temperatures while suppressing growth performance ( P < 0.05). It activated the transient receptor potential melastatin 2 (TRPM2) channel and elevated cyclooxygenase-2 (COX-2, PGE 2 synthase) content and PGE 2 concentration in the hypothalamus ( P < 0.05), and intracerebroventricular inhibition confirmed the role of TRPM2. Heat stress triggered intestinal barrier disruption, characterized by reduced tight junction protein expression ( P < 0.05), particularly in the jejunum; In vitro PGE 2 treatment of intestinal epithelial cells recapitulated this observation. Mechanistically, both in vivo heat stress and in vitro PGE 2 treatment upregulated intestinal EP 4 (PGE 2 receptor), inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate (IP 3 ), transient receptor potential vanilloid 4 (TRPV4), the nuclear factor-κB (NF-κB) signaling pathway, and pro-inflammatory cytokine production ( P < 0.05); In vitro blockade of E P 4 , IP 3 or TRPV4 attenuated PGE 2 -induced intestinal epithelial inflammation ( P < 0.05). We therefore infer that hypothalamic TRPM2, together with intestinal EP 4 , IP 3 and TRPV4, may contribute to PGE 2 -mediated intestinal inflammation under heat stress. Intestinal interleukin-6 (IL-6) was elevated under heat stress in vivo and in PGE 2 -treated intestinal epithelial cells; IL-6 stimulation of hypothalamic neurons enhanced PGE 2 synthesis ( P < 0.05), implying a potential intestine-to-hypothalamus feedback loop. Collectively, these findings indicate that PGE 2 participates in heat stress-triggered intestinal inflammation, potentially through the brain-gut axis. This study provides a novel immunological insight and theoretical basis for understanding heat stress-related intestinal disorders and optimizing broiler health management under high-temperature conditions.

titre: The Association Between Prenatal Anxiety and Depression and Autism Spectrum Disorder With Gastrointestinal Symptoms in Children: Case-Control Study
resume: Background: Studies have indicated that maternal anxiety and depression during pregnancy can contribute to neurodevelopmental disorders and gut flora dysbiosis in children. However, it is unclear whether these factors increase the risk of autism spectrum disorder (ASD) with gastrointestinal (GI) symptoms in children. Objective: This study aimed to analyze the relationship between maternal anxiety and depression during pregnancy and ASD with GI symptoms. Methods: A total of 470 children with ASD and 486 children with typical development were enrolled in the study. The caregivers of all enrolled children completed questionnaires, including information on maternal mental health and GI symptoms. Results: <.001). Children whose mothers experienced anxiety or depression during pregnancy had substantially higher risk of developing ASD than those whose mothers did not experience these conditions (unadjusted odds ratio [OR] 4.274, 95% CI 2.799-6.526; adjusted OR 3.897, 95% CI 2.481-6.119). For children with ASD, those whose mothers had prenatal anxiety or depression had a significantly higher risk of GI symptoms than those whose mothers did not have these conditions (unadjusted OR 1.883, 95% CI 1.209-2.934; adjusted OR 1.943, 95% CI 1.236-3.054). Conclusions: Mothers who experience anxiety or depression during pregnancy may have a higher likelihood of their children developing ASD with GI symptoms.

titre: Gastrointestinal medication use patterns and incident depressive symptoms among adults aged 50 years or older: a prospective multicohort study
resume: Background Depressive symptoms contribute substantially to disability and loss of independence in later life, and gastrointestinal illness frequently co-occurs with affective vulnerability. However, evidence linking gastrointestinal medication use to subsequent depressive symptoms remains largely confined to single countries and cross-sectional assessments. We investigated whether baseline gastrointestinal medication use and longitudinal two-wave medication-use patterns are associated with incident depressive symptoms across three prospective ageing cohorts. Methods We analysed community-dwelling adults aged 50 years or older from the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study (CHARLS), the US Health and Retirement Study (HRS), and the Survey of Health, Ageing and Retirement in Europe (SHARE) who scored below cohort-specific depressive-symptom thresholds at baseline, followed for a median of 8–11 years. Baseline medication use was compared with non-use; two-wave patterns comprised continued non-use (reference), initiation, discontinuation, and persistent use at both waves. Cohort-specific Cox proportional hazards models with cluster-robust standard errors adjusted for sociodemographic, behavioural, and chronic health covariates (multiple imputation for missing data); estimates were synthesised using random-effects meta-analysis. Negative- and positive-control medications and Fine–Gray competing-risk regression models evaluated specificity and survival bias. Results The baseline analysis included 50,467 participants (median age 59–65 years; 44.4%–56.8% female) with 16,896 incident depressive events; the two-wave analysis included 32,686 participants with 8,069 events. Pooled adjusted hazard ratios (HRs) were 1.31 (95% CI 1.21–1.41; I ² = 29%) for baseline use and 1.34 (95% CI 1.22–1.47; I ² = 0%) for persistent use; initiation (1.27, 1.13–1.43) and discontinuation (1.25, 1.11–1.40) showed consistent risk elevations across cohorts. Antihypertensive and lipid-lowering medications (negative controls) showed null associations with incident depression, whereas psychiatric medications (positive control) showed the expected strong relationship (pooled HR 1.99, 95% CI 1.79–2.22). The association remained robust after further adjusting for continuous baseline subthreshold depressive symptoms (pooled HR 1.21, 95% CI 1.14–1.27; I ² = 0%), and medicated digestive disease carried higher risk than untreated digestive disease (pooled HR 1.18, 95% CI 1.05–1.32; I ² = 0%). Accounting for competing mortality did not alter the estimates. Conclusions Baseline and persistent gastrointestinal medication use were consistently associated with increased risk of incident depressive symptoms across three cross-national ageing cohorts with negligible heterogeneity. These findings support integrating routine affective screening into medication reviews for older adults receiving gastrointestinal pharmacotherapy, while maintaining guideline-directed management of digestive conditions.

titre: Difficult-to-Catheterize Continent Channel Revision: Techniques and Outcomes in an Adult Cohort
resume: Introduction Continent catheterizable channels allow patients who cannot void volitionally to maintain quality of life. However, catheterizable channels are susceptible to various pathologies, which may necessitate revision. Outcomes after catheterizable channel revision in adults are poorly described and are the focus of this investigation. Methods We conducted a retrospective review of adult patients undergoing continent catheterizable channel revision at a single institution between 2011 and 2024. Indications for revision included stomal or channel stenosis, redundancy, false passage, and parastomal hernia resulting in difficulty catheterizing. Revisions performed solely for channel incontinence were excluded. Surgeries were categorized by repair type: (1) suprafascial, involving superficial revision with a local skin flap, (2) subfascial, requiring mobilization of the intraperitoneal channel, and (3) channel replacement with a new bowel segment. The primary outcome was freedom from reoperation for recurrent stenosis. Results We identified 45 patients who underwent 54 revisions. Common surgical indications were stomal stenosis (24/54, 44%) and channel stenosis (27/54, 50%). Over a median follow-up of 46 months, 41/54 (76%) revisions were successful: 13/19 (68%) for suprafascial revision, 18/20 (90%) for subfascial revision, and 10/15 (67%) for channel replacement (p = 0.178). Eight patients (15%) developed new channel incontinence after surgery; two (4%) developed a parastomal hernia. Study limitations include its retrospective design. Conclusions Adult continent catheterizable channel revision can be accomplished with satisfactory success rates. When abdominal entry is necessary for reconstruction, efforts should be made to preserve the existing channel. Patients should be counseled about the risks of de novo stress incontinence and parastomal hernia.

titre: The effects of zinc supplementation on olfactory disorders: a systematic review with meta-analysis
resume: Objectives This systematic review aimed to evaluate the efficacy of zinc supplementation for treating olfactory disorders, including quantitative and qualitative symptoms, in adults. Methods We conducted a comprehensive search of the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, Pubmed, Embase, and other relevant databases for Randomized Controlled Trials (RCTs) and observational studies evaluating zinc supplementation for olfactory dysfunction. Studies published up to April 2025 were included. Improvement in olfactory function was assessed with validated olfactory tests or subjective questionnaires. Qualitative symptoms (parosmia, phantosmia), adverse effects, patient-reported outcomes, and quality of life measured by questionnaires were evaluated. Results A total of 6 studies, including 3 RCTs and 3 observational studies, were included in the review. Sample sizes varied between 25 and 606 participants, with follow-up durations ranging from 1 to 15 months. The meta-analysis showed no significant difference in olfactory function improvement between the zinc-treated group and the control group (OR = 1.78; 95% CI 0.63-5.03; p = 0.28). In addition, the analysis of subjective perception of improvement, also did not demonstrate a statistically significant effect (OR = 0.69; 95% CI 0.25-1.93; p = 0.48). However, an individual study reported improvement in specific subgroups, such as those with posttraumatic anosmia. Adverse events were generally mild and primarily gastrointestinal. Conclusion Current evidence does not support a clear benefit of zinc supplementation for olfactory disorders. Further high-quality RCTs are necessary to determine its potential role, particularly in targeted subgroups. Level of evidence Level 2a.
